An explicit Euler primitive and Hensel radial normalization construct the entire tower. Its restricted p-adic limit is algebraic with radial field degree p^3+2p^2+p+1, while the original integer seed has characteristic-zero generic degree p^2. The normalized output coordinates cannot both be rational; this tower has unbounded polynomial degrees. Other lifting architectures and JC2 remain open.

results.scope: The Frobenius extension now proves all lower-one prime-power gaps at every terminal order: exact valuation v_pD_(n,p^s)(gamma)=(((p^s-1)/(p-1))-s)binom(n,2) for gamma inZp; rational positive p-integral shapes give squarefreeness and SFC. The prime-gap cyclic/Fitting argument proves all-terminal lower-one SFC for every prime gap and p-integral positive rational Gamma shape, and completes every ordinary binomial of degree at most four. Its terminal determinant is congruent(-1)^binom(n,2) modp as a polynomial in gamma. General lower exponents, remaining composite-gap lower-one cases, all positive real higher-gap shapes and unrestricted SFC remain open. For d=p^s, lower-one ordinary pairs are separated at N=m*p^r and m*p^r-1,1<=m<p,N>=2, retaining the no-carry and arbitrary-a prime-power criteria. For arbitrary gaps, a prime p>dN dividing some aN+j,1<=j<=d, exactly once gives irreducibility and the preceding pair; with a>=d,a>=2,N>=3 and prime aN+j, both adjoining pairs are separated. The resultant has exact degree dN(N-1) and positive stated leading coefficient. It does not refute coefficient positivity, the adjacent-gap proposal, or binomial SFC. For cubic factorial splitting at every nonnegative offset C=3q+c, an exact convergent 3-adic unit logarithm gives a diagonal Euler-operator deformation from the gap-one base at every precision3^K with explicit finite truncation. Its modulo81 profile and second-unit offset isometry are exact. The operator does not yet provide squarefreeness preservation in local weighted coordinates. nodes.title: Bounded full lift of a noninvertible rank-two frame
nodes.scope: Construct a full Weyl lift of a noninvertible polynomial symplectic map of affine four-space with one common finite ordinary spatial-degree bound. Canonical Long graded scalar lifts require degree at least 27 with arbitrary parity, or at least 28 for even Moyal symbols. Degree 27 is the sharp scalar minimum through h5 only. Matrix lifts with the prescribed Airy first coefficient require degree at least 27; the displayed scaled lower-family theorem remains at degree 25. Other matrix first data remain open. Finite positive jets and one-order covariant solvers do not establish bounded realization. As in QFL2, the admissible parameter may be ramified, h=t^e*u(t) with u(0)!=0. For this existential formulation one may pass to an algebraic closure of the coefficient field. The corresponding geometric condition is horizontal membership at some finite degree D.

For B=c(Z)W+u(Z), g=Wh(Z)+k(Z), all pure members are safe if deg c<=8, with unrestricted h,u,k. More generally, for nonconstant c whose root multiplicities are at most two, purity is equivalent to a=0, h,c divisible by Z^2, u,k divisible by Z. Thus nonconstant squarefree c of arbitrary degree has no pure members. For arbitrary multiplicities nonconstant c excludes purity when a!=0; unshared roots of c,h also have no multiplicity restriction. The same positive-weight classification holds if ord h>=ord c at every common root, including the entire c|h subfamily, without multiplicity bounds. The sharp four-level argument classifies the mixed family whenever every nonzero common root avoids ceil(2m/3)<=ord h<=m-3, m=ord c>=9. Polynomial cubic barriers realize nonpositive volume order at every pair in that strip but are not pure. For a nonzero constant lambda, every pure phase lambda W^2+Wh(Z)+c(Z)WY+aY^2+u(Z)Y+k(Z) is quadratic; nonconstant c(Z) admits no pure member, by a connected double-cover period argument retaining positive-genus cycles. For polynomial ell(Z) of degree at least two in place of lambda, no pure member exists when gcd(ell,c^2) has only simple/double roots and the explicit fixed and moving determinant sources are clean. Moving cleanliness is automatic unless ell/gcd(ell,c^2) is constant or proportional to Z. In particular gcd(ell,c)=1 admits no pure member, without multiplicity bounds. When c=0, no pure member exists if ell has only simple/double roots and ell(0)!=0 or h(0)!=0. Acyclicity on the determinant or reduced-root divisor proves that localization preserves the original seed. If the sole unclean fixed source is a simple origin under the stated volume hypotheses, a rank-one actual Gysin-kernel argument forces a=u(0)=k(0)=0 for purity. For every integer nu>=1 and every complex polynomial k, Z^(2nu+1)W^2+Z^nu WY-W/2+k(Z) is not pure: an exact all-order marked kernel and uniform factorial coefficient bound treat this moving-nullsource-zero branch directly. Analytic amplitudes extend it to all constant a and u divisible by Z^nu. More generally the entire R=0 branch e=ell/gcd(ell,c^2)=kappa Z with c(0)=0 admits no pure member, for arbitrary u,k and root multiplicities. An exact actual Wick-residue/Lagrange kernel, selected-sheet continuation and uniform contour coefficient bound prove this without localization at the degenerate moving source. nodes.title: An explicit right inverse for every fiber defect
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL1, the named sub-result states:

Let B be a commutative Q-algebra with derivation delta, put A=B[Z], and
extend delta by delta(Z)=0. Define
\[
 \{f,g\}=f_Z\delta g-(\delta f)g_Z,\qquad
 f\star g=m\exp\!\left({\hbar\over2}
   (\partial_Z\otimes\delta-\delta\otimes\partial_Z)\right)(f\otimes g).
 \tag{1}
\]
The two derivations commute, so the product is associative. It is a
well-defined product on A[[hbar]]. In fact, on two individual polynomials
the bidifferential sum is finite because each term differentiates their
combined Z degree.

Fix any S,T in A with {S,T}=1. Write
\[
 d_1(u,v)=\{u,T\}+\{S,v\},\qquad
 I_Z\!\left(\sum_{k\ge0}F_kZ^k\right)
       =\sum_{k\ge0}{F_kZ^{k+1}\over k+1}.
\]
Then
\[
 {\cal H}(F)=\bigl(S_Z I_ZF,\ T_Z I_ZF\bigr),\qquad
                 d_1{\cal H}(F)=F
 \quad\hbox{for every }F\in A.                       \tag{2}
\]

nodes.title: Every compatible finite jet extends formally
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose a finite pair S_h,T_h reduces to S,T and satisfies
\[
 {[S_h,T_h]_\star\over\hbar}
       =1+\hbar^mF_m+O(\hbar^{m+1}).
\]
Replace it by
\[
 (S_h,T_h)-\hbar^m{\cal H}(F_m).                     \tag{3}
\]
The coefficient at order m changes by -d_1 H(F_m)=-F_m; lower orders
are unchanged. Iterate. At every step the new coefficients belong to B[Z].
Completeness in hbar gives
\[
 S_h=S+\sum_{m\ge1}\hbar^m s_m,\quad
 T_h=T+\sum_{m\ge1}\hbar^m t_m,\qquad
 [S_h,T_h]_\star=\hbar.                              \tag{4}
\]
This extends any already compatible finite jet, including odd branches.

If the prescribed jet is even in hbar, the normalized Moyal commutator is
even. Equation (3) can then be applied only at orders 2,4,6,..., giving an
even lift. Odd corrections are therefore unnecessary for unrestricted
formal existence in this fiber problem.

Each coefficient is polynomial. No common bound on their Z orders, total
degrees or denominators is asserted. The result concerns the S,T relation.
If R is central in (1), its commutators with these lifts stay zero; the
connection equations involving a fourth image are separate.

nodes.title: Explicit escape from the QRT3 category
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL1, the named sub-result states:

Use the retained polynomial lower lift s,t from
[the frozen inputs](../dixmier-residue-transport/inputs.json). Its order-five
defect is
\[
 O_5=\{s,t\}+\Pi^3(s,T)/24+\Pi^3(S,t)/24+
                        \Pi^5(S,T)/1920.
\]
QRT3 gives Lambda_plus(O_5)=1 and annihilates its allowed current
corrections. Equation (2) instead gives the unrestricted corrections
\[
 u=-S_ZI_ZO_5,\qquad v=-T_ZI_ZO_5,\qquad
                  d_1(u,v)=-O_5.                   \tag{5}
\]
In particular Lambda_plus(d_1(u,v))=-1. The same formula works above
every compatible polynomial or finite-X-Laurent lower lift; it does not
depend on a selected point of that lower-lift space.

For the frozen lower lift the exact sizes are:

| Polynomial | Nonzero terms | Z order |
|---|---:|---:|
| O_5 | 55 | 4 |
| u | 162 | 9 |
| v | 135 | 8 |

Both corrections are polynomial in X,Q,Z, with minimum X exponents 12 and
14. QRT3 requires current Z orders at most 1 and 0. Thus (5) leaves that
category explicitly. It does not contradict QRT3.

More generally, for this seed deg_Z(S)=5 and deg_Z(T)=4. If
deg_Z(s)<=3 and deg_Z(t)<=2, then deg_Z(O_5)<=4, and (5) has Z orders
at most 9 and 8. This is an all-lower-lift bound, not a finite scan.

Starting at the classical seed, the same homotopy gives a fresh
third-order correction with Z orders 11 and 10. It leaves the restricted
lower-lift category but starts an all-orders even formal solution.

nodes.title: Full polynomial symplectic frames are formally unobstructed
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL1, the named sub-result states:

Let A=K[x_1,...,x_{2n}] in characteristic zero with a constant nondegenerate
Poisson matrix J and the corresponding Moyal product. Suppose
f=(f_1,...,f_{2n}) is polynomial and
\[
                       \{f_i,f_j\}=J_{ij}.          \tag{6}
\]
Then there are polynomials f_{i,2r} such that
\[
 F_i=f_i+\sum_{r\ge1}\hbar^{2r}f_{i,2r},\qquad
                         [F_i,F_j]_\star=\hbar J_{ij}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently f lifts to a continuous endomorphism of the hbar-adically
completed Weyl algebra. Any compatible finite jet extends; an even jet
admits an even extension.

Here is an elementary proof, requiring no assumption that f is invertible.

Put D_i={f_i,-}. The D_i commute by (6). Moreover the identity
Df J (Df)^t=J makes Df an invertible matrix over A. The D_i therefore
form an A-basis of Der_K(A). Their dual one-forms theta^i are constant
linear combinations of df_j, so they are polynomial and closed.
The cochain complex of this commuting frame is exactly the polynomial
de Rham complex, expressed in the theta basis:
\[
 (dc)_{ij}=D_i c_j-D_j c_i,\qquad
 (dE)_{ijk}=D_iE_{jk}+D_jE_{ki}+D_kE_{ij}.          \tag{8}
\]
In particular H^1=H^2=0. Explicitly, a closed polynomial p-form whose
coefficients are homogeneous of ordinary degree q has primitive
i_Euler(alpha)/(q+p), for p>0. Summing its homogeneous pieces gives a
polynomial primitive. This uses the original source coordinates and the
inverse Jacobian matrix, never an inverse polynomial map f^{-1}.

Suppose the normalized commutators of a compatible jet are
J_ij+hbar^m E_ij+O(hbar^{m+1}). Their Jacobi identity at the first
remaining order gives dE=0 in (8). Vanishing of H^2 supplies polynomial
c_i with dc=-E. Adding hbar^m c_i to every image removes that defect.
Induction proves (7); parity follows from the Moyal commutator as before.

nodes.title: Comparison with graph quantization
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL1, the named sub-result states:

[Baranovsky, Ginzburg, Kaledin and Pecharich, Theorem 1.1.4](https://arxiv.org/html/1403.3493v2)
give existence criteria for a line bundle on a smooth closed Lagrangian
subvariety to quantize as a complete flat module over a fixed formal
quantization. For the graph of (6) in the product with opposite symplectic
form, the graph is affine space. Its canonical bundle is trivial, and
both degree-two cohomology groups in their criterion vanish by the
polynomial Poincare lemma. Their criterion therefore permits the trivial
graph line bundle to quantize. This is consistent with (7), whose regular
left module and right action through F give a formal graph bimodule.

This comparison concerns formal deformation quantization. It is not a
theorem about a characteristic-zero D-module with a prescribed family of
positive-characteristic arithmetic supports.

nodes.title: The algebra that bounded degree supplies
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL2, the named sub-result states:

For a characteristic-zero field K, put R=K[[t]], L=K((t)), and let
a(t) be a nonzero element of tR. Consider the finite PBW algebra
\[
 {\cal W}_R(a)=R\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n\rangle/
 ([p_i,x_j]-a(t)\delta_{ij},[x_i,x_j],[p_i,p_j]).
 \tag{1}
\]
An element has finitely many spatial PBW monomials; their scalar
coefficients may be arbitrary power series in t. Its t-adic completion
is larger: spatial degrees may grow with t order.

Suppose the images F_i of a formal lift satisfy
\[
                \deg_{\rm spatial}F_i\le D
 \quad\hbox{for every image and every t coefficient}.       \tag{2}
\]
There are finitely many spatial monomials of degree <=D, so all F_i
belong to the uncompleted algebra (1). They therefore define an
endomorphism phi_R of (1). After inverting t, rescaling each p_i by
a(t)^{-1} identifies W_L(a) with A_n(L). This rescaling preserves spatial
degree.

No convergence or algebraicity of the scalar coefficient series is
required. This is the first useful improvement over demanding termination
of the formal series.

nodes.title: A valuation lemma makes nonsurjectivity automatic
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL2, the named sub-result states:

Assume the commutative reduction
\[
        f^*:K[x_1,\ldots,p_n]\longrightarrow K[x_1,\ldots,p_n]
\]
of phi_R is injective. For any nonzero g in W_L(a), define v(g) as the
minimum t valuation among its finitely many PBW coefficients. Then
\[
                         v(\phi_L(g))=v(g).         \tag{3}
\]

To prove this, write g=t^m g_0 with g_0 in W_R(a) and nonzero reduction
bar(g_0). Reducing phi_R(g_0) gives f^*(bar(g_0)), which is nonzero by
injectivity. Thus phi_R(g_0) has valuation zero, proving (3).

If phi_L were surjective, take a finite PBW preimage g_i of each standard
generator. Equation (3) gives v(g_i)=0, so every g_i already belongs to
W_R(a). Reduction supplies a polynomial preimage of every generator
under f^*. Hence f^* is surjective. We have proved
\[
 \boxed{\quad f^*\text{ injective and not surjective}
             \ \Longrightarrow\ \phi_L\text{ not surjective}.\quad} \tag{4}
\]

A polynomial symplectic map has invertible Jacobian, hence is dominant
and induces an injective polynomial-ring map in characteristic zero.
Thus (4) applies to every noninvertible f in the opening statement.
The argument also permits ramification a(t)=t^e u(t), u(0) nonzero.

The injectivity hypothesis matters. In the commutative example x -> t*x,
the generic inverse x/t has a pole and the special reduction is zero.
There is no such pole cancellation when f^* is injective.

For completeness, the counterexample over L yields one over C. The
finitely many PBW coefficients of its generator images generate a
finitely generated characteristic-zero field K_0 over Q. The restricted
A_n(K_0) endomorphism is not surjective, since surjectivity would persist
over L. Nonsurjectivity also persists under any field extension: the
nonzero vector-space cokernel tensors faithfully. Embed K_0 into C.
This proves the opening criterion.

nodes.title: Finite type geometry of the same condition
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL2, the named sub-result states:

Fix n and D. Let M_(n,D) be the affine finite type scheme over K[h]
whose coordinates are the coefficients of 2n spatial polynomials of
degree <=D and whose equations are
\[
 { [F_i,F_j]_{\star_h}\over h}=J_{ij}.                \tag{5}
\]
These are polynomial equations in h and the finitely many coefficients.
The numerator is universally divisible by h. At h=0, equation (5)
is the full set of classical Poisson relations. At h nonzero it is
the full set of Weyl relations.

Write V_e for the spatial polynomials of degree <=e, and put
\[
                         E=D^{2n-1}.
\]
For each point m of M_(n,D), substitution through its assignment gives
\[
       T_m:V_E\longrightarrow V_{DE},\qquad g\mapsto\phi_m(g).
 \tag{6}
\]
Its matrix entries are polynomial in the parameters. At every geometric
point in characteristic zero, T_m is injective: at h=0 this follows
from the symplectic Jacobian, and at h nonzero from simplicity of the
Weyl algebra. Its rank is therefore the constant dim(V_E).

The inverse-degree theorem for polynomial automorphisms and its Weyl
analogue give degree(phi_m^{-1})<=E whenever phi_m is an automorphism.
For the Weyl statement see
[Lauritzen--Thomsen, Theorem 2.5](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.09384v2);
their Theorem 4.3 states the polynomial bound, and they reference
[Bavula's extension](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0512215).

Consequently phi_m is an automorphism exactly when every standard
generator belongs to im(T_m). With the rank already constant, these
are closed determinantal conditions on [T_m | x_i] and [T_m | p_i].
The inverse-degree bounds are used only on field-valued geometric points.
They are not being asserted over truncated h rings with nilpotents; the
reduced-ring hypothesis in Lauritzen--Thomsen's Theorem 2.5 matters.
Thus:

> Within M_(n,D), the locus of automorphisms is Zariski closed.
> Its complement is a Zariski open locus of non-surjective assignments,
> including the classical noninvertible points at h=0.

nodes.title: What Artin approximation does and does not provide
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL2, the named sub-result states:

Suppose a degree-D formal lift exists. Its finitely many scalar
coefficient series solve the finite polynomial system (5).
[Artin approximation, Stacks Theorem 16.13.2](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07QX)
gives a solution over an etale neighborhood of the local ring K[h]_(h)
with the same prescribed finite jet. Taking the approximation order
one preserves f. After shrinking and taking the component through that
point, this is an algebraic curve family with h nonconstant.

For algebraically closed K, the curve meets U and h nonzero, giving
actual non-surjective Weyl endomorphisms over K. Over general K the
coefficient-field argument above already gives a counterexample over C.

Approximation replaces the original scalar series by algebraic ones
with the same selected jet. It does not assert that the original series
is algebraic or has a value at h=1.

Without (2), QFL1 has infinitely many potentially nonzero spatial
coefficients. There is no single finite system (5) to which this
application of Artin approximation applies. Applying approximation
separately at each growing degree does not supply a common bound.

Equivalently, one may seek a finite-dimensional spatial carrier for
one full formal lift, rather than a terminating h expansion.

nodes.title: Horizontal components and the all-degree question
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL2, the named sub-result states:

At a fixed D, let H_D be the scheme-theoretic closure in M_(n,D) of
the open set h nonzero. In coordinate-ring terms its ideal is the
saturation I_D:h^infinity of the equations (5).

Any degree-D formal lift puts f in H_D. Conversely, over an algebraically
closed characteristic-zero field, a point of H_D can be reached by an
algebraic curve through f with h not identically zero. Normalize the
curve at a point above f and complete: h=t^e u(t) with u(0) nonzero.
This gives a bounded-degree ramified formal lift of f of the kind
allowed in (1). This is the usual curve-selection argument for the
closure of a dense open in an affine finite type scheme. More generally,
[Stacks Lemma 32.15.1](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0CM2) supplies
a discrete valuation ring reaching a point in the closure of a finite
type image; the valuation proof above works directly over such a ring.

Thus the decisive construction question is
\[
 \boxed{\quad
  \text{Does a known noninvertible polynomial symplectic map belong to }
               H_D\text{ for some finite }D?
       \quad}                                      \tag{7}
\]
A positive answer already gives a Weyl counterexample by (4).
It does not need the stronger condition of a lift with integral h
powers or a terminating h series.

If DC_n is true, every noninvertible classical symplectic point is
vertical in every finite M_(n,D). QFL1 is compatible with this: its
formal solution may use increasing spatial degrees and never factor
through a single finite M_(n,D).

This is a structural reformulation, not a proposal to compute the
saturations for increasing D. The remaining unproved condition concerns
horizontal membership or its failure for all D simultaneously.

The property "some bounded-degree formal lift exists" is preserved by
source and target changes admitting exact quantum automorphisms with
bounded spatial degree, and with inverses having the same property.
Composition multiplies finite degree bounds. Positional polynomial
Weyl shears are included. An arbitrary formal gauge need not preserve
boundedness of a chosen representative.

nodes.title: Classical reduction does not prescribe arithmetic support
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFL2, the named sub-result states:

The bounded polynomial quantum shear
\[
                     x\mapsto x,\qquad p\mapsto p+h^2x^2       \tag{10}
\]
also reduces to the identity at h=0. At h=1 it is a nontrivial Weyl
automorphism. In every prime characteristic ell>3,
\[
                  (p+h^2x^2)^\ell=p^\ell+h^{2\ell}x^{2\ell}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Thus its specialized Frobenius center map is a nontrivial shear, while
the identity lift of the same classical map has identity center action.

Here is an elementary all-prime proof of (11). Let A=p+h^2x^2.
The constant commutator [A,x]=h shows A^ell commutes with x.
It also commutes with A, hence with p=A-h^2x^2. Therefore A^ell is
central. The difference A^ell-p^ell has p order <ell, and commutation
with x forces it to belong to K[h,x]. A word containing j copies of
h^2x^2 contributes to its p-order-zero part only with exponents
h^(ell+j) x^(3j-ell). Centrality forces 3j-ell divisible by ell.
Since ell>3 and 0<=j<=ell, the only nonnegative surviving case is
j=ell. Its coefficient is one, proving (11). Finite PBW checks at
ell=5,7,11 are implementation controls, not the all-prime proof.

Accordingly, the
[Kanel-Belov--Fedorov preprint's arithmetic nonlifting theorem](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.33919v1)
for Long's prescribed Frobenius center map does not by itself decide
(7) for Long's classical map. A new comparison would be required.
Bounded spatial degree implies a genuine Weyl assignment, but its
arithmetic center map need not equal the classical h=0 map.

nodes.title: A centralizer theorem for every full polynomial symplectic frame
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QCR1, the named sub-result states:

Let A=K[z_1,...,z_(2n)] in characteristic zero, and suppose
\[
 \{d,r\}=1,\qquad
 (r,d,s_1,t_1,\ldots,s_{n-1},t_{n-1})
\]
is a full polynomial symplectic frame. Define
\[
 C=\{g\in A:\{g,r\}=\{g,s_i\}=\{g,t_i\}=0
                                    \text{ for all }i\}.
\]
Then
\[
                                  C=K[r].              \tag{1}
\]

Indeed the symplectic Jacobian identity makes the differentials
of the full frame a polynomial basis of Omega_A^1. Expanding dg
in this basis, the bracket constraints force
\[
                                   dg=b\,dr
\]
for some b in A. In characteristic zero, dg wedge dr=0 implies
that g and r are algebraically dependent.

We use the classical polynomial dependence theorem:
algebraically dependent nonconstant polynomials lie in one
polynomial algebra K[u]. This is
[Arzhantsev--Petravchuk, Lemma 2](https://publications.hse.ru/pubs/share/direct/219130966.pdf),
following their generative-polynomial lemma. Write r=P(u), g=Q(u).
The polynomial Hamiltonian mate d gives
\[
                       1=\{d,r\}=P'(u)\{d,u\}.
\]
Units of A are scalars, so P'(u) is a nonzero scalar. Since u is
nonconstant and the characteristic is zero, P has degree one.
Thus g belongs to K[r]. Constants cause no exception.

Consequently all polynomial choices d' completing the same
remaining 2n-1 images are exactly
\[
                                  d'=d+P(r),\qquad P\in K[u].
 \tag{2}
\]
No inverse polynomial map is assumed. The theorem applies to
noninvertible symplectic endomorphisms just as to automorphisms.
It assumes an admitted classical frame; it does not establish
admission from an arbitrary partial tuple.

nodes.title: Formal quantum centralizers have exactly the completed ambiguity
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QCR1, the named sub-result states:

Let the fixed formal images
\[
                  \mathsf R,\mathsf S_i,\mathsf T_i\in A[[h]]
\]
have the above classical reductions and satisfy their exact mutual
Weyl relations. In particular \(\mathsf R\) commutes with every
\(\mathsf S_i\) and \(\mathsf T_i\). Its formal joint centralizer is
\[
 \left\{\sum_{\nu\ge0}h^\nu P_\nu^\star(\mathsf R):
                                      P_\nu\in K[u]\right\}.     \tag{3}
\]
The notation means star-polynomial evaluation. There is no common
bound on the degrees of the P_nu in (3).

To prove this, let C commute with all the fixed images. The
coefficient of h in each commutator shows that its reduction C_0
lies in the classical centralizer (1), so C_0=P_0(r). Subtract
\(P_0^\star(\mathsf R)\), which commutes with all the fixed images, and
divide the remaining series by h. Repeat. The resulting sum
converges h-adically, and subtraction is unique: at the first
differing order, a nonzero polynomial in the nonconstant r cannot
vanish. Conversely every series in (3) commutes with the tuple.

If two formal conjugate images \(\mathsf D\) and \(\mathsf D'\) exist for
this fixed partial tuple, their difference is exactly an element
of (3). For a prescribed common classical image, its h^0 term
must vanish. This classifies the ambiguity, not existence of a
conjugate for an arbitrarily prescribed quantum tuple.

nodes.title: Apply the theorem to the corrected Long triple
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QCR1, the named sub-result states:

For
\[
 R=x(2-3xq)
\]
and the retained S,T of Long's full map, (1)--(2) give
\[
 \operatorname{Cent}_{\{,\}}(R,S,T)=K[R],\qquad
                       D'=D_{\rm Long}+P(R).           \tag{4}
\]
The [retained exact transcription](../dixmier-audit/verify_long_pbw.py)
has
\[
 \deg D_{\rm Long}=23,\qquad
 \operatorname{ord}_{p,z}D_{\rm Long}=5,\qquad \deg R=3.
\]
Here momentum order is the maximum combined exponent of p and z
in the original polarization. Exact nonzero witnesses in D_Long are
\[
                 [x^{12}q^6z^5]D_{\rm Long}=144/5,
             \qquad [x^6z^5]D_{\rm Long}=32/405.         \tag{5}
\]
The full support bounds are checked, not inferred from these two
monomials alone.

Since P(R) has momentum order zero, every completion in (4) has
momentum order exactly five. For nonconstant P of degree k,
deg P(R)=3k. No multiple of three equals 23. Thus
\[
                     \deg(D_{\rm Long}+P(R))
                          =\max(23,3k)\ge23.            \tag{6}
\]
Constants leave the degree unchanged. There is no lower-degree
or lower-momentum-order fourth image for the retained triple,
irrespective of the degree allowed in the search.

polarization changes the problem. It does not establish an
intrinsic minimum over Long's full canonical orbit.

nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QCR1, the named sub-result states:

For Long, keeping R exact is possible at the formal level. Begin
with any full formal lift supplied by [QFL1](PROOF.md). In the

coefficient. Its h-adically small inner gauge preserves all Weyl
relations and removes that term. Repeat. Every coefficient remains
a polynomial, so this produces a full formal lift with first image
R exactly. Applying (7) then normalizes its completing fourth image
without changing the classical Long map, since D_Long is already
normalized.

a proved bounded algebraic normalization of every bounded lift.
Consequently a failure for all R-fixed triples, were it established,
would still need a bounded-normalization comparison to exclude all
possible lifts. No such failure or comparison is proved here.

nodes.title: Why the undeformed R hypothesis matters
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QCR1, the named sub-result states:

For a general deformed first image, formal centralizer closure
does not become a finite polynomial algebra merely because an
individual centralizer element is spatially bounded.

For example, in normal order with [p,x]=h, set
\[
                  X=x+h^2x^2,\qquad
                  P=(1+2h^2x)^{-1}p.
\]
Then [P,X]=h exactly in the h-adic algebra, with classical
identity reduction. The element x has spatial degree one and
commutes with X, but
\[
                              x\notin K[[h]][X].
\]
Over K((h)), any nonconstant polynomial in X has even positive
x degree. Nevertheless x belongs to the completed algebra:
\[
       x=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k C_k h^{2k}X^{k+1},
       \qquad C_k=\frac{1}{k+1}{2k\choose k}.           \tag{10}
\]
Thus (3) genuinely needs h-adic completion. In fact this fixed X
has no spatially bounded polynomial Weyl mate at all. Over K((h)),
a finite normal PBW operator Q of p order m>0 has leading
commutator coefficient h*m*q_m(x)*(1+2h^2*x). A scalar nonzero
commutator forces m=1 and q_1(x)*(1+2h^2*x)=1, impossible for a
polynomial coefficient. The same p-order argument works with any
number of spectator pairs as coefficients.

So even a spatially bounded first image with identity classical
reduction can force its completing mate to have unbounded spatial
degrees. The identity formal gauge class still has the bounded
representative (x,p). This is failure of the specified first-image
choice, not intrinsic nonliftability of its formal class.

nodes.title: Valuation and the exact hypothesis
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVM1, the named sub-result states:

Let C be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, let h be
a nonzero differential constant, and let F/C(v) be any finite
algebraic function-field extension. Extend
\[
             \delta=v^{1-d}\partial_v,\qquad d\ge2
\]
uniquely to F, and work in the finite scalar Ore ring F[a;h*delta].
At a point over v=infinity, use Puiseux series in v^(-1/e).
Define deg_v(f) as its leading v exponent, and for an operator
sum f_j*a^j use the maximum of those coefficient exponents.
All such exponents are rational.

Assume S has
\[
 S=vH(a)+S_{<1},\qquad
 H\in C[a],\quad \deg H\ge2,\quad \deg_v S_{<1}<1 .            \tag{1}
\]
There is no order bound on S_<1. Its coefficients may have
arbitrary algebraic poles away from infinity. Write
H=c*product_i(a-alpha_i)^(n_i), with c nonzero, and require
\[
                            \gcd_i n_i=1.                   \tag{2}
\]
Thus H is not a proper power after a constant rescaling over C.
In particular every squarefree H of degree at least two qualifies.

**Theorem.** Under (1)--(2), no finite T in any such algebraic
coefficient field satisfies
\[
                             [S,T]=\kappa,\qquad
                           0\ne\kappa\in C .                \tag{3}
\]
The constant fields may first be extended algebraically; the
result descends to any characteristic-zero constant field.

nodes.title: The leading commutator
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVM1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose T has leading term v^M*K(a), with M rational and K nonzero
in C[a]. Since delta decreases v exponent by d, the Ore product gives
\[
 \deg_v[S,T]\le M+1-d,\qquad
 [S,T]_{\rm leading}
   =h\,v^{M+1-d}\bigl(MH'K-HK'\bigr).                        \tag{4}
\]
The displayed coefficient is interpreted as the coefficient at
that exponent; it may vanish. All repeated contractions and all
terms from S_<1 or lower terms of T have strictly smaller exponent.
The bound and formula are valid on every finite Puiseux cover.

If M>d-1, equation (3) forces
\[
                         MH'K-HK'=0 .
\]
Comparing residues of the logarithmic derivatives K'/K and H'/H
at the roots of H gives
\[
             \operatorname{ord}_{\alpha_i}K=M n_i.
\]
There are no other roots of K, because K'/K=M H'/H.
Condition (2) forces M to be an integer, and hence
\[
                              K=c_0 H^M.                    \tag{5}
\]
Here M>d-1>=1, so S^M is a finite operator. Replace T by
T-c0*S^M. This preserves (3) and strictly lowers deg_v(T).
Every exponent still greater than d-1 must again be an integer
by the same argument. Thus this reduction terminates after finitely
many subtractions; no infinite subtraction or completion is used.

We may consequently assume M<=d-1. If M<d-1, (4) makes the
commutator have negative v degree, contradicting (3). Thus
M=d-1, and its leading coefficient must obey
\[
                     (d-1)H'K-HK'=\kappa/h .                \tag{6}
\]

nodes.title: The polynomial leading equation has no solution
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVM1, the named sub-result states:

Put n=deg H>=2 and t=deg K. Unless t=(d-1)n, the leading term
on the left of (6) is nonzero and has degree n+t-1>=1.
It cannot be a nonzero constant.

If t=(d-1)n, subtract a constant multiple of H^(d-1) from K to
reduce its degree. This does not alter the left side of (6).
If the result is zero the left side is zero. Otherwise its degree
is now below (d-1)n, so the preceding nonconstant leading-term
argument applies. Both outcomes contradict (6), proving the theorem.

nodes.title: Why the restrictions matter
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVM1, the named sub-result states:

For degree-one H=alpha*a+beta, with alpha nonzero, the exact pair
\[
       S=v(\alpha a+\beta),\qquad
       T=\frac{v^{d-1}}{\alpha(d-1)}
\]
satisfies [S,T]=h. Thus the degree threshold cannot be discarded.

For H=(a^2+1)^2, the homogeneous leading equation in (4) has the
fractional-exponent solution M=3/2, K=(a^2+1)^3.
Such a leading term cannot be removed by subtracting an integer
power of S. This demonstrates the boundary of the reduction proof;
it does not give a finite Weyl mate for this proper-power H.

The assumption deg_v S_<1<1 is also essential to the method.
Terms on a different top face can change both (4) and the finite
reduction. Ordinary polynomial coordinate equivalence or formal
Hamiltonian equivalence does not preserve this specified face.

For the classical leading-bracket and proportional-power framework, see
[Han--Tan, Theorem2.8](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00257) and
[Guccione--Guccione--Valqui, Remark1.13 and Section2](https://arxiv.org/html/1111.6100).
Those polynomial and fractional-Weyl results are context; the proof above
establishes the stated whole-curve, arbitrary-Puiseux-cover version directly.

The [quadratic finite-mate theorem](QUADRATIC_OPERATOR_MATE_CLASSIFICATION.md)
gives the complementary low-order input.
This proof uses only the finite Ore calculus, polynomial roots and
characteristic-zero Puiseux expansions. No novelty priority or
independent theorem review is asserted.

nodes.title: An h-small cubic candidate passes the Fourier rank test
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVM1, the named sub-result states:

The [QKR1 rank budget](FOURIER_CYCLIC_RANK_BUDGET.md) makes a
generic inverse-Fourier rank-two proposal insufficient for a
bounded full exact-R scalar Long lift. The next natural local
test is
\[
              S_*=v(2+h a^3)+4a-3ra^2,\qquad q=v^2/2 .
                                                               \tag{7}
\]
Its special operator symbol is the retained Long S, while its
generic differential order is three. It therefore escapes the
order-two hypothesis of QSO2.

This candidate also passes the algebraic branch and minimum-rank
tests. For a source eigenvalue s, the connection S_*-s has rank
three over C(v). In the basis 1,a,a^2 its ordinary v derivative
matrix is
\[
 A(v)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 0&0&(s-2v)/h^2\\
 v/h&0&-4/h^2\\
 0&v/h&3r/h^2
 \end{pmatrix}.                                               \tag{8}
\]
It is polynomial of degree at most one, so the connection is
nonsingular at every finite v and has slopes at infinity at most
two. Its quadratic pushforward has rank six, local characters
1^3 direct_sum K_(1/2)^3 at q=0, no other finite singularities,
and slopes at infinity at most one. The Fourier rank formula
therefore gives exactly
\[
                       N=6,\qquad r(E_*)=3.                 \tag{9}
\]
It saturates the quadratic rank budget.

For completeness, write A(v)=A0+v*A1 and put
C0=h*A1, Cminus=h*A0. Its a-connection is
C(v)=C0+Cminus/v. The pushed-forward q matrix is
\[
 H_*=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 C0&Cminus\\
 Cminus/(2q)&C0+hI/(2q)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
With V=[[0,2qI],[I,0]], the two algebraic projectors
(I+V/v)/2 and (I-V/v)/2 are horizontal after q=v^2/2.
Their image connections are C0+Cminus/v and C0-Cminus/v.
Thus the rank-three inverse model genuinely permits extraction;
a missing algebraic projector is not its failure.

However H(a)=2+h*a^3 in (7) is squarefree over the generic constant
field: H'=3h*a^2 and H(0)=2. It has degree three.
Equations (1)--(6) exclude every finite T satisfying [S_*,T]=h,
over all finite algebraic coefficient covers. The exclusion
continues to hold after arbitrary finite lower-v-degree corrections
to S_*. It is independent of the inverse-Fourier rank computation.

nodes.title: A nonlinear ordinary infinity limit has no finite mate
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

Let C be algebraically closed of characteristic zero, let h be a
nonzero differential constant, and let F/C(u) be any finite
algebraic function field with derivation partial_u. At a point
over u=infinity, use the leading Puiseux exponent as deg_u.
Consider a finite scalar operator
\[
 P=\sum_j p_j(u)E^j,\qquad [E,f]=h f_u,\qquad
 \deg_u p_j\le0,\qquad
 P_\infty(E)=\sum_j \lim_{u\to\infty}p_j(u)E^j .
                                                               \tag{1}
\]
If deg P_infinity>=2, there is no finite Q over any finite
algebraic coefficient cover such that [P,Q]=kappa is a nonzero
differential constant. Higher-order coefficients of P are allowed
to tend to zero; P_infinity need not have P's generic order.

nodes.title: Transport through algebraic canonical changes
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

Return to a coefficient field with derivation delta and
[a,f]=h*delta(f). After a finite algebraic extension choose
f nonzero, alpha and u in that field such that
f*delta(u)=1. Then
\[
          E=f(a-\alpha),\qquad
                 a=\alpha+f^{-1}E,\qquad [E,u]=h .            \tag{4}
\]
Both directions preserve finite scalar differential order.
Any hypothetical finite mate remains a finite mate after this
change. Consequently (1)--(2) apply whenever u tends to infinity
and the transformed coefficients have the stated limits.
A change with f*delta=v*partial_v instead uses (3).

These changes need not be regular at h=0. In particular a root
alpha may have an h pole. This is legitimate for a generic-fiber
nonexistence proof: a finite regular mate would still become a
finite generic mate. It is not a bounded formal normalization
theorem for arbitrary quantum lifts.

nodes.title: Repeated roots produce a nonlinear limit
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

Let q=v^d/d with d>=2, so delta=v^(1-d)*partial_v.
Suppose
\[
       S=vH(a)+S_0,\qquad H\in C[a],\qquad
              \deg_v\text{ every coefficient of }S_0\le0 .
                                                               \tag{5}
\]
Let alpha be a root of H of multiplicity k>=2, and put
\[
 E=v^{1/k}(a-\alpha),\qquad
 u=\frac{v^{\,d-1/k}}{d-1/k},\qquad [E,u]=h .                 \tag{6}
\]
This takes only a finite algebraic coefficient extension, and
u tends to infinity with v. Write b=a-alpha.
If H(alpha+b)=sum_(j>=k)c_j*b^j, then in the new normal order
the leading coefficient term of b^j is v^(-j/k)*E^j.
Each internal contraction decreases its coefficient v exponent
by the additional positive amount d-1/k.

Thus all coefficients of v*H(a) become bounded; its limit is
c_k*E^k. Every term from S0 remains bounded and contributes
only a scalar to the limit. If sigma0 is the value at alpha
of the polynomial made from S0's coefficient limits, then
\[
                          S_\infty(E)=c_kE^k+\sigma_0 .      \tag{7}
\]
The degree is k>=2, so (1)--(2) exclude every finite mate.
This covers repeated roots whether or not their multiplicities
have gcd one.

Combining with QVM1 gives the complete conclusion for (5):
\[
             \deg H\ge2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
       \text{no finite algebraic-coefficient Weyl mate for }S.
                                                               \tag{8}
\]
If H is squarefree, QVM1 applies. If it is not squarefree,
choose a repeated root and use (6)--(7). These two cases
exhaust every polynomial H of degree at least two.

The boundedness requirement on S0 is precise. QVM1's primitive
case permits coefficient exponents strictly below one. The new
proper-power conclusion assumes exponents at most zero.
It does not silently cover arbitrary fractional positive growth.

nodes.title: A finite Newton support test beyond bounded lower terms
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

There is a useful sufficient criterion for more general finite
Laurent-polynomial operators. After a constant shift b=a-alpha,
write S=sum c_(j,l)*v^j*b^l. Choose rational rho with 0<rho<d.
If every nonzero support point satisfies
\[
 j-\rho l\le0,\qquad
           F(E)=\sum_{j=\rho l}c_{j,l}E^l,\qquad \deg F\ge2,
                                                               \tag{9}
\]
then E=v^rho*b and u=v^(d-rho)/(d-rho) transport S to (1).
The coefficient exponent of each contraction drops further by
d-rho>0, so its limiting polynomial is exactly F(E).
No finite mate is possible.

This test can include positive intermediate v powers absent from
(5), when their momentum vanishing order is sufficient. It needs
a finite support certificate, not a partner-order search.

At rho=d the change has Euler derivation rather than an
algebraic ordinary coordinate. Under the same support inequality,
the limiting polynomial is
\[
 F_{\rm Euler}(E)=
    \sum_{j=dl}c_{j,l}
                    \prod_{t=0}^{l-1}(E-thd).                \tag{10}
\]
If this is nonconstant, (3) excludes every finite mate.
The product records all ordering corrections; replacing it by
E^l would omit terms at the same infinity degree.

For the quadratic chart d=2, (10) and the repeated-root
normalization also give a second complete bounded-lower class:
S=v^2*H(a)+S0 has no finite mate whenever H is nonconstant.
A simple root uses E=v^2*(a-alpha) and the Euler limit.
A root of multiplicity k>=2 uses E=v^(2/k)*(a-alpha),
an ordinary coordinate tending to infinity, and a degree-k limit.

This quadratic-growth corollary retains the bounded-coefficient
hypothesis on S0. It does not cover every higher-v-degree
deformation of Long: its existing 2v term would be an unbounded
lower term unless additional root-vanishing conditions such as
(9) were actually verified.

nodes.title: The proper-power Long repair is excluded in every degree
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

A natural replacement for QVM1's rejected cubic coefficient is
\[
             S_k=2v(1+ha)^k+4a-3ra^2,\qquad k\ge2 .         \tag{11}
\]
It has the correct classical Long S and a proper-power leading
polynomial. The preceding primitive-root test alone did not
exclude it.

Its root alpha=-1/h has multiplicity k. Formula (6) gives
\[
             (S_k)_\infty=
                2h^k E^k-\frac4h-\frac{3r}{h^2}.             \tag{12}
\]
Thus no S_k has a finite Weyl mate, on any finite algebraic
coefficient cover, in any partner order. Arbitrary finite
corrections with bounded v coefficients are still excluded.

For k=3 the spectral connection (S_3-s) also passes the earlier
minimum-rank and branch-splitting tests. In the basis 1,a,a^2 its
ordinary v matrix is polynomial of degree one, because the
leading a coefficient is 2h^3*v and multiplication by v/h clears
its v denominator. QKR1 therefore gives pushforward rank six
and inverse-Fourier rank three, with the usual algebraic branch
projectors. The missing full Weyl action is still impossible by
(12). There is no need to compute more quantum corrections
inside this proper-power family.

nodes.title: A surviving linear growth Long model costs at least rank four
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

For a rational Laurent-coefficient operator in (5), let m be its
generic a order and p=deg H. If m>p, the coefficient of a^m is
bounded at infinity, while some coefficient of order at most p
has v degree one. The commutative Newton polynomial therefore has
a root with positive v exponent: otherwise its elementary symmetric
functions, after division by the leading coefficient, would all
be bounded.

For such a growing a branch, a=(h/v)*partial_v gives a v
exponential slope strictly greater than two. On the quadratic
q-line its slope is strictly greater than one. This is a formal
Newton-polygon assertion: derivative contractions are lower at
every positive a exponent, so they do not remove that upper edge.
The strictly positive infinity contribution rho_infinity is an
integer and is at least one.

The quadratic pushforward of (S-s) has rank2m and a Kummer
self-twist. QKR1 gives its q=0 contribution at least m,
whether or not the v=0 connection is nonsingular. Hence
\[
                       r(E)\ge m+1 .                        \tag{15}
\]
Any other finite singularities add nonnegative cost.

For a bounded full scalar Long lift with exact undeformed R,
[QSO2](QUADRATIC_OPERATOR_MATE_CLASSIFICATION.md) gives m>=3.
Equation (8) forces p<=1 in the v-linear bounded-lower class.
Thus m>p and (15) forces r(E)>=4. This closes the rank-three
proposal throughout that class; it does not exclude the remaining
higher-rank models or change the scalar-reduction hypothesis.

For example S=v*(2+h*a)+4a-3ra^2+h^2*a^3 has m=3 and p=1.
It has one bounded momentum branch and two growing like
v^(1/2). Its v connection is nonsingular at every finite point;
the q infinity contribution is one and its inverse rank is
exactly four. No full mate for this example is supplied.

nodes.title: A commuting Darboux algebra still cannot supply a Weyl generator
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QVL1, the named sub-result states:

The bounded-coefficient setting also occurs in bispectral research;
compare [Horozov, Section2](https://arxiv.org/html/math-ph/0206029).
Bispectrality and a finite Weyl mate impose different requirements,
and no classification theorem from that paper is used here.

For an explicit rational Darboux example, with [E,u]=h, set
\[
 \begin{split}
 A&=E-h/u,\\
 L_2&=E^2-2h^2/u^2,\\
 L_3&=E^3-3h^2u^{-2}E+3h^3u^{-3}.
 \end{split}                                                  \tag{16}
\]
Direct multiplication gives L2*A=A*E^2 and L3*A=A*E^3.
Cancellation in the Ore domain gives [L2,L3]=0 and L3^2=L2^3.
Every nonconstant element of C[L2,L3] has a nonlinear ordinary
infinity limit in C[E^2,E^3], so (1)--(2) exclude every finite
Weyl mate, of every order and on every finite coefficient cover.
The limit map is injective: in the normal form p(L2)+L3*q(L2),
the even and odd highest E orders cannot cancel.

This rules out choosing a scalar Weyl generator inside this whole
commuting Darboux algebra, not only its quadratic member. It does
not exclude a full action using other noncommuting operators in a
larger idealizer, or identify this algebra with every projective
Long carrier.

The remaining scalar constructions lie outside the excluded
v-linear Laurent class or have leading H of degree at most one
and satisfy this stronger rank cost, together with the full
right action and global admission.
Arbitrary nonpositional first images and projective or matrix
carriers remain separate possibilities. No all-representative
Long nonlifting is inferred.

For the leading-bracket framework compare
[Han--Tan, Theorem2.8](https://arxiv.org/html/2210.00257) and
[Guccione--Guccione--Valqui, Remark1.13 and Section2](https://arxiv.org/html/1111.6100).

are proved directly; no classification of bispectral operators
or centralizers is imported.

nodes.title: Hypotheses and conclusions
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QET1, the named sub-result states:

Retain the algebra and classical-centralizer assumptions of
[QFC1](FINITE_CENTRALIZERS_AND_COMPLETION.md): E is an h-torsion-free,
h-separated K[[h]]-algebra with commutative reduction; the commuting Fi
have independent reductions fi and full joint Poisson centralizer K[fi].
Actual integral Ti satisfy [Fj,Ti]=h*delta_ij. One may also start
with actual generic mates: the parameter-pole lemma below normalizes
them integrally before applying this theorem. Write
\[
 L=K((h)),\quad P=L[F_1,\ldots,F_m],\quad
 B=\operatorname{Cent}_{E[h^{-1}]}(F_1,\ldots,F_m),\quad
 Q=\operatorname{Frac}P,\quad H=\operatorname{Frac}B.        \tag{1}
\]
QFC1 makes B commutative, and its commuting translation derivations
nabla_i=-ad(Ti)/h extend partial_(Fi). Their joint constants in B are L.

Assume additionally that B is finitely generated as an L-algebra,
H/Q is finite, and
\[
                            P\cap B^\times=L^\times.      \tag{2}
\]
For E the scalar finite-PBW algebra of rank m, the finite-field
hypothesis and (2) are automatic once B is finitely generated.
The dimension input is the classical commutative-subalgebra bound
trdeg C<=m in A_m. It follows from
[Bavula, Corollary1.6](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0401263):
extend scalars faithfully to an algebraic closure, apply that bound,
and descend dimension. Since B contains P of transcendence degree m,
its finitely generated fraction field is finite over Q.
For units, Bernstein degree is additive on products, so a unit of
A_m(L) has degree zero and is scalar.

**Centralizer geometry theorem.** Under these hypotheses:

1. B is smooth over L and P->B is etale. The open image of Spec B
   in Spec P contains every height-one point.
2. In the finite normalization C of P in H, above each base prime
   divisor at least one unramified prime meets Spec B. Thus every
   geometric codimension-one inertia generator has a fixed sheet.
3. If H=Q, or more generally H/Q is Galois, then B=P.
4. The integral centralizer is K[[h]][F]. Polynomial curvature
   homotopy gives a finite full completion; corrections can be h-small
   if the prescribed classical individual conjugates are flat.

nodes.title: Finite generation makes the centralizer etale
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QET1, the named sub-result states:

Now impose finite generation. Omega_(B/P) is a finite B-module and
has connections
\[
         \nabla_i(b\,dc)=(\nabla_i b)\,dc+b\,d(\nabla_i c). \tag{4}
\]
Separability of H/Q gives Omega_(B/P) tensor_B H=0.
Since Omega is finite, its annihilator is a nonzero ideal of B.
The connections preserve that annihilator: differentiate a*omega=0.
Differential simplicity forces the annihilator to be B, so
\[
                     \Omega_{B/P}=0.                     \tag{5}
\]
The exact sequence of differentials and the derivations give mutually
inverse maps
\[
 B^m \xrightarrow{e_i\mapsto dF_i}\Omega_{B/L}
       \xrightarrow{db\mapsto(\nabla_i b)_i} B^m.           \tag{6}
\]
Surjectivity of the first map is (5), and the composite is the identity.
At every closed point the residue field is finite separable over L,
so (6) makes the cotangent-space dimension m. The integral finite-type
L-algebra B has dimension m, and every closed local ring has dimension
m. Thus every such point is regular; the Jacobian criterion in
characteristic zero makes B smooth over L. The differential of the
map to affine m-space is an isomorphism by (6), so that map is etale.
This proves flatness as well as unramifiedness; vanishing relative
differentials alone would not have sufficed.

nodes.title: Weyl units retain all base divisors
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QET1, the named sub-result states:

An etale morphism is open. Let U be the image of Spec B in Spec P.
If the generic point of an irreducible divisor q(F)=0 were absent
from U, its whole divisor would be absent: an open set containing
any point of an irreducible divisor contains its generic point.
Then q(F) would vanish at no prime of B, hence be a unit. By (2),
q would have to be constant, a contradiction. Therefore
\[
       \operatorname{Spec}P\setminus U
                         \text{ has codimension at least two}. \tag{7}
\]
This asserts no rational point over a base field; it retains geometric
points over every generic divisor, possibly with nontrivial separable
residue-field extensions.

Let C be the integral closure of P in H. It is finite over P, since P
is a polynomial ring over a field and H/Q is finite. Smoothness makes
B normal, so C is contained in B. Zariski's Main Theorem identifies
\[
          \operatorname{Spec}B\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}C
                  \longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}P     \tag{8}
\]
as an open immersion followed by a finite map. We use the
[normalization form of Zariski's Main Theorem, Stacks02LR](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02LR).
In this normal dominant setting its normalization is precisely C.
The result is an external geometric input, not a finite experiment.

At each height-one base prime, (7) gives a point in Spec B over that
prime. There (8) identifies the local normalization with the etale
source, so this is an unramified prime of C. In characteristic zero
all residue extensions are separable and inertia is tame. Over a
geometric generic divisor the cycle lengths of an inertia generator
are the ramification indices, repeated by residue degree. Hence
\[
       \text{each codimension-one inertia generator has a fixed point}.
                                                               \tag{9}
\]
This does not supply one sheet fixed by the whole monodromy group.

nodes.title: Birational and Galois fields collapse to polynomiality
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QET1, the named sub-result states:

If H=Q, then C=P because P is normal. Equation (8) makes B an affine
open subring in the same function field. Every b in B is regular
at all height-one points of P by (7). Since P is a factorial normal
domain,
\[
                  B\subset\bigcap_{\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=1}
                                      P_{\mathfrak p}=P.  \tag{10}
\]
Thus B=P. This is the birational case; no module-finiteness hypothesis
on B/P was needed.

Suppose next that H/Q is Galois. At a base prime divisor the Galois
group acts transitively on the primes of C above it, preserving
ramification indices. Since at least one is unramified, all are.
This standard DVR fact is recorded in
[Stacks09E3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09E3).
Consequently the finite map Spec C->Spec P is unramified in
codimension one. The source is normal and the target regular;
[purity of the branch locus, Stacks0BMB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BMB)
makes this finite map etale everywhere.

Finite etale covers of affine space over characteristic-zero fields
are constant, using the same explicit external covering theorem as
QFC1, [Milne, Remark3.3(c), Theorem3.4 and the fundamental group sequence](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/LECc.pdf#page=27).
Thus C is C0 tensor_L P for a finite etale L-algebra C0. Because C
is a domain, C0 is a field. It lies inside B, and its elements are
annihilated by all the nabla_i, being separably algebraic over L.
The joint constants in B are L, so C0=L, H=Q, and the birational
argument gives B=P.

For scalar Weyl algebras one can also exclude C0 directly: an element
algebraic over L in A_m(L) has Bernstein degree zero and is scalar.
The formal-horizontal-constant argument permits the more general
algebra hypotheses in (1)--(2).

Return now to the integral algebra. QFC1's valuation argument gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cent}_{E}(F)=K[[h]][F],\qquad
                   h^{-1}[T_i,T_j]\in K[[h]][F].          \tag{11}
\]
Its finite polynomial de Rham homotopy kills all mixed curvature
inside E, and is h-small when the classical tuple is flat.
Thus Galois or birational field data furnish a second positive
completion certificate after the individual conjugates are found.

nodes.title: Degree and inertia restrictions without a degree cutoff
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QET1, the named sub-result states:

If all hypotheses hold and B is not polynomial, then
\[
                         [H:Q]\ge3,\qquad H/Q\text{ is not Galois}.
                                                               \tag{12}
\]
Every quadratic extension in characteristic zero is Galois; degree
one was treated separately. A cubic nonpolynomial survivor must have
normal closure S3 and may have generic inertia type (2,1), but not
(3). Two transpositions can each fix a different sheet and generate
transitive S3, so no common branch or algebraic rank-one extraction
follows from (9).

The lower degree three is sharp in rank at least three.
The retained rescaled cotangent examples of
[QNI1](IDENTITY_LIFTS_AND_UNBOUNDED_INVERSES.md) have B=L[x1,x2,x3]
and P=L[f_(h^N)] with identity classical reduction and all full
relations. [QDI1's cubic chart](QUANTUM_DIVISION_AND_COMPLETION.md)
proves their position-field extension has degree three. With its
unnormalized output parameters A,B,C and source parameter w, the
equation is
\[
                        Cw^3-2w^2+Bw-2A=0.               \tag{13}
\]
Its discriminant is
4B^2-4CB^3+72ABC-64A-108A^2C^2.
As a quadratic in A its discriminant is
64*(4-3BC)^3, nonzero, so it is squarefree in A over L(B,C)
and not a square. Therefore the normal closure is S3. These
centralizers are etale but nonfinite over their position-image rings,
as QFC1's cotangent boundary shows. This is a reused higher-rank
control, not a rank-two or Long construction.

The degree in (12) is [Frac B:L(F_i)]. It is distinct from QDI1's
left/right indices of whole noncommutative Weyl division rings and
their completed degrees. No equality between them is inferred.

nodes.title: Remove parameter poles inside the actual generic algebra
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QET1, the named sub-result states:

This lemma needs only QFC1's algebra and polynomial classical
centralizer hypotheses, not finite generation, a field-degree
condition or the unit condition. Suppose actual generic Ti in E[h^-1]
satisfy [Fj,Ti]=h*delta_ij. There are unique polynomial polar parts
\[
 T_i=U_i+a_i(F),\qquad U_i\in E,\qquad
       a_i\in h^{-1}K[h^{-1}][t_1,\ldots,t_m].             \tag{17}
\]
To construct them, if Ti has pole order N>=1, multiply by h^N.
Its reduction Poisson-commutes with all fj, since
[Fj,h^N Ti]/h is divisible by h. Write that reduction uniquely
as a polynomial q(fi), subtract h^-N*q(F), and the pole order
drops by at least one. After at most N steps Ti is integral.
There are finitely many polynomial corrections, so this remains
in the actual finite algebra. Uniqueness follows because a
nonzero polynomial in F with only negative h coefficients cannot
lie in E: its first coefficient is nonzero in the independent fi.

Subtracting ai(F) does not change the translation derivations on
B. Thus the geometric theorem above can start with actual generic
individual mates; one first applies (17). Their classical images
can be matched to any prescribed classical individual conjugates:
each difference lies in K[f], and its polynomial lift can be
subtracted finitely.

There is an extra full-tuple statement with no centralizer-finiteness
hypothesis. Direct commutation gives
\[
 h^{-1}[U_i,U_j]=h^{-1}[T_i,T_j]
                         +\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i. \tag{18}
\]
If the original curvature divided by h is integral, then the last
term is integral too. But its F-coordinate coefficients have only
negative h powers. By the same independence argument it is zero.
In particular, a generic flat tuple stays flat after (17), with
no additional curvature correction.

If its integral classical tuple is to equal a prescribed flat
tuple t_i^0, the differences are polynomials
\[
             \bar U_i=t_i^0+q_i(f),\qquad
                         \partial_i q_j-\partial_j q_i=0. \tag{19}
\]
Closedness follows from the two classical flatness relations.
Replacing Ui by Ui-qi(F) preserves every quantum relation exactly
and attains the prescribed full classical tuple. Hence an actual
generic full tuple with the regular Long positions already suffices
for a finite integral full Long lift. This is a parameter-pole
descent theorem, not a bounded comparison between arbitrary lifts.

nodes.title: The algebra and the positive criterion
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

Let K have characteristic zero, R0=K[[h]], L=K((h)), and let E be an
R0-algebra that is h-torsion-free and h-separated. Assume D=E/hE is
commutative; its Poisson bracket is the reduction of [ , ]/h.
Choose actual elements F1,...,Fm,T1,...,Tm in E such that
\[
 [F_i,F_j]=0,\qquad [F_j,T_i]=h\delta_{ij}.                 \tag{1}
\]
Write fi for the reduction of Fi. Assume the fi are algebraically
independent and their full joint Poisson centralizer in D is
\[
                   \operatorname{Cent}_{\{\,,\,\},D}(f_1,\ldots,f_m)
                         =K[f_1,\ldots,f_m].              \tag{2}
\]
Put
\[
 P=R0[F_1,\ldots,F_m],\quad B=\operatorname{Cent}_{E}(F_1,\ldots,F_m),
 \quad P_L=L[F_1,\ldots,F_m],\quad B_L=B[h^{-1}].            \tag{3}
\]
Algebraic independence and h-separatedness identify P with a polynomial
ring over R0. Central localization shows B_L is the centralizer in
E[h^-1].

**Finite centralizer theorem.** Under (1)--(2), the following are equivalent:
B is module-finite over P; B_L is module-finite over P_L; and B=P.
Under these equivalent conditions there are bi in P with
\[
 [T_i+b_i,T_j+b_j]=0,\qquad [F_j,T_i+b_i]=h\delta_{ij}.      \tag{4}
\]
If the reductions of the Ti already commute in the Poisson bracket,
the bi can all be chosen in hP. Thus the entire prescribed classical
tuple is preserved.

The scalar finite-PBW algebra and finite idempotent corners with
scalar rank-one classical reduction satisfy the separation, torsion
and commutative-reduction hypotheses. For Long's pair, (2) is QSC1.
An arbitrary partial graph module needs its own proof of these hypotheses;
a completed frame alone is not being used as an algebraic frame.

nodes.title: Formal centralizer and actual translation derivations
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

The reduction of any b in B lies in K[f]. Subtract its polynomial lift
in P and divide by h. The result is again in B: h is a nonzerodivisor
and the Fi commute with b. Repeating gives a unique expansion in the
h-adic completion,
\[
              b=\sum_{\nu\ge0}h^\nu Q_\nu(F),\qquad
                       Q_\nu\in K[t_1,\ldots,t_m].         \tag{5}
\]
Uniqueness follows by taking the first nonzero h coefficient and using
independence of the fi. Separation makes the map from E into its
completion injective. Polynomial partial sums of two such expansions
commute, so B is commutative. The same induction works for the full
completed centralizer. Laurent localization permits only finitely many
negative h powers. In particular B_L is a domain.

Since D is commutative, every commutator in E is in hE. Division by h
is unique and remains in the actual algebra. The derivations
\[
 \nabla_i=-h^{-1}\operatorname{ad}(T_i):B\longrightarrow B,\qquad
                    \nabla_i(F_j)=\delta_{ij}              \tag{6}
\]
therefore preserve B and extend to B_L. Jacobi puts [Ti,Tj] in B, and
commutativity of B implies [nabla_i,nabla_j]=0 on B. On (5) these
derivations act coefficientwise as partial_(ti). Consequently
\[
                  \bigcap_i\ker(\nabla_i:B_L\to B_L)=L.    \tag{7}
\]
This excludes nontrivial algebraic constant extensions even though
L=K((h)) need not be algebraically closed.

nodes.title: Two elementary differential algebra lemmas
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

Let A be any commutative Q-algebra. If an ideal I in A[t1,...,tm] is
stable under every coordinate partial derivative, then
\[
                      I=(I\cap A)A[t_1,\ldots,t_m].        \tag{8}
\]
For a polynomial q, the finite Taylor projector
\[
             q(0)=\sum_\beta\frac{(-t)^\beta}{\beta!}
                                      \partial^\beta q    \tag{9}
\]
lies in I when q does. Apply this also to all derivatives of q:
each coefficient of q belongs to I intersect A. This proves (8) in
every degree and over a ring with nilpotents as well.

If a finite module N over a noetherian A[t] has operators Di satisfying
Di(pn)=(partial_i p)n+pDi(n), all its Fitting ideals are stable under
partial_i. Indeed, over dual numbers, sigma(p)=p+epsilon*partial_i p
is a base automorphism, and 1+epsilon*Di is an invertible
sigma-semilinear module map. Functoriality and base change of Fitting
ideals give sigma(Fitt_k(N))=Fitt_k(N), hence derivative stability.
The required basic Fitting facts are
[Stacks, Lemma15.8.4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07ZA).

Over a characteristic-zero field, (8) says each such Fitting ideal is
zero or the unit ideal. If r is the generic rank, Fitt_(r-1)=0 and
Fitt_r=the unit ideal, so N is locally free of rank r. This follows
locally by choosing r generators: vanishing Fitt_(r-1) forces every
entry of the relation matrix to vanish. In particular a generically
zero finite module with these connections is zero. Integrability
is not needed for this Fitting argument.

nodes.title: Integral module finiteness removes escaping support
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

Assume first that B is finite over P. The finite P-module N=B/P inherits
the connections (6). The reduction argument before (5) gives B=P+hB,
hence N/hN=0. Its zeroth Fitting ideal is, by (8),
\[
                      \operatorname{Fitt}_0(N)=JP,\qquad J\subset R0.
                                                               \tag{10}
\]
Fitting base change and N/hN=0 imply JP+hP=P. Evaluation at t=0 gives
J+(h)=R0. Since R0 is local, J=R0, so Fitt_0(N)=P and N=0. Thus B=P.

It would be invalid to apply Nakayama directly to P: h is not in the
Jacobson radical of R0[t]. For example P/(1-h*t1) is nonzero but equals
h times itself. It cannot carry a partial_1 connection, since its
annihilator would have to contain both 1-h*t1 and its derivative -h,
which generate the unit ideal. The connections remove precisely this
possible escape to t1=1/h.

nodes.title: Generic module finiteness also suffices
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

Assume only that B_L is finite over P_L. Equations (6) and the Fitting
lemma make B_L a finite locally free P_L-module. Its relative
differentials Omega_(B_L/P_L) are finite over P_L and inherit connections
\[
       \nabla_i(b\,dc)=(\nabla_i b)\,dc+b\,d(\nabla_i c).    \tag{11}
\]
This respects d(p)=0 because partial_i p is again in P_L.
The domain B_L becomes a finite field extension after passing to
Frac(P_L), and that extension is separable in characteristic zero.
Thus Omega is generically zero and the same Fitting lemma gives
Omega=0. Hence B_L is finite etale over P_L.

We use the standard external fact that finite etale covers of affine
space over a characteristic-zero field are constant. Over an algebraic
closure this follows from Riemann existence and simple connectedness
of complex affine space, with invariance under algebraically closed
base extension; see [Milne, Remark3.3(c), Theorem3.4 and the fundamental
group exact sequence](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/LECc.pdf#page=27).
Descent identifies every such algebra with C tensor_L P_L for a finite
etale L-algebra C. Each element of C is killed by the derivations,
because it is separably algebraic over L. Equation (7) forces C=L.
Therefore B_L=P_L. The covering theorem is an explicit external
dependency; it is not inferred from a finite control.

Finally, B=P, not merely B_L=P_L. Express b in B as a finite polynomial
in the Fi with coefficients in L. If the minimum coefficient valuation
were negative, multiply by the opposite power of h and reduce modulo h.
A nonzero polynomial in the independent fi would become zero. Thus
all coefficients are in R0. This proves the theorem's equivalence of
the integral and generic finiteness conditions.

nodes.title: Polynomial curvature has a finite integral primitive
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

Write
\[
                 P_{ij}(F)=h^{-1}[T_i,T_j]\in B=P.         \tag{12}
\]
Jacobi and (6) show partial_i Pjk+partial_j Pki+partial_k Pij=0.
Thus the polynomial two-form with coefficients Pij is closed.
The radial polynomial homotopy gives
\[
 b_j(t)=\sum_i t_i\int_0^1 s\,P_{ij}(st)\,ds,\qquad
                     \partial_i b_j-\partial_j b_i=P_{ij}. \tag{13}
\]
The integral is coefficientwise finite: a monomial t^alpha receives
the denominator |alpha|+2, invertible in K. Commutativity of B and (6)
now give (4). If the classical Ti commute in the Poisson bracket,
[Ti,Tj]/h is zero modulo h. Independence of the fi makes P h-saturated
in E, so all coefficients Pij and bj are h-divisible.

For rank two one may instead choose the particularly simple primitive
\[
              b_1=0,\qquad b_2=\int P_{12}(t_1,t_2)\,dt_1. \tag{14}
\]
No h-pole correction or new spatial completion is needed.

For E the actual scalar finite-PBW algebra, this is a full bounded
quantum lift, so [QFL2](BOUNDED_REALIZATION.md) applies to a noninvertible
classical map. For a finite projective corner it supplies a full corner
action. This does not construct the required Long input or supply a
scalar free frame for an arbitrary projective carrier.

nodes.title: A certificate from leading Poisson geometry
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

Here is a sufficient all-degree gate for the generic finiteness
hypothesis. In the scalar Weyl algebra over L, use the Bernstein
filtration and put di=deg Fi and gi=sigma(Fi). Suppose the gi are
algebraically independent and their entire polynomial Poisson
centralizer is module-finite:
\[
 \operatorname{Cent}_{\{\,,\,\},L[x,p]}(g_1,\ldots,g_m)
               \text{ is finite over }L[g_1,\ldots,g_m].  \tag{15}
\]
Then gr(B_L) is a graded L[g]-submodule of that centralizer. Since
L[g] is noetherian, gr(B_L) is finite over L[g]. Lift homogeneous
generators to B_L and subtract their polynomial Fi combinations in
descending filtration degree. Degree decreases at every step, so
this terminates and proves B_L finite over P_L. No degree sweep is
used. The independence assumption ensures gr(P_L)=L[g].
The same argument works for another nonnegative algebra filtration
if its associated graded algebra is commutative and the stated
Poisson and finite-module hypotheses actually hold. A projective
idealizer does not acquire these filtration hypotheses automatically.

In rank two, leading-symbol independence also gives an explicit
correction bound. If ei=deg Ti and C=[T1,T2] is nonzero, then
\[
 \deg b_2\le\deg(C/h)+d_1\le e_1+e_2-2+d_1,\qquad
 \deg(T_2+b_2)\le\max(e_2,e_1+e_2-2+d_1).                 \tag{16}
\]
There is no cancellation of distinct top weighted monomials in P(F),
because the gi are independent. Integrating in t1 raises weighted
degree by d1; the Bernstein commutator drops degree by at least two.
The bound is conditional on the actual certificate (15), not on a
finite approximation to the full Poisson centralizer.

nodes.title: Why the finiteness gate is substantial
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFC1, the named sub-result states:

The escaping-boundary algebra in QSC1 has
B=R0[x,y,(1-h*x)^-1,(1-h*y)^-1]. It is finitely generated as an
R0-algebra and has polynomial formal centralizer, with individual
conjugates, but is not module-finite over R0[x,y] or after inverting h.
For example the valuation at 1-h*x is negative on its inverse,
whereas every element integral over the polynomial ring has
nonnegative valuation. Its nonzero curvature residue prevents
finite or rational flattening. It is an Ore boundary control, not
a subalgebra example in the finite Weyl algebra.

Even actual full Weyl relations and identity classical reduction
do not force the new finiteness hypothesis in all ranks.
For any Keller map f, the exact cotangent construction has
\[
 \operatorname{Cent}_{A_n}(f_1(x),\ldots,f_n(x))=K[x],
 \quad K[x]\text{ finite over }K[f]\ \Longleftrightarrow\
                                  f\text{ is an automorphism}. \tag{19}
\]
Indeed the Jacobian is invertible, so the leading differential symbol
of a positive-order centralizer element would have all its momentum
partials zero; hence every centralizer element has order zero.
Finiteness makes f a finite etale self-map of affine space, and the
same covering theorem makes it an automorphism. The converse is
immediate. The inverse-Jacobian conjugates commute already.

For a normalized f, rescale f_t=t^-1*f(t*x) and set t=h^N as in
QNI1. The classical position images become the identity, so (2) holds,
while the generic centralizer is still L[x]. Its module finiteness
over L[f_(h^N)] is equivalent to invertibility of f. Thus a universal
centralizer-finiteness assertion even in this planar identity-reduction
cotangent subclass would imply JC2. This is a precise obstacle to
deducing it merely from the Weyl relations. The rescaled full
identity examples in [QNI1](IDENTITY_LIFTS_AND_UNBOUNDED_INVERSES.md)
supply higher-rank instances where the relations, bounded forward
images and every desired finite identity contact hold but this
centralizer finiteness fails. This is not an equivalence between
JC2 and Long-specific finiteness, nor a cotangent normalization of
Long.

nodes.title: A self twist uses up inverse Fourier rank
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QKR1, the named sub-result states:

Let K be the Kummer line with residue 1/e at q=0, with e>=2, and
suppose
\[
                         E\simeq E\otimes K .                 \tag{3}
\]
No irreducibility assumption is needed for this part.
Put i_0=irr(V_0), and let N_reg be the rank of its slope-zero part.
Then
\[
           r(E)\ \ge\ N+i_0-\frac{N_{\rm reg}}e
                    \ \ge\ (1-1/e)N+i_0 .                   \tag{4}
\]
To prove this, the e pairwise nonisomorphic formal Kummer lines
1,K,...,K^(e-1) have the same Hom dimension into V_0, by (3).
That dimension is h_0. Their images give a direct sum of e*h_0
regular rank-one submodules. Distinct simple lines have no common
simple submodule; the corresponding evaluation maps are injective.
Thus e*h_0<=N_reg. Substitute in delta_0=N+i_0-h_0 and use (2).

Also e divides N, by taking determinants in (3). Every possible
self-twist order is covered by the same inequality. Neither local
regularity nor a bound on Stokes matrices is assumed.

For the quadratic twist, N=4 and r=2 is a rigid equality case.
It forces i_0=0, h_0=2, and the complete local module
\[
                       V_0\simeq 1^{\oplus2}\oplus
                                           K_{1/2}^{\oplus2}.
                                                               \tag{5}
\]
There are no nontrivial Jordan extensions: the four independent
line submodules already exhaust its rank. Every other finite
delta_x and rho_infinity must vanish. Thus there are no other
genuine finite singularities, and every slope at infinity is at
most one. This necessary condition does not construct such a
Long-compatible family.

nodes.title: Reducibility on a cyclic cover forces a self twist
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QKR1, the named sub-result states:

Assume now that E is irreducible and let pi(v)=v^d/d.
If pi^*E is reducible, then (3) holds for some nontrivial Kummer
character of order e dividing d. Here is the descent argument.

Restriction of an irreducible differential Galois representation
to a finite-index normal subgroup is semisimple: an irreducible
submodule exists, its finitely many conjugates span the original
representation, and that span is a sum of simple submodules.
Consequently a reducible restriction has more than scalar
horizontal endomorphisms.

The projection formula for the cyclic cover gives
\[
 \operatorname{End}_{\nabla}(\pi^*E)=
       \bigoplus_{j=0}^{d-1}
          \operatorname{Hom}_{\nabla}(E,E\otimes K_{j/d}).
                                                               \tag{6}
\]
The trivial character contributes only scalars. An additional
endomorphism supplies a nonzero Hom for a nontrivial character;
irreducibility makes that Hom an isomorphism. Equation (4) follows.
In particular
\[
 N>2r(E)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \pi^*E\text{ is irreducible for every cyclic power cover }\pi .
                                                               \tag{7}
\]

If E has at most one finite singularity, N>2r(E) also excludes
reducibility over every finite algebraic function-field extension.
Its Picard--Vessiot component cover is unramified away from that
singularity and infinity; Riemann--Hurwitz makes it cyclic, as in
[QFT1](RATIONAL_LINE_FOURIER_OBSTRUCTION.md). Translate the puncture
and apply (4). Translation does not change inverse-Fourier rank,
since it corresponds to a rank-one exponential twist on the other side.
This extension permits an irregular finite puncture.

With several finite singularities, arbitrary covers with additional
branch points need not give a Kummer self-twist. In that generality
(7) concerns cyclic power covers, not all finite extensions. This
distinction must be retained when testing higher-rank models.

nodes.title: Finite pushforward gives a direct test for an extracted branch
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QKR1, the named sub-result states:

Let L be any rank-m connection over k(v), and put E=pi_*L on the
unramified locus of q=v^d/d. Restriction of scalars gives rank N=d*m.
The projection formula gives E tensor K_(1/d) isomorphic to E,
since pi^*K_(1/d) is trivial. Therefore
\[
                    r(\pi_*L)\ge(d-1)m .                    \tag{9}
\]
If L is nonsingular at v=0, E has the d Kummer characters each
with multiplicity m there, h_0=m and irr_0=0. Its contribution
at q=0 is exactly (d-1)m. All other finite singularities and
slopes greater than one at infinity add nonnegative cost.

This result holds even when E is reducible. It does not infer
generic rank from a formal classical rank. The numerical rank
must be computed for the actual generic algebraic connection.
