nodes.title: An explicit family really does split in every polynomial degree
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QKR1, the named sub-result states:

Take g(a)=sum_(j=0)^m g_j*a^j with g_m nonzero and m>=1.
Put q=v^2/2, a=(h/v)*partial_v and
\[
 S_{\rm naive}=g(a)+2v,\qquad
 L_g=k(v)\langle a\rangle/
                  k(v)\langle a\rangle(S_{\rm naive}-s).
                                                               \tag{10}
\]
The source eigenvalue s is included in the constant field.
This is a rank-m connection in v. In the basis
1,a,...,a^(m-1), the ordinary v derivative has matrix
(v/h)*C(v), where C(v)=C0+v*C1 is the companion matrix of
g(a)+2v-s. This matrix is polynomial in v.
Consequently L_g extends nonsingularly across every finite v,
including v=0.

Its pushforward E_g has rank2m, has no finite singularity other
than q=0, and has local module
1^m direct_sum K_(1/2)^m there. At infinity its single slope is
\[
                      1+\frac1{2m}.
\]
Indeed g_m*a^m balances -2v, and a=(h/v)*partial_v.
The exponential phase in v has leading power 2+1/m;
on the q-line this becomes 1+1/(2m).
Equivalently the scalar operator below has a single Newton edge
balancing a^(2m) against q. Its 2m distinct leading exponential
factors form one ramification orbit. Standard formal Newton-polygon
theory therefore also makes E_g formally irreducible at infinity,
and hence generically irreducible. No bounded coefficient search
is used here.

Its infinity contribution in (2) is one. Thus the exact rank is
\[
                   r(E_g)=m+1,\qquad \operatorname{rank}E_g=2m .
                                                               \tag{11}
\]
After the quadratic cover, E_g splits into the two connections
g(a)+2v-s and g(a)-2v-s. This gives genuine algebraic extraction,
rather than merely a formal branch expansion.

For an explicit horizontal projector, use the restriction-of-scalars
matrix
\[
 H=\begin{pmatrix}
       C_0&2qC_1\\ C_1&C_0+hI/(2q)
    \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 V=\begin{pmatrix}0&2qI\\I&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
One has V^2=2qI and
h*partial_q V+[H,V]=hV/(2q). Since partial_q v=1/v,
\[
                e_\pm=\tfrac12(I\pm V/v)                    \tag{12}
\]
are idempotent horizontal projectors after q=v^2/2.
The image frames (I,+v^-1 I)^t and (I,-v^-1 I)^t
carry the matrices C0+v*C1 and C0-v*C1, respectively.

nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QKR1, the named sub-result states:

For m=2 the extracted positive operator is precisely
S_naive=4a-3ra^2+2v. It has differential order two, unit leading

[QSO2](QUADRATIC_OPERATOR_MATE_CLASSIFICATION.md) excludes this
for every finite partner order, on every finite algebraic coefficient
curve. In particular no extra partner terms, finite pole enlargement
or algebraic cover supply that missing action while S_naive is fixed.

More generally, QSO2 forces every bounded full scalar Long lift with
exact undeformed R into generic fiber order m>=3 for S.
For its spectral connection L=(S-s), the actual generic v rank is m.
Equation (9) therefore forces inverse-Fourier rank at least three.
A proposed rank-two model in this category fails before further
quantum corrections are attempted.

This last application assumes the bounded exact-R scalar reduction
used in QSO2. It does not normalize every deformed first image, supply
a scalar frame for every projective carrier, or exclude a nonpositional
full carrier.

The linear case is a positive full-pair control. For g=lambda*a+mu,
\[
 S=\lambda a+\mu+2v,\qquad
 T=-\lambda a^2/8-va/2-h/(4v)
\]
satisfy [S,T]=h exactly. This control and the QFT1 rank-one/rank-two
split keep the numerical inequality separate from the additional
Long mate obstruction.

An actual finite carrier must satisfy the rank budget,
the full right Weyl action, global admission and a finite-left lattice
together. Branch splitting alone is now explicitly achievable and
explicitly insufficient. The finite-left Long carrier in
the full compatible left/right module conditions and the bounded
scalar target remain open.

The rank inequalities and all-degree splitting construction are written
arguments above. The scalar classification's finite controls are retained
separately; no formal verification or independent external review is claimed.

nodes.title: An all-degree construction from any Keller map
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

Let K have characteristic zero and let
\[
 f: {\mathbb A}^n\longrightarrow{\mathbb A}^n,\qquad
 \det Df=1,\quad f(0)=0,\quad Df(0)=I.
\]
Any Keller map can be put in this form by affine changes.
For an independent parameter t set
\[
                    f_t(x)=t^{-1}f(tx),\qquad
                    A_t(x)=(Df_t(x))^{-1}.          \tag{1}
\]
Since f has no constant term, f_t is polynomial in t,x.
The inverse Jacobian is polynomial as well, by the adjugate
formula, and
\[
 f_0=x,\qquad A_0=I,\qquad Df_t(x)=Df(tx).           \tag{2}
\]
If deg f=d, then
\[
             \deg_x f_t\le d,\qquad
             \deg_x A_t\le(n-1)(d-1).              \tag{3}
\]
The scalar parameter t contributes no spatial degree.

In the finite PBW algebra over K[h,t] with [p_i,x_j]=h*delta_ij,
define
\[
 X_i=f_{t,i}(x),\qquad
 P_i=\sum_j(A_t)_{ji}(x)p_j.                         \tag{4}
\]
These satisfy every Weyl relation exactly:
\[
 [X_i,X_j]=[P_i,P_j]=0,\qquad [P_i,X_j]=h\delta_{ij}. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed the polynomial vector fields
delta_i=sum_j(A_t)_(ji) partial_(x_j) are dual to df_(t,i).
They satisfy delta_i(f_(t,j))=delta_ij and commute.
Their commutator kills all f_(t,j), and the invertible
Jacobian makes such a vector field zero. First-order
differential-operator commutators are exactly these vector
field brackets. Thus no quantum correction or infinite
recursion is needed for (5).

The resulting endomorphism Phi_(h,t) has common spatial bound
\[
              D=\max(d,(n-1)(d-1)+1).              \tag{6}
\]
If f is not invertible, its generic cotangent Weyl lift is
not surjective. This classical transfer is recalled, for
example, in Bavula,
[Holonomic modules and 1-generation in the Jacobian Conjecture](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/crmath.556.pdf).
The next argument supplies the exact implication needed here.

nodes.title: Differential order detects generic nonsurjectivity
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

Work over any characteristic-zero field in which h,t are
nonzero. Differential order in p is preserved by Phi:
the leading p-symbol is substituted through the invertible
matrix A_t(x), and coefficient substitution through f_t
is injective because its Jacobian is a unit. Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_p\Phi(Q)=\operatorname{ord}_p Q,\qquad
 \Phi(A_n)\cap K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]=K[f_{t,1},\ldots,f_{t,n}].
                                                               \tag{7}
\]
All fields in (7) can be extended to include the parameters.

If Phi were surjective, preimages of the standard positions
would have p-order zero. They would give polynomial inverse
coordinates for f_t. But f_t is conjugate to f by nonzero
scalar dilations, so this would make f invertible.
Conversely, a polynomial inverse of f gives the inverse
cotangent Weyl map. Thus
\[
                 \Phi\text{ surjective}
                       \Longleftrightarrow f\text{ invertible}.
                                                               \tag{8}
\]
This does not assume that a formal inverse is polynomial.

nodes.title: Arbitrarily high identity contact with fixed forward degree
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

Choose any integer N>=1 and specialize t=h^N. Then the
finite-PBW map
\[
                       \Phi_h=\Phi_{h,h^N}
\]
satisfies all relations (5), has the same spatial bound (6),
and
\[
                       \Phi_h=\operatorname{id}+O(h^N).
                                                               \tag{9}
\]
Its h-adic completion is an automorphism: the inverse of
the continuous linear map id+O(h^N) is its convergent
Neumann series. As Phi is an algebra map, that inverse
is an algebra map too. Every coefficient of every inverse
image is polynomial, since a fixed h-order uses finitely
many polynomial operations.

Nevertheless, for noninvertible f the generic finite-PBW
map is not surjective by (8). Its unique completed inverse
therefore has no common finite spatial bound.

This failure is visible explicitly on the positions. Let
\[
                    g(x)=x+\sum_{k\ge2}g_k(x)
\]
be the formal inverse at the origin of f, with g_k homogeneous
of degree k. Then
\[
                \Phi_h^{-1}(x)=h^{-N}g(h^Nx)
                      =x+\sum_{k\ge2}h^{N(k-1)}g_k(x). \tag{10}
\]
If only finitely many g_k were nonzero, the two formal inverse
identities would be polynomial identities, making f a
polynomial automorphism. Thus a noninvertible input gives
nonzero coefficients of arbitrarily high spatial degree in
(10). Increasing N postpones the failure to higher parameter
orders and leaves the forward bound unchanged.

nodes.title: A retained rank-three control of forward degree twelve
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

Use [F1's certified input](../../foundations/verified/FOUNDATIONAL_GEOMETRY.md).
With u=1+xy, write its outputs as
\[
 a=u^3z+y^2u(4+3xy),\quad
 b=y+3xu^2z+3xy^2(4+3xy),\quad
 c=2x-3x^2y-x^3z.
\]
Take
\[
                              f=(c/2,b,a).          \tag{11}
\]
It satisfies the normalization in (1), has component degrees
(4,6,7), and has the three distinct rational collision points
\[
 (0,0,-1/4),\quad (1,-3/2,13/2),\quad
 (-1,3/2,13/2)
\]
over the common value (0,0,-1/4). The retained F1 theorem
already establishes the determinant and collision; its
provenance is not reclassified by the present result.

For this input the inverse Jacobian column degrees are
(11,9,8), so the six Weyl images in (4) have degrees
\[
                             (4,6,7,12,10,9).        \tag{12}
\]
The common bound12 holds for every N. The scaled collision
points are the displayed points divided by t, with common
image (0,0,-1/(4t)). They belong to K((h)) when t=h^N,
so generic nonsurjectivity is exact.

Identity padding gives the same examples in every n>=3.
This does not descend from rank three to rank two. Higher-rank
Weyl counterexamples are already known; the new use here is
as a fully compatible control for proposed bounded comparison
and inverse arguments.

nodes.title: Even completed graph isomorphism does not give a bounded gauge
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

For N>=2 the completed automorphism in (9) is inner by an
h-adic unit:
\[
                       \Phi_h(a)=U a U^{-1},\qquad
                       U\in1+h^{N-1}\widehat A.     \tag{13}
\]
Here is the precise formal input. At a first difference of
order k>=N, the linearized full Weyl relations form a closed
polynomial one-form. Polynomial H1 vanishes, as in
[QFL1](PROOF.md), so that difference is a normalized
Hamiltonian derivation. Remove it by conjugation with
exp(h^(k-1)*G_k). Since k>=2 this exponential is an h-adic
unit. The successive product converges, proving (13).
No finite spatial bound on U, or on the inverse map, follows.

Let M_Phi be the algebraic graph bimodule: its underlying left
module is the regular finite PBW algebra A and its right
action is m*a=m*Phi_h(a). It is left free of rank one and
carries the full right Weyl action. It is a coherent bimodule,
being cyclic over the Noetherian algebra A tensor A^op.

Multiplication m to mU is an isomorphism from its completion
to the completed identity graph, by (13). Generically M_Phi
is not an invertible bimodule: invertibility would make the
right-action map A^op to End_left(M_Phi)=A^op an isomorphism,
forcing Phi to be surjective. The identity graph is invertible.
Thus these algebraizations cannot be compared by bounded
source and target Weyl automorphisms. Surjectivity is preserved
by every such two-sided change.

This is stronger than a failure of finiteness for a selected
lattice: both left modules here are already free, and the full
right actions exist. It does not contradict any uniqueness
theorem requiring prescribed arithmetic support. The common
classical h=0 map does not prescribe that support.

nodes.title: Two consequences for degree and jet arguments
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

At t=0 with h=1, (4) is the identity of a fixed Weyl algebra;
for generic t it is not surjective. Hence the automorphism
locus in a bounded-degree endomorphism scheme need not be
open at the identity. The same conclusion holds at the
classical identity point in QFL2's h-relation scheme, after
the degree-nonincreasing change from normal to Weyl symbols.
Its automorphism locus being closed does not imply openness.

For every m, the reduction of (9) modulo h^m is an automorphism,
by a finite Neumann series. Their inverse degrees are unbounded
as m grows, by (10). Thus an inverse-degree theorem over
fields or reduced rings cannot be applied to all these
nonreduced jets. Any fixed inverse bound for all the jets
would give a common bound for the unique completed inverse,
contradicting (8).

nodes.title: The rank-two comparison gap contains JC2
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QNI1, the named sub-result states:

For fixed n and N>=2, consider the statement P_(n,N):

> Every exact finite-PBW Weyl assignment over K[[h]] equal to
> the identity modulo h^N has a finite-PBW inverse.

For characteristic-zero fields, with the usual passage from
finitely generated coefficient fields to C,
\[
                    {\rm DC}_n\ \Longrightarrow\
                    P_{(n,N)}\ \Longrightarrow\ {\rm JC}_n.
                                                               \tag{14}
\]
For the first implication, DC makes the generic Weyl map an
automorphism. QFL2's valuation argument, applied to its
injective identity reduction, puts its finite inverse
coefficients back in K[[h]]. For the second implication,
apply P to (1)--(9) for an arbitrary normalized Keller map
and use (8). Over C one can state all three assertions over
that field; a generic counterexample over a coefficient
field extension yields one over C by the standard
finitely-generated-field argument of QFL2.

Restricted to the cotangent rescalings (1), the inverse or
bounded-comparison assertion is equivalent to JC_n. If f is
invertible, its normalized inverse g gives the polynomial
inverse family t^{-1}g(tx), regular at zero. Conversely (8)
recovers invertibility of f.

Accordingly, a universal bounded gauge comparison for full
identity lifts is not a routine consequence of formal
Hamiltonian equivalence. It is false in every n>=3 and,
even on the cotangent subclass in n=2, would settle JC2.
No equivalence P_(n,N) to DC_n is claimed, and no assertion
P_(2,N), JC2 or DC2 is proved or refuted here.

nodes.title: The classical joint centralizer
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSC1, the named sub-result states:

Use the actual global Long R,S and the retained rational canonical
chart from [QPH1](QUINTIC_PHASE_AND_BRANCH_OBSTRUCTION.md). Put
r=R, v=X^-1, with conjugate momentum a and parameter momentum d:
\[
 A_0[X^{-1}]=K[r,v,v^{-1},a,d],\quad
 \{d,r\}=1,\quad\{a,v\}=1/v,\quad
 s=S=g(r,a)+2v,\quad g=4a-3ra^2.                            \tag{1}
\]
The other chart brackets vanish. This is an equality of localized
polynomial algebras, not only an equality of their fraction fields.
The inverse expressions for X,Q,P,Z in QPH1 are Laurent in v.

Replacing v by (s-g)/2 gives the ring
K[r,s,a,d,(s-g)^-1]. Commutation with r first removes d.
On the remaining ring the Hamiltonian of s is
\[
                 \{s,-\}=-\frac4{s-g}\partial_a
                     \quad\hbox{with r,s held fixed}.     \tag{2}
\]
Its fraction-field kernel is K(r,s). The intersection
K[r,s,a,(s-g)^-1] intersect K(r,s) is exactly K[r,s]:
a reduced denominator in K[r,s] would have to divide a power
of s-4a+3ra^2. But no nonconstant element of K[r,s] divides
that polynomial, whose a-linear coefficient is the unit -4.
It follows that
\[
                       \operatorname{Cent}_{\{,\}}(R,S)
                                      =K[R,S].             \tag{3}
\]
No bound on a potential invariant, and no assumption on its
momentum order, enters this proof. This is a special feature
proved for this pair, not a theorem for all Lagrangian pairs.

nodes.title: Every commuting quantum deformation has commutative centralizer
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSC1, the named sub-result states:

Let A_R be the finite PBW h-Weyl algebra over R0=K[[h]], and
Ahat its h-adic completion. Let F1,F2 in Ahat commute, with
classical reductions R,S. Their complete joint centralizer is
\[
 Bhat=\left\{\sum_{j\ge0}h^j P_j(F_1,F_2):
                                  P_j\in K[u_1,u_2]\right\}.
                                                               \tag{4}
\]
Indeed a centralizer element has classical reduction in (3).
Subtract its corresponding polynomial in the commuting F_i,
divide by h, and repeat. Algebraic independence of R,S makes
this representation unique. Conversely every such series
commutes with both F_i. In particular Bhat is commutative.

This argument permits arbitrary h-small corrections to both
images. It uses no positional normalization, scalar differential
order, finite Fourier comparison or prescribed arithmetic support.
The finite or generic algebraic centralizer can be strictly smaller
than (4), but it is commutative whenever it embeds faithfully there.
It is not automatically K[[h]][F1,F2].

nodes.title: Finite projective carriers retain this commutativity
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSC1, the named sub-result states:

For a finite idempotent corner e*Mat_s(A_R)*e with e mod h=e11,
the completed left module is free of rank one. Its completed
corner identifies with Ahat. The finite corner embeds faithfully
in its completion, since its matrix coefficients are h-separated.
If two right images reduce to R,S, their finite joint centralizer
is therefore commutative by (4). No finite conjugating frame is
being inferred.

More generally, consider a rank-one torsion-free generic left module P
over the Weyl algebra A=A_R tensor K((h)), with a finite h-lattice M whose
completion is free of rank one. The same conclusion holds for its generic
endomorphism algebra under these explicit hypotheses. Here is the
faithfulness argument.
An embedding P into A is obtained by a fractional-ideal realization.
After clearing h poles on finitely many generators of its lattice M,
there is an injection M into A_R. Thus M is h-separated.

Every generic endomorphism of P, multiplied by a sufficiently high
power of h, preserves M. It extends to its free completion. If that
extension is zero, separatedness makes it zero on M, hence on P.
Consequently the generic algebra E=End_A(P)^op embeds faithfully
in Ahat[h^-1]. Its centralizer of the two Long right images is
commutative by (4).

A partial finite-left module does not automatically meet the
rank-one, torsion-free or faithfulness hypotheses. Nor does
formal left freeness imply generic left finiteness; QGM1 remains
the countercontrol. The carrier consequence uses the stated QMC1
hypotheses and its external generic-projectivity dependency.

nodes.title: Universal spectral translation classes in the actual algebra
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSC1, the named sub-result states:

Let E be a unital characteristic-zero algebra with central
nonzerodivisor h, and fix two commuting elements F1,F2.
The generic version has h invertible; integral applications
below use h-torsion-free algebras. Introduce central
spectral parameters u1,u2 and set
\[
 {\cal M}=E[u_1,u_2]\big/
       \big(E[u](F_1-u_1)+E[u](F_2-u_2)\big).               \tag{5}
\]
As a left E-module this is the regular module E: right evaluation
sends sum a_ij*u1^i*u2^j to sum a_ij*F1^i*F2^j.
The parameter ui acts by right multiplication by Fi.

The two commuting monic expressions Fi-ui have the free Koszul
resolution. Exactness follows successively by monic division in
the central variables, which gives injectivity at each step.
Applying Hom(-,M) gives the finite-algebra complex
\[
 E\xrightarrow{d_0}E^2\xrightarrow{d_1}E,\qquad
 d_0(T)=([F_1,T],[F_2,T]),\quad
 d_1(A,B)=[F_1,B]-[F_2,A].                                 \tag{6}
\]
Thus its cohomology computes the spectral self-Ext groups.
The closed vectors (h,0) and (0,h) define canonical classes alpha1,
alpha2 in H1. They vanish exactly when there are elements T1,T2
of the actual E satisfying
\[
                      [F_j,T_i]=h\,\delta_{ij}.            \tag{7}
\]
These are finite elements when E is the finite operator algebra
or finite corner; completing E changes the question.

Equivalently, right multiplication by Ti defines an E-linear
spectral connection with [nabla_i,ui]=h. This is a relative
connection interpretation of the explicit Koszul calculation.
For a finite projective left Weyl module P, use P[u] in the same
resolution. Its self-Ext complex has coefficients End_A(P)^op,
so the criterion is independent of a free left frame.

The connection viewpoint is standard context; compare the
[principal-parts sequence](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09CN)
and the canonical first-order classes in
[Lauritzen--Thomsen, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.16636).
No identification with that paper's Hochschild class, or with QRF2,
is asserted. The calculation (5)--(7) is direct.

nodes.title: The full completion obstruction is one curvature class
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSC1, the named sub-result states:

Assume alpha1=alpha2=0, choose T_i satisfying (7), and suppose
B=Cent_E(F1,F2) is commutative. This is now known for Long pairs
under the hypotheses above. Put
\[
 C=[T_1,T_2]\in B,\qquad
                 \delta_i(b)=[T_i,b]\quad(b\in B).         \tag{9}
\]
Jacobi gives preservation of B and
[delta1,delta2]=ad_C=0 on B.
Every other choice of individual mates is Ti+bi with bi in B.
Because B is commutative,
\[
 C\longmapsto C+\delta_1 b_2-\delta_2 b_1,\qquad
 [C]\in B/(\delta_1 B+\delta_2 B).                          \tag{10}
\]
The derivations on B are independent of the choice of Ti.
Hence the quotient and curvature class are canonical for the pair
once the two translation classes vanish.

All four Weyl relations are realizable in E exactly when
alpha1,alpha2 vanish and the class in (10) is zero. This is an
all-partner criterion: there is no degree, pole or order cutoff.
It does not supply the commuting pair F_i in the first place.

Actual algebra isomorphisms transport the complex, B, derivations
and curvature class. This includes finite Weyl coordinate changes,
with the images transported too, and changes of a projective frame.
The result uses an actual finite algebra, without selecting a
position-field or pseudodifferential completion.

If B=K((h))[F1,F2], curvature can always be removed finitely.
Here delta_i=-h*partial_(Fi), and choose
\[
         b_1=0,\qquad
         b_2=\frac1h\int C(F_1,F_2)\,dF_1.                 \tag{11}
\]
For polynomial degree at most N in the F_i this primitive has
degree at most N+1. If the F_i have spatial degree at most D,
the correction has spatial degree at most D*(N+1).
This is a sufficient bound given the polynomial representation
of C; it does not bound N from a formal representation alone.

For h-regular finite Long images and h-regular individual mates,
(4) makes (11) possible coefficientwise in the completion.
Commutators are divisible by h, so C/h has an integral formal
centralizer expansion. Generic mates with h poles use its Laurent
version; integrality is not asserted for those choices. If the
h-regular classical individual mates are already flat, the
correction can be h-small and preserve them.
The resulting series need not belong to the actual B.
Thus the algebraic curvature class vanishes after completion,
without being proved zero before completion.

nodes.title: Matrix padding with scalar positions adds no completion freedom
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSC1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose Fi*I_m are the two position images and arbitrary finite
matrices Ui in Mat_m(E) satisfy
[ Fj*I_m,Ui ]=h*delta_ij*I_m and [U1,U2]=0.
Assume B=Cent_E(F1,F2) is commutative. Then the normalized traces
\[
             T_i=\frac1m\operatorname{tr}_{\rm matrix}(U_i)
                                                               \tag{12}
\]
are already a full scalar completion in E.

To prove the mixed relation, write Ui=Ti*I_m+Bi.
Every entry of Bi belongs to B, and tr(Bi)=0.
Taking normalized trace of [U1,U2] gives
\[
 0=[T_1,T_2]
   +\tfrac1m\operatorname{tr}([T_1I,B_2]+[B_1,T_2I])
   +\tfrac1m\operatorname{tr}[B_1,B_2]=[T_1,T_2].            \tag{13}
\]
The middle terms vanish by tracelessness; the last vanishes
because the matrix coefficients belong to the commutative B.
Ordinary matrix trace does not have this property for arbitrary
noncommutative coefficient algebras.

Consequently fixed Long scalar positions admit a matrix completion
if and only if they admit a scalar one. The normalized trace
does not increase spatial degree and preserves h regularity.
A bounded full formal matrix lift with scalar position images
and Long's classical graph would therefore yield a bounded scalar
lift, and QFL2 would give its nonsurjective Weyl realization.

For a projective carrier the scalarization takes place in E,
not automatically in a scalar Weyl algebra. Stafford's generic
two-copy frame may make both positions genuinely matrix-valued.
No free rank-one frame or scalar DC2 consequence is obtained
from the existence of an arbitrary projective carrier alone.
The QPH1 phase has a genuinely nonscalar S, so (12) does not
apply to it.

Identity Weyl stabilization also preserves completion of the
fixed positions. Add spectator positions y_j. Any mate of an
old Fi must commute with every y_j, hence has no spectator
momentum terms and belongs to E[y]. Evaluation y=0 is an
algebra homomorphism and gives an old flat completion.
Conversely an old completion extends by the identity pairs.
This does not normalize all deformed positions into a fixed pair.

nodes.title: Normalization and the universal differential polynomials
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSO2, the named sub-result states:

Extend the constants to an algebraic closure C and choose a component
of the coefficient field after constant extension. The constants of a
nonzero derivation on a one-variable function field over C are exactly C.
Derivations extend uniquely to algebraic field extensions.

Writing P=a_2 D^2+... and Q=b_m D^m+..., the coefficient of order m+1
in the commutator is 2a_2 delta(b_m)-m b_m delta(a_2). Adjoin
rho=sqrt(a_2), set E=rho D and replace its derivation by epsilon=rho delta.
Then P is monic, and Q's leading coefficient b_m/rho^m is constant.
The coefficient-preserving Ore change E -> E-ell_1/2 removes the linear
coefficient ell_1 of P. Hence we may work with L=E^2+u and primes
meaning epsilon. No assumption about an algebraic primitive of 1 is used.

Use the differential-polynomial algebra C[u,u',u'',...] with derivative
partial. Define R_j by B(s)=sum_{j>=0} R_j s^j, R_0=1/2, and
\[
       4B^2-4usB^2-2sBB''+s(B')^2=1.
\]
At each positive s-degree the new coefficient is 4R_j plus known
terms, so this defines differential polynomials uniquely. Differentiation
and cancellation of the unit 2B give the Lenard identity
\[
       R_{j+1}'=\tfrac14R_j'''+uR_j'+\tfrac12u'R_j.              \tag{4}
\]
For example R_1=u/4 and R_2=(u''+3u^2)/16. Each R_j has weight 2j
for wt(u^{(i)})=i+2, with
\[
 R_j=4^{-j}u^{(2j-2)}+\cdots,\qquad
 [u^j]R_j=\beta_j=\frac{\binom{2j}{j}}{2\,4^j}\ne0
                 \quad(j\ge1).                               \tag{5}
\]
The first coefficient follows inductively from (4); setting all
derivatives to zero gives B=1/(2sqrt(1-us)) and the second coefficient.

Define the finite monic odd operators
\[
 B_{2j+1}=\sum_{\ell=0}^j(2R_\ell E-R_\ell')L^{j-\ell}.
\]
Direct Ore multiplication gives
\[
 [L,2RE-R']=4R'L-(R'''+4uR'+2u'R).
\]
Using (4), the sum telescopes:
\[
                         [L,B_{2j+1}]=-4R_{j+1}'.               \tag{6}
\]

nodes.title: Every odd mate supplies a forced Painleve hierarchy
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSO2, the named sub-result states:

For any finite Q with [L,Q] scalar, its highest positive-order
coefficient is constant, by the next coefficient of its commutator.
Subtract that constant times L^{m/2} at even order m, or B_m at odd
order m. Both subtractions retain a scalar commutator. Repetition
ends in a scalar coefficient whose derivative must vanish. Hence
\[
 Q=A(L)+\sum_{j=0}^g c_j B_{2j+1},\qquad c_j\in C,              \tag{8}
\]
where a nonzero commutator requires at least one odd summand.
If the remaining highest odd order is 2g+1, take c_g nonzero.
Equations (1) and (6) imply
\[
       \tau=-\frac4\kappa\sum_{j=0}^g c_j R_{j+1}(u),
                       \qquad \tau'=1.                        \tag{9}
\]
Thus the relation itself creates an algebraic time coordinate. The
coefficient field is finite over C(tau). For g>=1, an algebraic u
would solve
\[
      \sum_{j=0}^g c_jR_{j+1}(u)=\alpha\tau+\beta,\qquad
                   c_g\ne0,\quad\alpha\ne0.                    \tag{10}
\]
Allowing beta and arbitrary lower constant c_j will be useful below.

nodes.title: Integer indicial exponents at every hierarchy pole
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSO2, the named sub-result states:

Write z=tau-tau_0. A pole u~a z^p with p<0 in (10) must have p=-2.
For p<-2 the pure power u^{g+1} is uniquely most singular. For
-2<p<0 the highest linear derivative u^{(2g)} is uniquely most
singular. To see both assertions in every order, a weight-2j monomial
with m factors of u and its derivatives has exponent
m(p+2)-2j. Its extreme is m=j or m=1 respectively.

At p=-2 put
\[
 R_j(az^{-2})=C_j(a)z^{-2j},\qquad
 C_j(a)=\beta_j\prod_{\ell=0}^{j-1}(a+\ell(\ell+1)).
\]
This follows from (4), which gives
C_{j+1}=(2j+1)(a+j(j+1))C_j/(2j+2), starting with C_0=1/2.
The leading coefficient of (10) forces
\[
                         a=-k(k+1),\qquad1\le k\le g.           \tag{11}
\]

Define d_j(a,rho) by linearizing at this pole:
\[
 DR_j[az^{-2}](z^{\rho-2})
                         =d_j(a,\rho)z^{\rho-2j}.
\]
Here d_1=1/4. Linearizing (4) gives the exact recurrence
\[
\begin{split}
(\rho-2j-2)d_{j+1}
 &= (\rho-2j-1)
       \left(\frac{(\rho-2j)(\rho-2j-2)}4+a\right)d_j\\
 &\quad+\frac{\rho-4j-2}{2}C_j(a).                             \tag{12}
\end{split}
\]
In particular the last numerator is rho-4j-2, not rho-2j-2;
the variation of both u R_j' and u' R_j/2 contributes.

We prove all the needed roots are integers without assuming a
closed resonance formula. At u_k=-k(k+1)z^{-2}, X_k=0, while for
0<=m<k the lower field X_m is a nonzero constant times z^{-2m-3}.
Commutativity of X_k and X_m gives
\(\partial(DR_{k+1}[u_k]\,X_m)=0\). By homogeneity the expression being
differentiated has strictly negative z-degree, so it is zero.
Consequently d_{k+1} has the k roots -1,-3,...,-(2k-1).

Set T=DR_{k+1}[u_k], an operator of order 2k with leading coefficient
4^{-(k+1)}. Homogeneity gives T=z^{-2k}p(z partial), with
p(s)=d_{k+1}(a,s+2). Formal selfadjointness and
(z partial)^*=-z partial-1 imply
p(s)=p(2k-1-s). The roots of d_{k+1} are therefore paired by
rho -> 2k+3-rho. The k reflected roots and k negative roots are
distinct and exhaust its degree 2k. Hence
\[
 d_{k+1}(-k(k+1),\rho)
   =4^{-(k+1)}
       \prod_{m=0}^{k-1}(\rho+2m+1)(\rho-(2k+4+2m)).             \tag{13}
\]
For j>=k+1, C_j(-k(k+1))=0, so (12) becomes
\[
 d_{j+1}
   =\frac{(\rho-2j-1)(\rho-2j-2k-2)(\rho-2j+2k)}
                 {4(\rho-2j-2)}\,d_j.                         \tag{14}
\]
Every displayed zero or possible pole is at an integer. Thus
d_{g+1}(-k(k+1),rho) is nonzero for every noninteger rho.
No convergence or full analytic Painleve property has been assumed.

nodes.title: Algebraic solutions cannot exist
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSO2, the named sub-result states:

Suppose u is algebraic over C(tau) and satisfies (10), with g>=1.
Use a Puiseux expansion at a finite tau_0. At a pole, (11) gives
the leading term. If its first nonintegral exponent is rho-2,
then rho>0 is noninteger. At the first fractional order in (10),
the highest hierarchy term contributes
c_g b d_{g+1}(-k(k+1),rho)z^{rho-2g-2}, with b nonzero.
Earlier integer terms cannot cancel it, lower hierarchy terms
have larger exponents, and terms using more than one fractional
correction also have larger exponents. Equations (13)--(14)
make its coefficient nonzero, a contradiction.

At a finite point where u is finite, a first noninteger exponent mu>0
contributes through 4^{-(g+1)}u^{(2g)}. The falling factorial
mu(mu-1)...(mu-2g+1) is nonzero. All nonlinear derivative monomials
and all lower hierarchy terms have strictly larger first fractional
exponents. This is again impossible.

Every branch at every finite point therefore has integral exponents.
The minimal function field C(tau,u) is unramified at every finite
tau, since its generating element u has all its branches in C((z)).
If its degree is d, its genus is G and it has r points over infinity,
[Riemann--Hurwitz](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0C1B) gives
2G-2=-d-r. This forces d=r=1 and G=0. Thus u is rational.

A rational u with positive integer pole degree m at infinity has
u^{g+1} as the unique term of highest degree, namely (g+1)m>1.
Indeed for a weight-2j monomial its degree is m times its number
of factors minus its total derivative order, strictly smaller than
jm unless it is the pure power. Lower hierarchy terms also have
smaller degree. If u is bounded at infinity, every term on the left
of (10) is bounded. Neither case can equal alpha*tau+beta with
alpha nonzero. This proves the all-hierarchy algebraic exclusion.

nodes.title: A valued order-drop obstruction with unrestricted partner order
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QSO2, the named sub-result states:

Let O be a discrete valuation ring in a one-variable algebraic
differential function field F over characteristic-zero constants.
Assume delta(O) is contained in O, so reduction defines differential
operators. Suppose P,Q belong to O[D;delta], satisfy (1), and:
P has generic order exactly two, its leading coefficient a_2 is a
valuation unit, and the reduction of Q has odd order at least three.
Then no such pair exists. The reduction of kappa may be zero.

Here is the argument that covers every generic partner order at once.
If Q has even order 2j, comparison at order 2j+1 gives
\[
          c=b_{2j}/a_2^j\in\ker(\delta)\cap O.
\]
The unit hypothesis ensures c is regular. Subtract c P^j.
The commutator and coefficient regularity persist and the order
strictly drops. Generic odd orders at least three are excluded by
the theorem. The process must end at order one, so
\[
 Q=A(P)+Q_1,\qquad A\in(\ker(\delta)\cap O)[t],
                     Q_1\in O[D;\delta],\quad\operatorname{ord}Q_1=1.
                                                                    \tag{15}
\]
After reduction, a nonconstant surviving A(P) has even order, because
the reduction of P still has order two and a nonzero leading
coefficient. The remaining summand has order at most one and cannot
cancel that leading even term. If no nonconstant A survives, the
reduction has order at most one. Either outcome contradicts the
assumed odd order at least three.

No estimate for ord(Q) is used. No square root of a unit in O is
needed: the normalization cover belongs only to the characteristic-zero
theorem; the regular even-power subtraction occurs in the original O.

nodes.title: Valuations on the quantum rational function fields
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Let K have characteristic zero, F=K((h)), and let A be the finite PBW
algebra over F on n canonical pairs, with
[p_i,x_j]=h*delta_ij and the other generator commutators zero.
Write Q=Frac(A) for its Ore division ring.

For a finite PBW sum define v as the minimum h valuation of its
scalar coefficients. It is multiplicative: normalized nonzero factors
reduce to nonzero commutative polynomials, because every commutator
is divisible by h. Hence v extends to Q, with value group Z, central
uniformizer h, and residue field
\[
                   \overline Q=K(x_1,\ldots,x_n,p_1,\ldots,p_n).
                                                               \tag{1}
\]
Indeed every rational function in the commuting residue variables is
the residue of a fraction of finite PBW polynomials. Let Qhat be the
valuation completion; it remains a division ring, with this residue
field. The usual geometric-series inverse proves the division claim.

Let psi be a polynomial symplectic endomorphism of affine 2n-space.
Its Jacobian is a unit, so its coordinate functions are algebraically
independent and the induced function-field extension is finite. Put
\[
 \delta=[K(x,p):K(\psi(x,p))].
\]
Let Phi be any full formal lift of psi, with polynomial coefficients
at each h order, as in [QFL1](PROOF.md). Its images belong to Qhat even
if their spatial degrees are unbounded. A finite source PBW polynomial
with its least scalar valuation removed has a nonzero classical
polynomial reduction; its image reduces to that polynomial evaluated
at psi, which is nonzero. Thus substitution preserves valuation.

It follows that Phi embeds the source Weyl division ring into Qhat
and extends isometrically to its completion. Denote the resulting
complete image by Ehat. Its residue field is exactly K(psi(x,p)).
When Phi has common finite spatial support, its images lie in A
over F; write E=Phi(Q) inside Q. In that case Ehat is also the
completion of this uncompleted image division ring. Without finite
support we do not claim E is a subring of Q.

nodes.title: A complete extension has the residue degree
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Here is the general valued-division-ring statement used throughout.

Suppose Ehat is a complete valued division subring of a complete
valued division ring Qhat. Both have value group Z with the same
central uniformizer h, and both residue division rings are fields.
If their residue extension has finite degree delta, then
\[
           [\widehat Q:\widehat E]_\ell
             =[\widehat Q:\widehat E]_r=\delta.                 \tag{2}
\]
Choose lifts b_1,...,b_delta of a residue-field basis.
They form a basis on either side. More precisely,
\[
 v\left(\sum_i b_i e_i\right)=\min_i v(e_i),\qquad
 v\left(\sum_i e_i b_i\right)=\min_i v(e_i).                    \tag{3}
\]
For a nonzero sum, remove its minimum h power and reduce. Residue
linear independence forbids cancellation. This proves (3) and
independence.

For spanning, first multiply an element by a power of h to give
nonnegative valuation. Expand its residue in the chosen basis with
coefficients in the residue of Ehat, and lift those coefficients
to elements of Ehat of nonnegative valuation. Subtract this finite
sum; the remainder has valuation at least one. Repeat after division
by h. For each basis element the successive coefficients converge
in Ehat. Completeness and (3) give the desired expansion. The same
construction on the other side proves both assertions.

No assertion about algebraicity of an arbitrary formal operator
coefficient is needed. This is a theorem about the completed
division rings, not about finite differential orders.

Consequently every full formal lift of psi has completed division
degree delta, without a spatial bound. Formal Hamiltonian gauge
equivalence alone cannot distinguish these completed degrees.

nodes.title: Finite PBW images give finite uncompleted indices
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose now that Phi has common spatial degree bound D. Its finite
PBW generic map has generator degrees at most D, so
Phi(A_{\le t}) is contained in A_{\le Dt} for the Bernstein
filtration. Both uncompleted indices obey
\[
       [Q:E]_\ell\le D^{2n},\qquad [Q:E]_r\le D^{2n}.             \tag{4}
\]
Here is a direct proof, independent of the new index-symmetry theorem.

Take m right E-linearly independent elements of Q. A common left
denominator puts all of them in A and preserves independence.
Call them b_i, and bound their Bernstein degrees by M. The
K((h))-linear spaces b_i*Phi(A_{\le t}) form a direct sum in
A_{\le M+Dt}. Therefore
\[
 m {t+2n\choose 2n}\le {M+Dt+2n\choose 2n}.
\]
Divide by t^{2n} and let t tend to infinity; this gives m<=D^{2n}.
An arbitrarily large independent set is impossible. For left
independence, use a common right denominator and the spaces
Phi(A_{\le t})*b_i. This proves (4) on both sides.

The same residue independence argument as (3), using basis lifts
chosen in Q, gives
\[
                    \delta\le[Q:E]_\ell,\ [Q:E]_r.             \tag{5}
\]
Lauritzen--Thomsen's cited Corollary 8.11 says that Weyl division
rings in characteristic zero are index-symmetric. With that
external theorem, the two finite indices agree; denote them by N:
\[
                         \delta\le N\le D^{2n}.                \tag{6}
\]
Finiteness, the individual bounds, and the completed-degree formula
do not depend on index symmetry.

nodes.title: The exact condition for equality
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Let O_Q and O_E be the valuation rings inside Q and E, respectively;
these are the elements of nonnegative h valuation. They are not
the polynomial PBW algebras. In particular, they contain fractions
whose reductions are arbitrary rational functions.

The following conditions are equivalent:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
{\rm (i)}&[Q:E]_r=\delta;\\
{\rm (ii)}&O_Q\text{ is finitely generated as a right }O_E
                       \text{-module};\\
{\rm (iii)}&\text{lifts of any residue basis form a right }E
                       \text{-basis of }Q.
\end{array}                                                    \tag{7}
\]
The corresponding left statements hold independently.

To prove (i) implies (iii), residue basis lifts are independent
by (3), so their number equals the dimension. Their valuation
formula also gives
O_Q=sum_i b_i O_E directly, proving (ii). Conversely O_E is a
local discrete valuation ring, possibly noncommutative, with
maximal ideal h O_E: a valuation-zero element has its inverse
inside O_E, and every nonzero element is h^k times a unit.
Moreover
\[
                    O_Q/hO_Q=\overline Q
\]
has dimension delta over O_E/hO_E. If O_Q is finitely generated,
Nakayama's lemma makes any lifts of a residue basis generate O_Q.
Inverting h makes them span Q over E, while (3) gives independence.
This proves (7). One can prove the Nakayama step directly by the
usual minimal-generator argument, since 1-hu is a unit in O_E.

There are also surjective linear maps
\[
 Q\otimes_E\widehat E\longrightarrow\widehat Q,\quad q\otimes e
                  \longmapsto qe,\qquad
 \widehat E\otimes_E Q\longrightarrow\widehat Q,\quad e\otimes q
                  \longmapsto eq.                            \tag{8}
\]
Surjectivity follows from the lifted residue basis in Q.
Their kernel dimensions are [Q:E]_r-delta and [Q:E]_ell-delta
over Ehat on the appropriate side. The tensors in (8) are vector
spaces; no tensor-product ring structure is asserted.

nodes.title: Application to every full Long lift
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Use the actual Long polynomials in the [retained source checker](../dixmier-audit/verify_long_pbw.py).
The rational coordinate change is displayed explicitly here:
\[
 r=R,\quad v=1/x,\quad a=v+Y,\quad d=D,\qquad
 s=2v+4a-3ra^2,\quad t=(ra^3-a^2-va)/2.
\]
The four variables r,v,a,d are birational coordinates in the
ambient classical function field. Explicitly,
\[
\begin{split}
 x&=1/v,&q&=(2v-rv^2)/3,&Y&=a-v,\\
 \beta&=5v^2-rv^3-3av,&M&=\beta+9q^2,&D_0&=d-H(x,Y,\beta),\\
 p&=3q^2 M+2(1-3xq)D_0,&
 z&=(1+3xq)M/2-3x^2D_0 .
\end{split}                                                     \tag{9}
\]
Here H is Long's retained correction, so d=D_0+H.
The two linear equations for p,z have determinant -1; hence
(9) is a rational inverse, not a claimed canonical coordinate
change. In particular d is independent of r,v,a.

We have
\[
 v=(s-4a+3ra^2)/2,\qquad
                  ra^3-2a^2+sa+4t=0.                         \tag{10}
\]
Over K(r,s,d), the output t is a polynomial of degree three
in the transcendental a. Thus the full classical function-field
degree, including the fourth image, is exactly three. Adding
the independent d does not change it.

Equations (2), (4), and (5) prove:
\[
 [\widehat Q:\widehat E]_\ell
  =[\widehat Q:\widehat E]_r=3,\qquad
 3\le[Q:E]_\ell,\ [Q:E]_r\le D^4.                             \tag{11}
\]
The first conclusion holds for every full formal Long lift.
The bounds apply whenever it has common spatial bound D.
There is no exact-R, positional-first-image, scalar-order,
ordering, or partner-degree hypothesis in (11).
With the cited index-symmetry theorem both finite indices are N.

This rules out a birational quantum division realization of Long,
but not a finite realization with N>=3. The statement controls
fraction division fields; it is weaker than surjectivity of the
finite Weyl algebra.

nodes.title: What bounded canonical changes preserve
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Precomposing a finite Weyl map with a Weyl automorphism leaves
its image division subring unchanged. Postcomposing transports
the extension by an ambient division automorphism. Hence the
individual uncompleted indices are invariant under arbitrary
finite source and target Weyl automorphisms.

For changes regular at h=0 whose inverses are regular and whose
classical reductions are polynomial canonical automorphisms,
the completed degree delta is preserved as well. Thus the
differences [Q:E]_r-delta and [Q:E]_ell-delta are invariants
under these changes.

Adding identity canonical pairs preserves both indices. For
example, adjoin spectator Weyl generators commuting with Q.
A right E-basis of Q remains independent over the spectator
extension E': clear a common denominator in E', expand in
spectator PBW monomials, and use independence in Q at each
coefficient. Its span over E' is stable under left multiplication
by Q and all spectator generators. Every nonzero such operator
acts injectively on this finite-dimensional right E'-space and
hence surjectively, so adjoining inverses does not enlarge it.
It spans the whole extended division ring. The left proof is
the same. The classical degree is preserved by adjoining
independent variables, so the differences are stable too.

These invariants are not invariant under arbitrary formal
Hamiltonian gauges. The next full example demonstrates that
distinction with every relation intact.

nodes.title: A full polynomial control: completed degree one, generic degree three
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

We first record a general differential-field fact. Let L/B be
a finite separable function-field extension of degree m in
characteristic zero. Suppose commuting derivations on B extend
to L and generate the same ambient rational differential-operator
field. Then the extension of quotient differential-operator
division rings has left and right degree m.

Indeed choose a field basis b_i of L/B. Their right span over
the smaller operator division ring is preserved by L and all
derivations, using
partial_j*b_i=b_i*partial_j+partial_j(b_i).
Every nonzero operator preserves this finite-dimensional space
injectively, hence surjectively, so its inverse also preserves
it. Thus the basis spans the ambient division ring. For
independence, clear a common denominator in the smaller operator
ring and compare PBW derivative coefficients, using the original
field basis. The left argument is identical. This proof applies
to any number of commuting derivations and to nonzero scalar h
multiplying them.

Apply this to the cotangent lifts in
[QNI1](IDENTITY_LIFTS_AND_UNBOUNDED_INVERSES.md).
For its retained three-variable map put u=1+xy and denote
the unnormalized outputs by A,B,C. On x!=0 set
w=y+1/x and rho=2/x. Then
\[
 A=w^2+\rho w/2-Cw^3,\qquad B=\rho+4w-3Cw^2,
\]
so
\[
 \rho=B-4w+3Cw^2,\qquad Cw^3-2w^2+Bw-2A=0.                  \tag{12}
\]
Over K(B,C), A is a cubic polynomial in the independent w.
The function-field degree is exactly three. The output
normalization (C/2,B,A) and scalar source and target dilations
do not change it.

QNI1 sets f_t=t^-1*f(tx), t=h^N for any N>=1, and takes its
inverse-Jacobian cotangent Weyl operators. It has all full
rank-three relations, common forward degree twelve, and
classical reduction the identity. Its generic division degree
is three by the differential-field fact, since nonzero t is
invertible in K((h)). Its completed degree is one by (2).
Thus each kernel in (8) has dimension two, and neither
valuation lattice in (7) is finite.

nodes.title: A rank-one rational control with arbitrary extra degree
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QDI1, the named sub-result states:

Let F=K((h)), Q=D_1(F), and use [p,x]=h.
For integers m>d>=1 set
\[
 f=x^d+hx^m,\qquad g=\partial_x f,\qquad
                       U=f,\quad V=g^{-1}p.                  \tag{13}
\]
Then [V,U]=h exactly. Both images are finite rational-coefficient
differential operators and are regular for the h Gauss valuation;
g reduces to d*x^{d-1}, a nonzero element of the residue field.

Over F, [F(x):F(f)]=m. Replacing the differential generator p by
g^-1*p and applying the preceding differential-field argument
gives uncompleted left and right division indices m. The
classical map is
\[
                     (x,p)\longmapsto
                  (x^d,p/(d x^{d-1})),
\]
of function-field degree d. Its completed degree is d by (2).
Thus d=3 gives completed degree three and every generic degree
m>3. The differences m-3 are unbounded.

The ordinary polynomial equation hX^m+X^d-u=0 explains where
the extra branches lie. Over the h-valued coefficient field
with u of valuation zero, its lower Newton polygon has a
horizontal segment of length d and a segment of slope
1/(m-d), length m-d. The latter roots have negative valuation
-1/(m-d). Completion at the selected Gauss valuation retains
the degree-d part.

This is a control for a general comparison theorem, not a
Long lift: the coefficients have x denominators, and the
classical map has a position-preserving form already excluded
for Long. A Long-specific global argument might exclude its
boundary mechanism. Generic index symmetry alone cannot.

nodes.title: The vector space cokernel records a necessary commutator condition
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QZM1, the named sub-result states:

Let A be an algebra over a characteristic-zero field K, V a left
A-module, and L,b in A. Suppose e in V satisfies
\[
       Le=0,\qquad
           \omega(L,V,e;b)=[be]\in V/LV .                    \tag{1}
\]
The quotient here is a K-vector-space cokernel; LV need not be an
A-submodule. If an operator T in A satisfies [L,T]=b, then
\[
                         be=L(Te),\qquad \omega=0.           \tag{2}
\]
Thus a nonzero class excludes every such T at once. No order,
coefficient-degree or matrix-size search is involved in this identity.

In particular take L=S-c and b=kappa, with kappa a nonzero
scalar constant. A Weyl mate [S,T]=kappa is excluded provided
[c,T]=0 and [e] is nonzero. The commutation with c is automatic
when c is scalar. When c is a function of another prescribed
image R, it is part of the full mixed-relation requirement.

nodes.title: Trace makes the class survive every finite coefficient cover
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QZM1, the named sub-result states:

Let F be a characteristic-zero differential field and E/F a finite
algebraic extension. Derivations extend uniquely. Each field embedding
into a normal closure therefore commutes with those derivations, so
normalized trace commutes with every finite differential operator over F:
\[
   \tau=\frac1{[E:F]}\operatorname{Tr}_{E/F},\qquad
          \tau P=P\tau,\qquad \tau|_F=\operatorname{id}.       \tag{3}
\]
Consequently F/PF -> E/PE is injective.

More generally, for any differential F-module V, the componentwise
map tau tensor id retracts E tensor_F V onto V and commutes with
the base-extended action. It therefore retracts the corresponding
vector-space cokernel. A nonzero class over F cannot acquire a
primitive on a finite algebraic coefficient cover.

For an inhomogeneous equation Pf=g over F, any algebraic solution
would yield the rational/base-field solution tau(f).
This is a linear statement. It does not assert that trace preserves
nonlinear quantum correction equations, specified spatial supports,
or a prescribed integral lattice.

nodes.title: Transport the module together with the canonical change
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QZM1, the named sub-result states:

For an actual algebra automorphism Phi:A->A, define V_Phi to have
the same vector space as V with action
a*v=Phi^(-1)(a)v. Then Phi(L) acts exactly as L on that vector
space and Phi(b)e acts as be. Thus
\[
 \omega(\Phi(L),V_\Phi,e;\Phi(b))
                          =\omega(L,V,e;b).                 \tag{4}
\]
For a finite Weyl automorphism this transports the class through
Fourier changes and polynomial Weyl shears. It is essential to
transport the module: after Fourier transformation the appropriate
module need not be the usual coefficient-function representation.
Changing the coefficient localization is a separate operation and
can kill a supported vector. In the Fourier control below, the new
position x annihilates e, so inverting that position would kill e.
The trace statement concerns finite extensions of an already valid
differential coefficient field; it does not justify this additional
localization.

Identity stabilization uses V tensor_K W for any nonzero module
W of the spectator Weyl algebra. Since L acts only on the first
factor, its cokernel is (V/LV) tensor_K W. A nonzero class remains
nonzero. Further actual finite canonical automorphisms, even ones
mixing the old and spectator pairs, are covered by (4).

This statement requires an actual algebra automorphism defined on
the algebra in question. A classical Poisson change without a proved
finite quantum action is not silently assumed to act. If an operator
belongs only to a rational coefficient localization, an arbitrary
polynomial Weyl automorphism need not preserve that localization.
For globally admitted operators, use the ambient Weyl module and
clear coefficient denominators as below.

nodes.title: A cyclic module gives a deformation interpretation
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QZM1, the named sub-result states:

For a domain differential-operator algebra D and L=S-c nonzero,
put M=D/DL and e=1 modulo DL. Right multiplication by L gives
the free left-D resolution
\[
 0\longrightarrow D\xrightarrow{\ \cdot L\ }D
             \longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0,\qquad
             \operatorname{Ext}^1_D(M,M)=M/LM .              \tag{5}
\]
The class [e] is the first-order eigenvalue-deformation class:
the relation (L-epsilon)e_epsilon=0 over epsilon^2=0 gives
L*e_epsilon=epsilon*e_epsilon. A finite commutator mate makes
that class zero by (2).

The standard relation between self-extensions and first-order
connection deformations is discussed in
[Arinkin, Section4.4](https://arxiv.org/html/0808.0699).
The particular identification (5) follows directly from the displayed
resolution. No rigidity or global lifting theorem is imported.

This is a necessary obstruction, not a complete mate criterion.
Vanishing of the class supplies neither a finite commutator identity
nor all the other right Weyl actions.

nodes.title: A complete all-degree linear coefficient exclusion
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QZM1, the named sub-result states:

Work over C(v), where C has characteristic zero, h is a nonzero
constant and a acts as (h/v)*partial_v. Let
\[
 S=v(\lambda a+\mu)+G(a),\qquad
 \lambda\ne0,\qquad G\in C[a],\quad\deg G=m\ge1 .             \tag{6}
\]
Then S has no finite scalar T with [S,T]=kappa a nonzero
constant, over any finite algebraic function-field extension.

Put alpha=-mu/lambda and apply the coefficient-preserving Ore
automorphism a->a+alpha. Subtract c=G(alpha). The transformed
operator is
\[
 P=\lambda va+\sum_{j=1}^m c_j a^j,\qquad c_m\ne0,\qquad
                              P1=0 .                       \tag{7}
\]
A mate would therefore give an algebraic coefficient function
\[
                        f=T1,\qquad Pf=\kappa.              \tag{8}
\]
By (3) it suffices to exclude rational f in C(v).

If m=1, equation (8) is
df=(kappa/h)*v/(lambda*v+c1) dv. At v=-c1/lambda its residue is
\[
                         -\frac{\kappa c_1}{h\lambda^2}
                                      \ne0 .                \tag{9}
\]
A rational derivative has zero residues, a contradiction.
The trace argument has already covered every finite algebraic cover.

Suppose m>=2. Away from v=0 the ordinary differential leading
coefficient of P is c_m*h^m*v^(-m), which is nonzero.
A rational pole of f there would give a uniquely highest pole
from the m-th derivative; it cannot match a constant forcing.
At v=0, if the first pole term is b*v^beta with beta<0, use
\[
 a^j v^\beta=
 h^j\beta(\beta-2)\cdots(\beta-2j+2)v^{\beta-2j}.              \tag{10}
\]
The j=m term has uniquely lowest exponent and nonzero coefficient.
No pole at zero is possible either. Thus f must be a polynomial.

For a nonconstant polynomial f of degree N, lambda*v*a lowers
its degree by one and every a^j term lowers it by at least two.
Equation (8) forces N=1 and f=(kappa/(lambda*h))*v+constant.
Substitution leaves
\[
 Pf-\kappa=
 \frac{\kappa}{\lambda h}
  \sum_{j=1}^m c_jh^j
       \prod_{t=0}^{j-1}(1-2t)\,v^{1-2j}\ne0 .               \tag{11}
\]
The j=m term is nonzero and has strictly lowest v power.
This proves [1] nonzero in C(v)/PC(v), and proves the theorem
for every polynomial degree m and every finite mate order.

nodes.title: Relative parameters and globally admitted canonical pairs
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QZM1, the named sub-result states:

The auxiliary value c may depend on a prescribed exact first image
R=r. The rational chart has [a,q]=[d,r]=h, q=v^2/2.
For alpha=alpha(r), the coefficient representation on K(r,v)
extends to the full chart by
\[
 a\mapsto(h/v)\partial_v+\alpha(r),\qquad
 d\mapsto h\partial_r+q\alpha_r .                             \tag{13}
\]
The mixed commutator vanishes because
alpha_r=(1/v)*partial_v(q*alpha_r).

The action of the original global generators uses the
[retained rational canonical chart](QUINTIC_PHASE_AND_BRANCH_OBSTRUCTION.md).
Suppose R,S are globally admitted finite Weyl operators and their
localized form is (6), with coefficients rational in r.
Write c(r)=g(r)/f(r), with nonzero polynomial f and polynomial g
over the generic scalar field. Use the finite polynomial operator
\[
             L=f(R)S-g(R),\qquad b=h f(R).                   \tag{14}
\]
Its coefficient zero mode is e=1. A full partner satisfying
[S,T]=h and [R,T]=0 would have [L,T]=b.
But its class [b e] is nonzero: multiplication by f(r) is
invertible in the coefficient field and the cokernel computation
is linear over that field of differential constants.

Consequently this actual quantum pair obstruction survives
every finite target Weyl automorphism and identity stabilization
by (4). This conditional global statement requires admission of
R,S themselves. It does not claim that every rational-chart
formula is globally polynomial, nor normalize every deformed R.

nodes.title: Rational canonical coordinates matching the retained Long map
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

Write the original Weyl generators as X,Q,P,Z, with
[P,X]=[Z,Q]=h. Put
\[
 \begin{split}
 r&=X(2-3XQ),\quad v=X^{-1},\quad q=v^2/2,\\
 F&=3v-\tfrac53rv^2+\tfrac13r^2v^3,\\
 a&=-X^3P-\tfrac23X(1-3XQ)Z+F,\\
 G&=-\tfrac5{12}v^4+\tfrac2{15}rv^5,\qquad
 d=-Z/(3X^2)+G .
 \end{split}                                                    \tag{1}
\]
These are finite rational operators on X!=0. All coefficients are
on the left. The cotangent vector fields commute, and
G_v=v F_r, so the gradient shifts give exactly
\[
 [a,q]=[d,r]=h,\quad [a,v]=h/v,\quad
               [d,v]=[d,a]=[r,v]=[r,a]=0.                     \tag{2}
\]
No h correction is omitted in (1). First-order normal-operator
commutators equal their Poisson brackets.

Define g=4a-3ra^2. The retained classical Long fiber is
\[
 s_+=g+2v,\qquad
 t_+=(ra^3-a^2-va)/2,\qquad
 D_+=d+a^4/4-3ra^5/10+va^3/2.                                \tag{3}
\]
The canonical fourth-coordinate expression in (3) equals the
actual corrected Long D, not its uncorrected cubic D0.
Substitution in the retained formula verifies this identity;
it is also checked against QPL1's retained classical seed.

nodes.title: The polynomial phase and its exact Fourier module
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

Use an auxiliary position s and the quintic polynomial
\[
 \mathcal F(r,s,a)
   =-\frac{as^2}{8}+\frac{a^2s}{2}-\frac{ra^3s}{4}
       -\frac{2a^3}{3}+\frac{3ra^4}{4}
       -\frac{9r^2a^5}{40}.
 \qquad
 \mathcal F_a=-\frac{(s-g)^2}{8}.                             \tag{4}
\]
For the phase mathcal F+a*q the critical equation is
q=(s-g)^2/8. On q=v^2/2 this has branches s=g+2v and s=g-2v.

There is no need to assume an oscillatory integral exists.
On finite polynomials in a,s with coefficients in K[r][[h]],
define left actions
\[
 a_{\rm left}=a,\qquad
 q_{\rm left}=-h\partial_a-\mathcal F_a,
 \quad
 s_{\rm right}=s,\qquad
 t_{\rm right}=h\partial_s+\mathcal F_s .                     \tag{5}
\]
Right operators compose in the opposite order as linear maps.
Thus (5) gives [a,q]=h on the left and [s,t]=h on the right;
the two actions commute by equality of mixed derivatives.

This is the partial Fourier transform of a polynomial exponential
module. The formal stationary-phase viewpoint is standard; compare
[Fang](https://msp.org/pjm/2011/254-1/pjm-v254-n1-p08-p.pdf) and
[Etingof--Kazhdan--Polishchuk, Section2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0003009v2).
Those papers are context, not an algebraization or splitting theorem
being applied here. The formulas and subsequent proofs are direct.

The module is free of rank two on the left over the q,a Weyl algebra,
with basis 1,s. Indeed q raises s degree by two with nonzero leading
coefficient 1/8; its derivative term and every remaining term have
smaller s degree. Leading-degree induction gives generation by 1,s
and proves independence in all degrees.

nodes.title: Four finite matrices satisfying every full relation
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

All matrix products below use the q,a Weyl product, [a,q]=h.
Abbreviate
\[
 c_0=8q-g^2,\quad t_0=a^2/2-ra^3/4,\quad
                       c=3a^4/4-9ra^5/20.
\]
The right fiber matrices and its parameter connection are
\[
 S=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\c_0&2g\end{pmatrix},\quad
 T=\begin{pmatrix}
 t_0&-a/4\\h-ac_0/4&t_0-ag/2
 \end{pmatrix},\quad
 C=\begin{pmatrix}
 c&-a^3/4\\-a^3c_0/4&c-a^3g/2
 \end{pmatrix}.                                               \tag{6}
\]
Expressions such as ac_0 have the indicated noncommutative order.
The connection h*partial_r+mathcal F_r commutes with the left q,a
actions and the right s,t actions. In the basis 1,s its matrix
part is C. Equivalently,
\[
 [S,T]=hI,\qquad [C,S]=hS_r,\qquad[C,T]=hT_r.
\]
Adjoin the independent left canonical pair r,d and set
\[
                         R=rI,\qquad D=dI-C.                  \tag{7}
\]
Then [D,R]=[S,T]=hI and all four mixed commutators vanish exactly.

Equations (6)--(7) give a homomorphism A_2 -> Mat_2(A_2), with
polynomial entries in this chart. It is not an endomorphism of
Mat_2(A_2): no commuting matrix-unit system is supplied. On replacing
the chart by (1), its coefficients are finite Laurent operators in X.
Its left rank is two, rather than QMC1's required rank one.

nodes.title: Why the algebraic fiber cannot separate its branches
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

Let L be any finite algebraic function-field extension of
K(r)((h))(v), with the derivation delta=(1/v)*partial_v extended
uniquely. Set O=L[a;h delta]. It is a left and right Euclidean
differential-operator ring. Work with the left module O^2 and its
right action (6).

Give its row basis weights 0,2. Right S has order at most two,
and right T has order at most three. Their leading graded matrices
are
\[
 \sigma_2(S)=
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-9r^2\xi^4&-6r\xi^2\end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 \sigma_3(T)=
 \begin{pmatrix}-r\xi^3/4&-\xi/4\\
                 9r^2\xi^5/4&5r\xi^3/4\end{pmatrix}.
 \quad
 \det\sigma_2(S)=9r^2\xi^4,\quad
 \det\sigma_3(T)=r^2\xi^6/4.                                  \tag{8}
\]
The displayed degrees include the basis shifts. Both determinants
are nonzero over the generic field r!=0.

Suppose N is a nonzero right-invariant rank-one left submodule.
Euclidean ideal theory makes N=O*w for a nonzero row w.
Write wS=P*w and wT=Q*w with finite scalar operators P,Q in O.
Additivity of the weighted order gives orders at most two and three.
The invertible matrices (8) prevent the leading row symbol from
being killed, so these orders are exactly two and three.

The full right relation gives [P,Q]=h. This contradicts
the [quadratic finite-mate theorem](QUADRATIC_OPERATOR_MATE_CLASSIFICATION.md), which excludes such
scalar operators over every algebraic coefficient curve and cover.
Therefore no such N exists. A rank-one quotient would have a
rank-one kernel and is equally excluded.

In fact this fiber bimodule is simple. A proper same-rank submodule
would have a torsion quotient over O, hence finite dimension over L.
Right S,T would act L-linearly on that quotient; taking traces in
[S,T]=hI forces its dimension to vanish. The only other possible
nonzero submodule rank was one, already excluded.

nodes.title: The obstruction also excludes full rank-one extraction
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

In the full chart let B=K((h))(r)[v,v^-1][a;h delta] and
mathcal A=B[d;h partial_r]. Suppose a rank-one left submodule of
mathcal A^2 is stable under the right R,S,T (and hence possibly D).
Left r and right R=rI show it is stable under differentiation
with respect to d. In the d-left PBW order the finite Taylor
projection sum_k (-d)^k*(partial_d)^k/k! extracts the constant
coefficient and preserves the submodule. Applying it after each
d derivative extracts all coefficients.

Consequently the submodule is induced from its d-free part N0,
which is a rank-one left B-submodule stable under S,T.
Localizing the position coefficients gives the forbidden rank-one
O-submodule above. Thus full algebraic submodules or direct summands
cannot isolate the Long branch either. This assertion concerns this
particular full matrix model, not every algebraization of its formal
branch.

nodes.title: Keeping both branches prevents global classical admission
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

In the chart X!=0 the second classical branch has
s_-=g-2v=s_+-4/X. The first branch s_+ is the actual polynomial Long S.
Thus the second branch has an unavoidable pole at X=0, and
\[
                    \operatorname{tr}S_0=2s_+-4/X             \tag{9}
\]
has a pole too.

There is no finite module over the normal ring K[X,Q,P,Z],
with this generic classical two-branch action and preserved by S.
The determinant trick would make both eigenvalues integral over
that ring. They belong to its fraction field, so normality would
make them polynomials, contradicting the pole of s_-.
This rules out a global finite-left flat carrier retaining both
classical branches of this model. It says nothing comparable about
a different carrier with only the Long classical graph.

nodes.title: Formal splitting gives a different global scalar Long lift
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

Let a row branch generator be (-g+L,1). Its S-invariance is equivalent
to the Riccati identity
\[
             L^2+[g,L]=4v^2,\qquad
             L=2v+\sum_{n>=1}h^nL_n.                         \tag{10}
\]
At each new h order the unknown coefficient is multiplied by 4v,
a unit in the chart. Thus there is a unique polynomial-in-a
coefficientwise solution over K[r,v,v^-1][[h]].

The negative branch starts at -2v and is constructed identically.
Their two row generators have an invertible classical determinant
4v. They therefore form a formal basis diagonalizing S.
Its two diagonal reductions differ by 4v. The off-diagonal
equations from [S,T]=hI and [D,S]=0 have an invertible leading
coefficient, forcing T,D to be diagonal too. The positive scalar
full tuple is
\[
 \begin{split}
  R_h&=r,\qquad S_h=g+L,\\
  T_h&=(ra^3-a^2)/2-La/4,\\
  D_h&=d+a^4/4-3ra^5/10+La^3/4 .
 \end{split}                                                   \tag{11}
\]
It satisfies every full Weyl relation in all orders, and (3) is its
complete classical tuple.

A finite-order L would have order at most one: for order m>=2,
L^2 has order 2m while [g,L] has order at most m+1, so (10) is
impossible. But the first two recurrence steps give
\[
 L_1=(3ra-2)/v^2,\qquad
       [a^2]L_2=-45r^2/(4v^5)\ne0.                            \tag{12}
\]
Thus even allowing arbitrary completed position coefficients, this
normalized branch vector has unbounded momentum. Algebraic
non-splitting above remains stronger for arbitrary algebraic frames.

nodes.title: All-order global admission and sharp growth
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

Write eta=ra and chi=rv. The recurrence in (10) gives
\[
 L_n=v^{1-3n}P_n(\eta,\chi),\qquad
 P_n\in\mathbb Q[\eta,\chi],\quad
 \deg P_n\le n,\quad\operatorname{ord}_a L_n\le n.              \tag{13}
\]
The polynomials are read with chi coefficients on the left of eta.
Here is an induction covering every order. In a normal product,
k contractions differentiate a k times and v by delta^k.
They contribute r^k*v^(-2k)=chi^k*v^(-3k).
For an h^n product the common factor is v^(2-3n).
Differentiating P in eta and multiplying chi^k does not increase
its degree. The first-derivative commutator with g raises degree
at most one from P_(n-1); its second derivative contributes one
chi from P_(n-2). Dividing the recurrence by 4v proves (13).

Both eta and chi are global polynomial operators in (1), and
v^(1-3n)=X^(3n-1). Hence every positive S correction is global.
Also a=X^-1+A with A a global first-order operator.
The normal coefficients of a^k have X pole order at most k:
the vector-field part of A has X component -X^3, so differentiating
a pole does not increase it.

The product P_n(eta,chi)*a^k has pole order at most n+k.
Its prefactor X^(3n-1) clears those poles for k=1,n>=1 and
for k=3,n>=2. This proves global admission of every positive T
term and all D terms from n=2 onward. The only remaining terms
are the finite base plus h*L1 terms in S,T,D-D0.
The retained Fraction seed checks their full normal-order
globality, including all their internal h corrections.
No later admission calculation is needed.

The coefficient of eta^n in P_n is c_n, where
\[
 c_1=3,\qquad
 c_n=-\frac14\left(
       \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}c_i c_{n-i}
           +6(3n-4)c_{n-1}\right)\quad(n>=2).                 \tag{14}
\]
The highest a-order terms in (10) give this recurrence.
Induction yields sign(c_n)=(-1)^(n-1), so c_n never vanishes.
In particular c2=-45/4 and c3=405/4.

nodes.title: The phase obstruction survives every finite polynomial g deformation
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

The quadratic-order proof is not the limit of this construction.
Let k be any characteristic-zero constant field, h a nonzero element,
and let g(a) in k[a] have arbitrary degree m>=1. Write G'=g and H'=g^2,
and use
\[
       \mathcal F_g=-as^2/8+sG(a)/4-H(a)/8,\qquad
       (\mathcal F_g)_a=-(s-g(a))^2/8.                        \tag{16}
\]
The Fourier module (5) is again left free of rank two over k<q,a>.
It has no proper nonzero right-invariant left submodule after
q=v^2/2 and after any further finite algebraic coefficient cover.
This includes every finite-degree g_h with classical reduction
4a-3ra^2: higher a powers multiplied by arbitrary positive powers
of h do not evade this phase-model obstruction.

Here is an all-degree proof independent of QSO1. Over k[a,s] the
rank-one polynomial exponential connection is simple: undo its
polynomial gradient shift of the derivatives, and a nonzero
polynomial ideal stable under both derivatives contains 1.
Partial Fourier transformation is an algebra automorphism, so
the Fourier module is simple too.

Regard that module instead over k[q,s]. Its operator q raises
a degree by 2m with nonzero leading coefficient g_m^2/8; all
other terms, including -h*partial_a, have smaller a degree.
Thus 1,a,...,a^(2m-1) form a free k[q,s] basis. Multiplication
by a and h*partial_s+mathcal F_s give an integrable connection
with polynomial matrices on the whole affine (q,s) plane.
It has no finite singularities and is generically irreducible.

We use the following elementary characteristic-zero fact.
A generically irreducible nonsingular flat algebraic connection
on affine space remains irreducible over every finite algebraic
extension of its function field. Over C, an algebraic horizontal
subspace over such an extension can be transported using a global
analytic fundamental matrix: affine space is simply connected and
the flat connection has no finite singularities. Its resulting
Grassmannian-valued map is single-valued on the entire affine space.
Its Plucker-coordinate ratios are algebraic meromorphic functions
and have trivial monodromy. They are rational: the normalization
of their algebraic function field would otherwise give a connected
finite covering with more than one branch over the complement of
its branch locus, whereas a single-valued branch is fixed by all
monodromy. Connectedness of that covering forces a single branch.
The horizontal subspace therefore descends to the original rational
function field, contradicting irreducibility. General characteristic
zero follows by descent of the finite coefficients to a finitely
generated field and an embedding into C. This does not assume
regular singularity at infinity. For differential-module and
monodromy background see
[Singer, Sections3 and6](https://arxiv.org/html/0712.4124).
Section6, immediately after Proposition9, gives the same entire-function
argument for connectedness in one variable; the affine-plane subspace
argument used here is written out above.

nodes.title: What this closes and what remains
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPH1, the named sub-result states:

The quintic phase gives an actual finite full matrix representation,
rather than a left module missing its right action. Its rank is two
and its second classical branch prevents global finite-left admission.
After the needed position cover, no algebraic rank-one extraction
exists in any finite coefficient cover. Formal extraction does exist
and yields the globally admitted but unbounded Riccati lift (11).

This closes the direct plan of extracting an algebraic rank-one
Long carrier from this phase form, including via a projective
summand and after any finite polynomial g_h deformation. The
nonconstant polynomial connection has an all-degree obstruction
independent of the special order-two/order-three classification. It does not exclude another algebraic model of the same
formal Long branch, just as QGM1 distinguishes a bad model from
intrinsic nonalgebraizability. The scalar and matrix targets in
the full finite-carrier conditions remain open.

The matrices, irreducibility and branch arguments above are the retained
written proof. The scalar-mate package retains complementary finite controls.
No new bounded Long lift, formal verification or external review is claimed.

nodes.title: Set-up and the classical Long coefficient
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

Let k have characteristic zero, let h be the central deformation parameter,
and initially work with constants in k((h)). Source positions and r may
be included in the constant field for the a-variable analysis. Let
chi_h(a) be rational in a, regular in h valuation, with reduction
\[
             \chi_0(a)\in k[a],\qquad \deg_a\chi_0=\ell>=3.
                                                               \tag{1}
\]
The coefficient field may itself be a function field such as K(r,s);
finite algebraic constant extensions cause no difficulty.

Consider the rank-one rational differential module represented by
h*partial_a+chi_h, and take its simple minimal extension M to the affine
a-line. Our sign convention under Fourier transformation is
\[
  a\longmapsto h\partial_q,\qquad h\partial_a\longmapsto-q.
\]
Thus the corresponding exponential-module presentation has
q_left=-h*partial_a+chi_h. For the Long phase in QPH1,
\[
             \chi_0=(s-4a+3ra^2)^2/8,\qquad \ell=4
                            \quad\hbox{over }K(r,s).          \tag{2}
\]
The geometric target chart then uses q=v^2/2.

**Theorem.** The Fourier transform of M is a nonzero connection on a
dense position open set. Its differential module over k((h))(q) remains
irreducible after algebraic closure of constants and every finite
algebraic function-field extension. Consequently no algebraic projector
can select a proper generic branch after q=v^2/2 or after any additional
finite coefficient cover.

The assertions are about a simple line connection and its minimal
extension. The algebraic full right action is still required separately
for a carrier. Additional compatible right actions cannot produce a
projector absent already for this connection.
