nodes.title: Remove apparent line poles before counting rank
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

After algebraic closure of constants, a finite simple pole has
\[
                          \chi_h/h=\alpha/(a-c)+\cdots .
\]
If alpha is an integer, replace the rational frame by (a-c)^alpha
times that frame, removing this apparent pole. The resulting gauge is
rational. Repeat at every apparent regular pole. Irregular poles remain.

A rational frame change f changes chi_h by
-h*(partial_a f)/f. It does not change the reduction in (1):
normalize f by a scalar of its h valuation. Its leading rational
coefficient is nonzero, so
\[
                     v_h((\partial_a f)/f)>=0.               \tag{3}
\]
This also holds after a finite ramified extension of the scalar
parameter field. Poles moving to infinity do not invalidate it.

Let the resulting rational coefficient be
\[
       \widetilde\chi_h=P(a)+B(a)/A(a),\qquad
       \deg B<d:=\deg A,\quad \gcd(A,B)=1.                    \tag{4}
\]
Every remaining regular pole has nonintegral residue and every irregular
pole is genuine. The polynomial part P is unchanged by rational gauges.

For this cleaned line module a cyclic presentation of its minimal
extension is
\[
 D_a/D_a L,\qquad
       L=A(a)h\partial_a+A(a)P(a)+B(a).                       \tag{5}
\]
Here D_a is the one-variable polynomial Weyl algebra over the generic
constant field.

We spell out why cleaning is necessary. At a pole of order j>=2,
the coefficient B(c) is nonzero. On a finite derivative-of-delta vector
the B(c) term has the highest delta-derivative degree, while
(a-c)^j*partial_a lowers it. Thus L has no kernel on a delta module,
so there is no point-supported quotient. Its formal adjoint has the
same nonzero constant term there and excludes point-supported submodules.
At a simple pole the corresponding leading coefficient is proportional
to alpha-n-1 on the n-th delta derivative; the adjoint replaces alpha
by 1-alpha. Nonintegrality excludes both possibilities.

nodes.title: A nonconstant polynomial part gives no finite singularities
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

The normal-ordered Fourier operator associated to A*h*partial_a+C is
\[
 \widehat L=-q A(h\partial_q)-h A'(h\partial_q)
                                  +C(h\partial_q).           \tag{6}
\]
If P in (4) has degree m>=1, then C=AP+B has degree d+m.
The transformed operator has order d+m and nonzero constant leading
coefficient. Consequently the entire Fourier module is a nonsingular
polynomial connection on the affine q-line. Fourier transformation is
an equivalence, so it is irreducible.

It remains irreducible after finite algebraic covers. A nonsingular
connection has a fundamental matrix of entire functions over C.
Every algebraic element of its Picard--Vessiot field is meromorphic
and unramified on the affine line, hence rational. Thus its differential
Galois group is connected. Finite algebraic base change cannot reduce
that connected group or split its irreducible representation.
The same argument and finite-coefficient descent were used in QPH1.

For the standard Picard--Vessiot finite-part theorem and the entire-function
argument, see [Singer, Corollary3.10 and Section6 after Proposition9](https://arxiv.org/html/0712.4124).
We use the standard Galois correspondence; no independent verification
of all the results in that source is asserted.

nodes.title: A constant polynomial part gives one finite singularity
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

It remains to handle P=c, including c=0. Replace q by z=q-c.
Then (6) becomes
\[
 \widehat L=-z A(h\partial_z)-h A'(h\partial_z)
                                      +B(h\partial_z).       \tag{7}
\]
Its order is d, with leading coefficient -A_d*h^d*z.
There is exactly one possible finite singular point, z=0.
Since all normalized coefficients have at most a simple pole there,
it is regular singular.

If d=0 the original cleaned coefficient is constant. It cannot satisfy
(1), because its rational degree and its reduction degree are zero.
In fact d>=ell: the rational function c+B/A has degree d, while
reduction of a rational function cannot increase its degree.
To verify this last statement even when c or pole locations have
parameter poles, choose a coprime numerator and denominator and
normalize their h valuations. Since the quotient has valuation zero,
their reductions are both nonzero. Cancellation on reduction only
decreases the rational degree. Equation (3) preserved chi_0, so
\[
                       N:=\operatorname{rank}\widehat M
                                   =d>=\ell>=3.              \tag{8}
\]

Let beta=B_(d-1)/(h*A_d), with beta=0 if that coefficient vanishes.
The indicial polynomial of (7), up to a nonzero scalar, is
\[
 \lambda(\lambda-1)\cdots(\lambda-d+2)
                                  (\lambda+1-\beta).        \tag{9}
\]
Only the top two differential coefficients contribute: the coefficient
of partial_z^(d-1), after normalization, has residue d-beta.
Therefore finite monodromy has at least N-1 eigenvalues equal to one.
Resonant Jordan blocks do not alter this eigenvalue statement.

nodes.title: One finite monodromy of this type excludes every finite-cover split
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

We use the following general criterion.

Let E be an irreducible connection of rank N>=3 on the punctured affine
line, with no other finite singularities, and suppose its monodromy A
at the puncture has at least N-1 eigenvalues one. Then its differential
Galois identity component acts irreducibly. E therefore stays irreducible
over every finite algebraic function-field extension.

nodes.title: The rank-two exception is real
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

For c nonzero consider the pre-Fourier line coefficient
\[
             \chi=-c/a^2+3h/(2a).
\]
Its Fourier equation, after multiplication by -1, is
\[
                  h^2 q\, y''+\tfrac12h^2 y'+cy=0.
\]
On q=v^2/2 it becomes
\[
                         h^2 y_{vv}+2cy=0.                  \tag{12}
\]
After adjoining kappa with kappa^2=-2c, the first-order system
h*partial_v*(y,h*y_v)^t=J*(y,h*y_v)^t, J=[[0,1],[-2c,0]],
has the constant horizontal projectors (I+J/kappa)/2 and
(I-J/kappa)/2. It really splits algebraically.

Its local monodromy eigenvalues are 1,-1, exactly the exceptional
case left by (11). This is a rank-two control, not a Long deformation:
its classical coefficient is rational of degree two rather than
a polynomial of degree at least three.

nodes.title: Consequences for amplitudes and rational phase changes
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

For every finite collection of nonzero rational functions f_j(a,s),
a logarithmic amplitude changes the Long coefficient by
\[
          \chi_h=\chi_0-h\sum_j\alpha_j\,\partial_a\log f_j.
                                                               \tag{13}
\]
Each logarithmic derivative is proper at a=infinity, even when
the f_j have mixed a,s divisors or parameter-dependent poles.
Thus the generic polynomial part remains the nonconstant quartic
chi_0. The first case of the theorem already excludes every finite
algebraic branch splitting. There is no degree, pole-number or
residue search to perform in this class.

More generally any finite rational chi_h with the same reduction (2)
is covered, including rational phase corrections that change its
polynomial part at generic h. This distinction matters:
chi_0/(1+h*a^5) is proper generically although its reduction is quartic.
It is handled by the one-singularity and monodromy argument, not by
assuming its behavior at infinity remains polynomial.

Tensoring the Fourier module by any rank-one connection afterwards
does not help: tensoring by a line is an equivalence and its
endomorphism connection is unchanged. The same statement holds
after every finite algebraic base extension.

The rational connection must still have a compatible s derivative,
and ultimately the full fourth-image action, to be a carrier.
Logarithmic amplitudes with constant residues have the expected
mixed-derivative compatibility. The theorem excludes splitting
already for the single a/Fourier-q connection, so adding the other
relations cannot repair it.

Minimal extension is part of the statement. Nonminimal extensions
may add puncture-supported constituents before Fourier transformation.
Their classical support, parameter lattice, global admission and
finite-left generation need a separate audit. No theorem here turns
such a constituent into a Long carrier or rules out every conceivable
different algebraization.

nodes.title: Why the generic pre-Fourier rank remains an actual gap
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QFT1, the named sub-result states:

Classical or formal position rank one does not force generic position
rank one. A small exact control is
\[
 \mathcal E_R=D_R/D_R(hA^2+A-a),\qquad [A,a]=h.                \tag{14}
\]
It is h-flat. If hQ=U*(hA^2+A-a), reduction modulo h in the
polynomial domain forces U divisible by h; cancel h to prove
h saturation of the left ideal. Its special module is the
rank-one graph A=a, and flatness gives a formally free rank-one
position completion. Its generic connection rank is two, because
the defining operator has order two when h is invertible.

This control carries no constructed full Long right action.
It demonstrates why the present theorem cannot silently be promoted
to all-representative nonlifting. A candidate may have additional
generic connection branches invisible in the formal classical frame.
One must prove or construct the relevant rank and lattice properties.

nodes.title: The differential algebra hypotheses
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

Let L have characteristic zero, let P=L[t1,...,tm], and let B be a
commutative domain containing P, with commuting derivations nabla_i
extending all coordinate partials. Put Q=Frac P and H=Frac B.
Assume H/Q is algebraic, not necessarily finite, and
\[
 \bigcap_i\ker(\nabla_i:H\to H)=L,\qquad
                              P\cap B^\times=L^\times.   \tag{1}
\]
No noetherian or finite-generation hypothesis is imposed on B.

These hypotheses hold for the actual generic scalar centralizer of m
commuting images in the rank-m Weyl algebra once QFC1's polynomial
classical-centralizer hypothesis and actual individual mates hold.
Commutativity is QSC1/QFC1. Algebraicity follows by applying
[Bavula's commutative-subalgebra bound, Corollary1.6](https://arxiv.org/html/math/0401263)
to each finitely generated P[b], not to all of B at once. Scalar extension
to an algebraic closure preserves that bound. Weyl units are scalar by
additivity of Bernstein degree.

For Long, let L=K((h)). QFC1 gives a unique Laurent formal expansion
sum h^j*P_j(F) for each actual centralizer element. Hence H embeds in the
commutative h-valued position-field completion K(t1,...,tm)((h)).
The nabla_i act there coefficientwise as partial_(ti), whose joint
constants are K((h))=L. This proves the first part of (1) for H itself,
without first proving B normal or finitely generated. QET1 removes
actual parameter poles in the mates, so generic individual mates suffice.

For an arbitrary projective endomorphism algebra, algebraicity and the
unit condition need their own proof. No scalar unit theorem is being
transferred automatically.

nodes.title: Formal Taylor maps over arbitrary residue fields
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

As proved in QET1, B is differentially simple. If a nonzero b lies in
a differential ideal I, clearing denominators in an algebraic equation
for b with nonzero constant term puts a nonzero element of P in I.
Coordinate partials then extract a nonzero scalar, so I=B.

Choose any maximal ideal n of B, put kappa=B/n, and write ci for the
image of ti. Its residue field may have arbitrary transcendence degree
over L. Commutativity and the Leibniz rule give the differential ring map
\[
 \tau_n(b)=\sum_{\alpha\ge0}
       {\overline{\nabla^\alpha b}\over\alpha!}s^\alpha
       \ \in R=\kappa[[s_1,\ldots,s_m]],\qquad
                         \tau_n(t_i)=c_i+s_i.             \tag{2}
\]
Every coefficient uses finitely many operations. The kernel is a
differential ideal, and tau(1)=1, so differential simplicity makes tau
injective. It extends to an embedding of H in Frac R.

The restricted coordinate map
\[
                         P\longrightarrow R,\qquad
                                      t_i\mapsto c_i+s_i  \tag{3}
\]
is flat. Factor it through the field extension kappa[t], translation
by c, localization at (t-c), and completion. The final flatness input is
[Stacks00MB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00MB). This argument
uses no finite presentation of B and no assumption that n contracts
to a closed point of Spec P.

nodes.title: Birational differential overrings are localizations
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

Here is a useful independent lemma. If a differential subring A of Q
contains P and is stable under all partial_i, then
\[
                    A=S^{-1}P,\qquad S=P\cap A^\times.    \tag{4}
\]
Finite generation of A is unnecessary.

Write b=p/q in A with coprime p,q in P. If q were not a unit of A,
choose a maximal ideal containing q and apply the Taylor ring map (2).
Its restriction (3) is flat even without differential simplicity.
Coprimeness makes multiplication by p injective on P/(q), and flatness
preserves this injection on R/(q). But p=q*tau(b) in R, so multiplication
by p there is zero. Since q maps into the maximal ideal of R,
R/(q) is nonzero, a contradiction. Thus q is a unit of A. This proves
both containments in (4).

In particular H=Q and (1) imply B=P, with no appeal to an etale
finite-type model.

nodes.title: Every base divisor has an unramified formal branch
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

Let pi be any irreducible polynomial in P. By (1), it is not a unit
of B. Choose a maximal ideal n containing pi and use (2). The nonzero
series pi(c+s) lies in the maximal ideal of R. The ring R is regular
local and factorial; see
[Stacks0AG0](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AG0).
Choose an irreducible factor rho of pi(c+s).

For any a in P not divisible by pi, the sequence pi,a is regular in
P, and flatness of (3) preserves injectivity of multiplication by a
on R/(pi). In a factorial ring this says that rho cannot divide a.
Moreover, choose i with partial_i pi nonzero and not divisible by pi,
possible in characteristic zero. If rho occurred with multiplicity
at least two in pi(c+s), it would divide every s derivative of that
series, contradicting the same regular-sequence argument for
a=partial_i pi. Consequently
\[
         v_\rho(\pi)=1,\qquad v_\rho(a)=0
                                  \quad(a\in P\setminus(\pi)). \tag{5}
\]
The discrete valuation of Frac R at rho therefore restricts to exactly
the pi-adic valuation on Q.

For any finite intermediate field Q subset J subset H, restrict the
same valuation to J. Its value group is contained in Z and contains
v(pi)=1, hence equals Z. Its ramification index over Q is one:
\[
 \text{for every base prime divisor and every finite }J/Q,
              \text{ some extension valuation has }e=1. \tag{6}
\]
The residue extensions are separable in characteristic zero, so the
corresponding prime in the finite normalization is unramified.
This is the divisor-retention statement needed by QET1, proved directly
without constructing Spec B as a finite-type etale scheme.

The point c may lie in the singular locus of pi=0. The argument uses
a prime factor in the formal completion, not total vanishing order
at that point. Equation (5) still holds for each such factor.

nodes.title: No finite Galois factor
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose J/Q in (6) is finite Galois. Galois transitivity gives the
same ramification index at all primes over each base divisor.
Thus every such prime is unramified. Normalize P in J; that
normalization is finite and normal. Branch purity over the regular
base makes it finite etale, hence a constant cover of affine space.
The explicit external inputs are
[Stacks09E3](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09E3),
[Stacks0BMB](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BMB), and
[Milne's characteristic-zero covering theorem](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/LECc.pdf#page=27).

Every resulting constant element is algebraic over L, so all nabla_i
kill it. Equation (1), now applied in H, excludes every new constant.
Therefore
\[
                  Q\subset J\subset H,\quad J/Q
                    \text{ finite Galois}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J=Q.
                                                               \tag{7}
\]
Only the normalization of the specified finite field J is used.
There is no normalization-finiteness assumption on all of B or H.

If H/Q is Galois, even an infinite algebraic Galois extension, it is
the union of its finite Galois subextensions, so H=Q. Equation (4)
and (1) then give B=P. In the quantum setting,
\[
  \operatorname{Cent}_{E}(F)=K[[h]][F],\qquad
                    \text{finite full completion follows}.   \tag{8}
\]
Use QET1 for actual parameter-pole removal and QFC1 for integral
polynomial curvature homotopy. A prescribed classical flat tuple can
be retained. For a fixed pair, a nontrivial finite Galois subfield
of its actual centralizer field instead forbids simultaneous
individual mates in all orders and degrees.

nodes.title: A stronger monodromy condition
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

For a finite intermediate J/Q let M be its normal closure,
G=Gal(M/Q), and S=Gal(M/J), the point stabilizer in the transitive
action. The largest Galois subfield of J is fixed by the normal
closure of S in G. Equation (7) therefore requires
\[
                           \langle gSg^{-1}:g\in G\rangle=G. \tag{9}
\]
Every codimension-one inertia generator must also have a fixed
sheet, by (6). Neither condition supplies a common sheet fixed by G.

The natural degree-four D4 action fails (9): a vertex stabilizer
is a reflection, and its normal closure has order four, index two.
Thus a D4 quartic centralizer subfield is excluded, although that
quartic field itself is non-Galois. In contrast the degree-three S3
stabilizer normally generates S3. QDI1/QNI1's retained cubic therefore
passes this condition. It remains a sharp degree-three boundary
in rank at least three.

For an explicit non-Galois field with a forbidden Galois factor,
the generic equation
\[
                  z^4+u z^2+v=0,\qquad
                      (z^2)^2+u z^2+v=0                 \tag{10}
\]
contains the quadratic field generated by z^2. The discriminant
u^2-4v is not a square. The quartic has degree four by the generic
polynomial map v=-z^4-u*z^2 over L(u). Its other squared root is
-u-z^2, not a square in L(u,z), so the quartic field itself is
non-Galois. If such a subfield occurred in an actual
centralizer under these hypotheses, individual mates would be
impossible. This is a field certificate, not a constructed Long
centralizer.

nodes.title: Radical certificates in the scalar Weyl algebra
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QTB1, the named sub-result states:

In the scalar Weyl application there are no new radicals:
\[
             \theta\in H,\quad \theta^k\in Q,\quad k\ge2
                                      \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta\in Q.
                                                               \tag{11}
\]
First suppose L contains the kth roots of unity. Q(theta)/Q is
Galois: all roots of the relevant binomial lie in Q(theta), even
if that binomial is reducible. Equation (7) makes this extension
trivial.

For general K, adjoin the kth roots of unity to the constant field.
The classical centralizer identity survives field extension, being
the kernel of finitely many K-linear Poisson maps. The actual
commuting operators and mates extend to the scalar Weyl algebra;
units remain scalar and the same argument applies there. Thus theta
lies in the constant extension Q'=L(mu_k)(t). Since Q'/Q is a
finite abelian Galois constant extension, its intersection with H
is a finite Galois subextension of H/Q. Equation (7) makes that
intersection Q.
This proves (11) without assuming K algebraically closed.

Accordingly a finite, checkable obstruction certificate consists
of commuting b,c in the actual joint centralizer, c nonzero, and
\[
                 q(F)b^k=p(F)c^k,\qquad
                     p/q\notin Q^{\,k}.                  \tag{12}
\]
Commutativity makes theta=b/c well-defined in H. Its kth power is
p/q, so (11) contradicts the nonscalar radical. To certify the last
condition it suffices to exhibit an irreducible polynomial pi
with valuation of p/q not divisible by k. The certificate needs
neither a finite presentation of B nor a description of all H.
A rational commuting operator outside Frac B cannot be substituted
without its own proof of membership.

For the older scalar boundary F1=x+h^2*x^2,F2=y, take
\[
                    b=1+2h^2x,\quad c=1,\qquad
                            b^2=1+4h^2F_1.              \tag{13}
\]
The right side has a simple spectral divisor. This finite square-root
certificate excludes every actual individual mate, including ones
with arbitrary parameter poles. Its rational mate remains outside
the actual generic Weyl algebra, as recorded in QET1.

nodes.title: Statement and linear trace descent
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPC1, the named sub-result states:

Let K be any characteristic-zero field, h in K nonzero, and
delta=v^-1*partial_v on F=K(v). For a finite algebraic extension E/F,
extend delta uniquely and form the finite Ore operator rings
\[
 D(F)=F[a;h\delta]\subset D(E)=E[a;h\delta],\qquad
 S=G(a)+\mu v,\quad
 G=\sum_{j=0}^n g_j a^j,\quad n\ge2,\quad g_n\mu\ne0.          \tag{1}
\]
There is no finite T in D(E) with [S,T]=kappa for nonzero kappa in K.
Scalars may belong to a Laurent-series field such as K0((h)).
The leading coefficient g_n need not be an h-valuation unit.

Normalized field trace tau=Tr_(E/F)/[E:F] commutes with delta.
Coefficientwise extension
\[
 \tau\left(\sum_i t_i a^i\right)=\sum_i\tau(t_i)a^i,\qquad
 \tau(P T Q)=P\tau(T)Q\quad(P,Q\in D(F))                     \tag{2}
\]
is a D(F)-bimodule retraction. Left multiplication by a uses
delta*tau=tau*delta; right multiplication uses the same identity
in the Ore Leibniz formula. Multiplication by base coefficients
commutes with tau. These generator checks prove the assertion.
Thus [S,T]=kappa implies [S,tau(T)]=kappa, reducing existence to F.
There is no bound on the extension degree or the mate's order.

This linear descent also works for matrix mates of the fixed scalar
S*I_m: take the normalized matrix trace first, then the coefficient
field trace. It does not descend a simultaneously unknown nonlinear
tuple or an idempotent. For example the quadratic-cover projector
e=(1/2)*[[1,w],[w^-1,1]], w^2=v, has e^2=e but coefficient trace
tau(e)=I_2/2, which is not idempotent.

nodes.title: The finite-characteristic necessity
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPC1, the named sub-result states:

Let A,B be N-by-N matrices over a field of characteristic p and
[A,B]=kappa*I_N, with nonzero kappa. Over dual numbers epsilon^2=0,
\[
 (I-\epsilon B)A(I+\epsilon B)=A+\epsilon\kappa I,\qquad
                       \chi_A'(z)=0.                       \tag{3}
\]
Indeed conjugacy preserves the characteristic polynomial, whereas
translation replaces chi_A(z) by chi_A(z-epsilon*kappa).
Consequently chi_A is a polynomial in z^p. When N=p it is
z^p+c, so Cayley--Hamilton makes A^p scalar.

Over a perfect field k of odd characteristic p, D=k(v)[a;h*delta]
has center and central degree
\[
 Z(D)=k(v^p)[a^p],\qquad
 \dim_{\operatorname{Frac}Z(D)}
   \left(D\otimes_Z\operatorname{Frac}Z(D)\right)=p^2.        \tag{4}
\]
For completeness put b=v*a. Then [b,v]=h and a=v^-1*b.
The ring D is the localization of the rank-one Weyl algebra
k[v,b] at all nonzero polynomials in v. Such polynomials are
invertible after central localization since f(v)^p is central.
The usual Weyl center is k[v^p,b^p], and the generic algebra is
central simple of degree p. Also delta^p=0 on k(v): each Laurent
monomial acquires p successive factors j,j-2,...,j-2(p-1),
one of which is zero. The p-th power of a derivation is a
derivation, so vanishing on v and k gives vanishing on k(v).
Thus a^p is central. The p^2 monomials v^i*a^j, 0<=i,j<p,
give the displayed center and dimension by PBW and commutation
with v and a. Generic splitting is faithful into p-by-p matrices.

Hence a scalar mate in D would make S^p central by (3).
This is a necessary condition, with no prescribed center map.
The standard Weyl-center and splitting framework is described in
[Lauritzen--Thomsen, Section1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/1508.02499)
and their [2026 paper, Section3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.23110).
Neither a lift modulo p^2 nor their Poisson-center lifting theorem
is used in the argument here.

nodes.title: One coefficient in every degree
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPC1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose p>2n+1. In normal order, the exact coefficient is
\[
 [v^{-2p}a^{J}]\,S^p
  =\frac{n^2-1}{24n}\,g_n^{\,p-2}\mu^2h^{\,p+1},
 \qquad J=(n-1)p-(2n+1).                                   \tag{5}
\]
It is nonzero: p>2n+1 excludes every prime divisor of
24*n*(n^2-1). Also J>0 and J is not divisible by p.
Therefore S^p is not central.

Here is a direct computation valid for every n and prime in that range.
A word with ell copies of v has p-ell polynomial factors.
If normal ordering uses c derivative contractions, then
\[
 \deg_v=\ell-2c,\qquad
 \operatorname{ord}_a\le n(p-\ell)-c.                       \tag{6}
\]
To reach v^-2p one needs ell even and c=p+ell/2.
With ell=0 no coefficients are differentiated and no such term occurs.
For ell>=4 the upper a order is strictly below J.
For ell=2 equality forces all p-2 polynomial factors to contribute
g_n*a^n. Thus lower G terms and words with any other v count
cannot cancel the coefficient in (5).

Put m=(p+1)/2 and c_r=product_(t=0)^(r-1)(1-2t).
The two-v words are a^(ni)*v*a^(nj)*v*a^(nk), i+j+k=p-2.
Their normal-order contribution with r+s=p+1 is
\[
 \binom{ni}{r}\binom{n(i+j)-r}{s}
       \delta^r(v)\delta^s(v),\qquad
 \delta^r(v)=c_r v^{1-2r}.                                  \tag{7}
\]
Since c_r=0 for r>=m+1, only r=s=m survives.
After removing the scalar factor g_n^(p-2)*mu^2*h^(p+1),
the desired coefficient is
\[
 c_m^2\sum_{u=0}^{p-2}
       \left(\sum_{i=0}^{u}\binom{ni}{m}\right)
                          \binom{nu-m}{m}.                 \tag{8}
\]

Work now in F_p[u]. Set
A(u)=binom(nu,m), B(u)=binom(nu-m,m), and let F(u) be the
polynomial summatory function sum_(i=0)^u A(i). It has degree m+1<p;
it exists by polynomial finite summation since m+1 is invertible.
Furthermore F(p-1)=sum_(i in F_p)A(i)=0, because deg A=m<p-1.
Thus the outer sum in (8) extends to all of F_p.
Since deg(F*B)=2m+1=p+2<2p-2, finite-field power sums give
\[
                    \sum_{u\in\mathbb F_p}F(u)B(u)
                         =-[u^{p-1}]F(u)B(u).              \tag{9}
\]

nodes.title: Return to characteristic zero
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPC1, the named sub-result states:

Suppose a finite rational mate exists in characteristic zero.
Adjoin to Z the finitely many scalar coefficients in S,T,h,kappa,
and invert g_n,mu,h,kappa and one nonzero coefficient from each
denominator polynomial in v. This gives a nonzero finitely
generated characteristic-zero coefficient ring R.
Clear rational denominators in the finitely many coefficients of
[S,T]=kappa to obtain polynomial identities over R.

There are good reductions to finite fields in arbitrarily large
characteristic. One elementary proof specializes the finite-type
Q-algebra R tensor Q at a maximal ideal. Zariski's lemma makes
the residue a number field. The image of R lies in O_L[1/N]
for some integer N, and the chosen units remain units after
excluding finitely many prime ideals. Reducing at primes of
arbitrarily large rational characteristic preserves the degree
of G, every required nonzero scalar, every denominator polynomial
and the commutator identity. This is the usual finite-type
reduction framework; see
[Lauritzen--Thomsen, Section1.4](https://arxiv.org/html/1508.02499).

Choose a good p>2n+1. The reduced pair would make S^p central
by (3)--(4), contradicting (5). Together with (2), this proves
the theorem for all finite coefficient covers.

This does not specialize h-adic series by evaluating h at 1.
Only finitely many field elements occur as coefficients of the
hypothetical finite operators, even if those elements themselves
are Laurent series. Finite generation and good reduction apply
to that scalar ring.

nodes.title: Complete pure separable classification
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of DIX-QPC1, the named sub-result states:

For S=v*H(a)+G(a), H,G in K[a], a finite scalar mate with
commutator h exists over a finite coefficient cover exactly
in the following cases, where it already exists over K(v).

- H=mu is constant, G=lambda*a+c is affine, and S is nonconstant.
  If mu is nonzero, an explicit mate is
\[
 T=-\frac{\lambda a^2}{2\mu^2}
       -\frac{va}{\mu}-\frac{h}{2\mu v},
                       \qquad [S,T]=h.                    \tag{14}
\]
  If mu=0 and lambda is nonzero, use
\[
                         T=\frac{v^2}{2\lambda}.           \tag{15}
\]
- H=lambda*a+mu with lambda nonzero and G constant. Then
\[
                              T=\frac v\lambda.            \tag{16}
\]

Every other case is excluded. Constant S has zero commutator.
For H constant nonzero and G nonlinear use the present theorem.
For H=0 and G nonlinear use QVL1's ordinary infinity lemma,
with coordinate u=v^2/2. For deg H>=2 use QVL1's complete
v-linear bounded-lower theorem. For deg H=1 with G nonconstant
use QZM1. These cases exhaust all polynomial H,G.

In particular no bounded full exact-R scalar Long lift can have
this pure separable polynomial form: its classical G is
4a-3r*a^2, so its generic G remains nonlinear. Every possible
finite momentum degree in H and G is covered, including
h-small highest coefficients. Finite matrix padding with S
unchanged as S*I does not help, by normalized matrix trace.
This is a structural closure of the ansatz, not a requirement
merely to increase a rank or order threshold.

nodes.title: 4. The missing multiplication estimate is EXACTLY L4
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of HESS-LW, the named sub-result states:

For ANY finite B-generating family lambda_1,...,lambda_m of Lambda,
the following conditions are equivalent:

1. every lambda_i belongs to L4(U);
2. every element of Lambda belongs to L4(U);
3. Lambda*Lambda subset Lambda;
4. the ordinary pairing Tr(Lambda*Lambda) is contained in B;
5. the Keller map is invertible.

lambda^2 belongs to R intersect H=Lambda. Polarization gives 3. A finite

inverse criterion gives 4 iff 5. Conversely an inverse makes U relatively
compact in the source, so every polynomial belongs to L4(U). This also
establishes the equivalence to 3 without assuming a primitive presentation.

E(w)=sum_i sum_(K(z)=w) |lambda_i(z)|^2.

exists. Indeed the square of a finite sum of nonnegative numbers is bounded
below by their squares and above by their number times the sum of squares;

nodes.title: 7. Entire coordinate multiplication need not have dense domain, even on Runge sets
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of HESS-LW, the named sub-result states:

For EVERY integer a>=3, consider the connected open polynomial polyhedron

W_a={|y|<1, |x^a*y|<1} subset C2.

It is complete Reinhardt and logarithmically convex, hence pseudoconvex.
Its Taylor series converge on compact subpolydisks; finite subcovers of a
compact set give uniform polynomial approximation, so it is Runge. It
contains the entire line y=0 and has finite volume. Direct integration gives

||x^m y^n||^2
      =pi^2 / ((m+1)*(n+1-(m+1)/a))
        iff m+1<a*(n+1),                           (9)

and divergence otherwise. Distinct monomials are orthogonal. In particular
Vol(W_a)=pi^2*a/(a-1), x is L2 for all a>=3, and x^(a-2) is an allowed
Bergman vector whose product with x is NOT L2. The coefficient functional
of x^(a-2)y^0 is continuous and nonzero. Every function in the natural
domain of M_x has that coefficient zero, since multiplication shifts it
to the forbidden monomial x^(a-1). Thus Dom(M_x) is NOT DENSE.

This whole-ambient-plane, Runge, finite-volume example rules out a generic
functional-analysis assertion of dense coordinate multiplication. It is
NOT an actual Keller pullback: the defining polynomial map (x^a*y,y) has
Jacobian a*x^(a-1)*y, which vanishes. No inference from this control to the
missing actual Keller density assertion is made.

nodes.title: 5. The flat dual endpoint retains the original global issue
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of HESS-MI, the named sub-result states:

For any polynomial unit-Hessian h, geodesic completeness of nabla^(1)
is equivalent to invertibility of grad(h). This is the standard developing-
map completeness criterion, not a new proposed independent HC4 criterion.
Here is the direct argument to avoid replacing it by a metric theorem.

The polynomial fields V_i=H^-1*e_i are parallel for nabla^(1), commute,
and satisfy V_i(Phi_j)=delta_ij. If all dual geodesics are entire, every
integral curve of each V_i is entire, since it is a geodesic with that
initial tangent. Their commuting complete flows give a holomorphic C^n
action. Its orbits are open because the fields span every tangent space;
connectedness makes the action transitive. Equivariance under Phi sends
this action to target translation, so its stabilizer is zero. Phi is
therefore a biholomorphism. A bijective etale polynomial morphism is an
algebraic isomorphism (equivalently use the usual birational Keller/Zariski
main argument). Conversely a polynomial inverse transports all target
straight lines to entire dual geodesics.

This argument applies to the FULL complex source in any dimension. It
does not follow from completeness of the standard source connection,
from the Levi-Civita connection, or from a positive-definite comparison.
The retained KZ complete-flow theorem is a different PLANE-specific
boundary theorem; its classification is not extended here to dimension4.

ord(y_p)>=ceil((2e*alpha+6beta)/ell)>=e*alpha+3beta,

nodes.title: 4. The central degree-two case forces a quadratic residue extension
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-PF162, the named sub-result states:

In the d=2 case, the two extra sheets from R are outside BOTH whole
charts; their source X and translated source coordinate are polar.
By Section2 their coframe is holomorphic, so the ACTUAL companion is
finite on every such end.

For a first p-dependent coefficient lambda after a finite p-independent
Puiseux truncation, PF159 gives H(lambda)=p with H polynomial. Its degree
is at most TWO: each root of H(Y)-p lifts to a distinct extra Puiseux root
with the same prior polar chart data, and there are only two extra sheets.
The leading coefficient of every polynomial source function is polynomial
in lambda. In particular the finite companion residue is G(lambda) with
G in C[lambda]. Later coefficients lie in C(lambda) by ordinary Hensel.

An affine H gives polynomial residue in p and is excluded by PF161's
closed-graph/full-normalization argument. The same is true if the closed
prime has residue degree1 over C(p): with quadratic H,
C[lambda] intersect C(p)=C[H(lambda)], so G is again polynomial in p.
The graph is a full closed image in the finite normalization, not a
punctured parameter curve. The retained Chau COMPONENT Remark excludes it.

The fundamental local degree sum for R is two. Consequently the only
remaining possibility is ONE original horizontal prime R0, with

ord_R0(t)=1, k(R0)=C(lambda), [C(lambda):C(P)]=2.          (14)

After an affine target P change and a constant lambda change take
P|R0=lambda^2. The actual Q residue is G(lambda). If G were in C[lambda^2],
its image would again be a forbidden graph. Hence C(P,G)=C(lambda),
and the residue degree of R0 over its target image is ONE.

nodes.title: 6. Complete global pole localization and the three surviving faces
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-PF162, the named sub-result states:

PF149 excludes constant b3 on every complete quadratic model. Thus b3
is nonconstant. Its infinity bound, with deg M>=2 and deg b3>0, makes
EVERY u-infinity coframe end holomorphic. Section2 covers every M-root
end. At a finite zero c of b3 off M, the specialization P*(c,w) has
degree>=2 by PF52; degree>=3 gives holomorphic ends by PF158.

An actual nonzero rational exact coframe on the complete generic curve
must have a pole of order at least TWO. Therefore EVERY actual ruling-six
coordinate has a bad point c off M with

b3(c)=a2(c)=b2(c)=a1(c)=0, b1(c)!=0.                    (21)

These are exactly the degree-two specialization conditions, not independent
assumptions on four unrelated divisors. On some polar branch at this c,
write u-c=s^alpha,w=c0*s^-h+..., c0!=0, and weighted initial I(Y).
PF159's multiplicity bound says r>=ceil(H0/ell)-h, H0>=2h.
If ell<=2 the end is holomorphic. Thus ell=3 or4. Its slope
L=h/alpha is an INTEGER: a denominator q>1 would give q conjugate
nonzero initial roots of multiplicity ell, whereas there are at most
four escaping roots. This yields exactly THREE face classes:

A: I=C*Y^2*(Y-c0)^4, H0=2h, L>=3.
    B: I=C*Y^2*(Y-c0)^3*K(Y), H0=2h, L>=4,
       deg K<=1, K(0)*K(c0)!=0.
    C: I=C*Y^3*(Y-c0)^3,
       ord_c p3=B0, 4<=B0<L,
       (ord p3,ord p4,ord p5,ord p6)
           =(B0,B0+L,B0+2L,B0+3L).                         (22)

All displayed C,c0 are nonzero constants. In A every face coefficient
has its binomial value and ord p_i=(i-2)L for i=2,...,6. In B only
nonzero face coefficients obey this order; an absent highest term is
above the face. Here p_i are coefficients of w^i in P*. The lower
bounds follow from r+alpha<0 at a pole of order>=2. In C, p2 is the
unit specialization term above the face, giving B0<L. These classes
include all cancellations and multiple roots; no simple-root subset is
substituted for the classification.

nodes.title: 2. Additive and multiplicative source symmetries at field level
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-PF52, the named sub-result states:

In any polynomial source coordinates, either of the following conditions
forces F to be an automorphism:

partial_x(K) subset K;
    E_(a,b)(K) subset K, E_(a,b)=a*x*partial_x+b*y*partial_y,
      (a,b) in Z^2 minus {(0,0)}.                         (2)

For the additive condition, (1) gives partial_x(A) subset A. Choose
f in A of positive x degree m, which exists by algebraic independence.
Its (m-1)-st derivative is in A and has form a(y)*x+b(y), a!=0.
On a line y=beta with a(beta)!=0 this is affine-linear in x. Apply the
one-line theorem.

For the multiplicative condition, (1) first gives E_(a,b)(A) subset A.
For a source polynomial f with finite weight support W, each homogeneous
component is obtained by the exact spectral projector

f_w = product_(v in W,v!=w) (E-v)/(w-v) applied to f.   (3)

Hence every component of every f in A belongs to A. Suppose a!=0.
The invertible differential of F at the source origin gives some f in
{P,Q} with a nonzero linear x term. Its weight-a component restricts
on y=0 to c*x, c!=0: the only surviving monomial of that weight on the
axis is x. This is an element of A, so F is injective on that line.
If a=0, use b!=0 and the y axis instead. This proof includes positive,
negative and zero weight patterns; it requires no linearization theorem
for an action on the target and no homogeneity of the chosen P,Q.

nodes.title: 1. The object being classified
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-MONODROMY, the named sub-result states:

Work first over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic zero.
A Keller map is a polynomial morphism F:X=A^m -> Y=A^m with
det DF in k*. It is dominant, generically finite and etale. Write

\[
 K=k(Y),\quad L=k(X),\quad M=\text{Galois closure of }L/K,\qquad
 G=\operatorname{Gal}(M/K),\quad H=\operatorname{Gal}(M/L).
\]

The degree is n=[L:K]=[G:H]. Analytic continuation over C, or the geometric
etale fundamental group in general, acts on the cosets G/H. This is the
monodromy action. It is faithful because M is the Galois closure.

The action must be recorded together with H. The deck group of the generic
cover is N_G(H)/H, equivalently the centralizer of G in S_n. It need not
equal G. Polynomial source symmetries covering target symmetries form yet
another object. These three meanings of "symmetry group" must be kept separate.

For a nonclosed ground field, geometric and arithmetic monodromy are
different groups, G_geom normal in G_arith <= S_n. Their quotient describes
the algebraic constant field of the Galois closure. The F11 example below
makes this distinction necessary, even with an explicit rational formula.

The absolute spectrum consists of actions realized by polynomial Keller
self-maps of affine space, allowing dimension to vary. The chart spectrum
allows smooth affine source and target varieties and a chosen volume form.
A field-versal spectrum additionally asks to realize all torsors of a
specified action. These are different problems.

nodes.title: 2. Three distinct realization steps
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-MONODROMY, the named sub-result states:

A finite etale algebra in a special fiber does not prescribe the generic
monodromy group. A special target slice can have a smaller group than the
ambient cover. The universal pencil H(W)-sW+t has group S_n for every
characteristic-zero degree-n polynomial H; choosing a Chebyshev or a
monomial seed alone does not preserve its dihedral or cyclic slice group.
See the retained [universal-pencil proof](../../foundations/verified/UNIVERSAL_SYMMETRIC_MONODROMY.md).

There is, however, a general cover-preserving chart construction. If
f:V -> U is a finite etale map of smooth affine curves with coordinates x,t
on open subsets of the projective line, write t=f(x). On a chart where x
is a coordinate and f' is a unit,

\[
 (x,z)\longmapsto (f(x),z/f'(x))
 \tag{2.1}
\]

has determinant one and preserves the function-field extension after adding
one independent transcendental variable. A monic root presentation
P(t,x)=0 gives the analogous derivative-unit construction.

Such charts can have many nonconstant units. Since A^m has only constant
units, adjoining affine coordinates does not make these charts affine
spaces. Changing the boundary through affine modifications is a separate
problem. A candidate absolute realization must exhibit polynomial
coordinates everywhere, a nonzero constant full Jacobian, an exact generic
field identification, and actual affine source and target spaces.

nodes.title: 3. Every affine divisor is met without ramification
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-MONODROMY, the named sub-result states:

**Lemma.** Let F:A^m -> A^m be Keller over k. For every prime divisor
D=V(q) in the target there is a prime divisor E in the source dominating D,
and its ramification index in L/K is one.

Indeed q(F) is nonconstant, since F is dominant. A nonconstant polynomial
over an algebraically closed field is not a unit and has a prime factor.
Every component E of V(q(F)) has dimension m-1. The restriction of a
quasi-finite morphism is quasi-finite, so its image has dimension m-1;
its image closure is D. At the generic points the local rings are DVRs.
The local map is etale, hence has ramification index one and separable
residue extension. This works for m=1 as well.

In fact q(F) is squarefree: every component just considered has index one.
Distinct target prime divisors have disjoint sets of source prime-divisor
factors, since such a factor cannot dominate two different divisors.
Consequently pullback on the free divisor groups is a primitive injection:
each target prime maps to a nonempty sum of distinct source primes, and
the supports of these sums are disjoint. Choosing one source prime over
each target prime gives a splitting. The cokernel is free.

One elementary consequence, useful for quadratic resolvents, is

\[
 b(F)\in k(X)^{*d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 b\in k(Y)^{*d}\qquad(d\ge2).
 \tag{3.1}
\]

Write the divisor of b in target prime divisors and compare valuations on
one source prime over each. Every exponent must be divisible by d; the
remaining constant is a d-th power in algebraically closed k. This
argument needs neither a prescribed primitive polynomial nor a Jacobian
ansatz. It cannot be applied to a selected target slice instead of the
whole affine target.

nodes.title: 4. The fixed-sheet inertia theorem
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-MONODROMY, the named sub-result states:

**KMFI1.** For every prime divisor D of the affine target, a geometric
inertia group I_D of M/K fixes at least one sheet of G/H. The normal
subgroup generated by all these inertia groups is G. Consequently

\[
 \boxed{\langle gHg^{-1}:g\in G\rangle=G.}
 \tag{4.1}
\]

Here "geometric inertia" means inertia after strict henselization at D;
it is cyclic in residue characteristic zero. The group is determined up
to conjugacy. The theorem concerns divisors of A^m, not arbitrary
divisors at infinity on a compactification.

To prove the first assertion, use E from Section 3. In the standard
inertia action on embeddings of L into M, the orbits have sizes equal to
ramification indices of geometric branches. Index one gives a fixed
sheet. Equivalently, for a suitable conjugate of H one has I_D <= gHg^-1.
An unramified branch may have a nontrivial residue-field extension before
strict henselization; this does not remove its inertia fixed points.

For the second assertion, let N be the normal subgroup generated by all
the I_D, and normalize Y in M^N. This normalization is finite, since Y
is excellent and M^N/K is finite. All codimension-one inertia is killed,
so the finite morphism is unramified in codimension one. Its source is
normal and its target regular. Purity of the branch locus makes it
finite etale everywhere. Affine space over an algebraically closed
characteristic-zero field has no nontrivial connected finite etale cover.
Thus M^N=K and N=G. Since every I_D lies in a conjugate of H, (4.1) follows.

The purity input is [Stacks, Lemma 58.21.4](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BMB).
For simple connectedness, descend the finite etale cover to a finitely
generated characteristic-zero field, embed it in C and use comparison
with the contractible analytic space C^m. Equivalence between algebraic
finite etale covers and finite analytic covers is the Riemann-existence
comparison of SGA 1, Expose XII, Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.2.
Isomorphism and geometric connectedness descend/extend with algebraically
closed constants. These are the only global inputs in this proof.

nodes.title: 5. Absolute exclusions beyond regular actions
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-MONODROMY, the named sub-result states:

**KMFI2.** The following are necessary consequences of KMFI1.

1. No nontrivial regular action occurs: H=1 cannot normally generate G.
   This recovers the classical Galois-case obstruction.
2. No nontrivial nilpotent group occurs in any faithful transitive action.
   For a finite nilpotent group every maximal subgroup is normal. A proper
   H lies in such a subgroup, so its normal closure is proper.
3. No proper normal block stabilizer is allowed. Under the
   block/intermediate-field correspondence, a normal block stabilizer
   would give a nontrivial Galois intermediate field. This does not
   exclude all imprimitive actions or algebraize arbitrary intermediate
   fields into polynomial factors.
4. H must surject onto every quotient in which its normal closure would
   otherwise be proper; in particular H -> G_ab is surjective. This last
   test alone is weaker than (4.1), for example for perfect groups.

For the natural degree-n action of
D_n=<r,s | r^n=s^2=1, srs=r^-1>, of order 2n, the point stabilizer is <s>.
Conjugating s by r gives r^2s, so

\[
 \langle\!\langle s\rangle\!\rangle
   =\langle s,r^2\rangle
   =\begin{cases}D_n& n\text{ odd},\\
                 \text{an index-two subgroup}&n\text{ even}.
     \end{cases}
 \tag{5.1}
\]

Thus **every even-degree natural dihedral action is impossible absolutely,
in every affine dimension**, irrespective of masks, blowdowns or
stabilization. For even n both reflection classes fail. In fact these and
the regular action exhaust faithful transitive dihedral actions: the
rotation part of any stabilizer is a normal subgroup contained in its
core, so a core-free stabilizer is trivial or a reflection. Therefore
D_n for even n has no absolute faithful transitive realization at all.

There is an independent elementary check of both exclusions. Every
quadratic subextension has the form K(sqrt(b)); equation (3.1) forbids
such a subextension inside L. More generally, over algebraically closed
k every cyclic prime-degree extension is Kummer, so (3.1) forbids it.
A finite nilpotent group has a normal maximal subgroup of prime index
containing any given proper stabilizer. The even dihedral action has
the explicit quadratic quotient (5.1). Thus these exclusions do not
depend on the global purity proof of KMFI1. On the even Dickson cover
itself, the identity P_(2m)(a,u)+2u^m=P_m(a,u)^2 displays the quadratic
resolvent directly.

nodes.title: 6. The PSL2(11) local sieve
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-MONODROMY, the named sub-result states:

**KMFI3.** For the natural degree-twelve action of PSL2(F_11), the complete
element-order and cycle dictionary is

| order | number of elements | cycles | allowed nontrivial affine-divisor inertia? |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1^12 | unramified |
| 2 | 55 | 2^6 | no |
| 3 | 110 | 3^4 | no |
| 5 | 264 | 5^2 1^2 | yes |
| 6 | 110 | 6^2 | no |
| 11 | 120 | 11 1 | yes |

The dictionary follows either by the split/nonsplit/unipotent
classification or by enumerating SL2(F_11)/{+/-I}; the replay does both
the projective action and its fixed-point test. In general the natural
PSL2(q) action permits only split semisimple and unipotent nontrivial
divisor inertia. Nonsplit semisimple inertia is a derangement.

The modular (2,3,11) cover on X_0(11) has two derangement branch values.
A Mobius rechoice of the target point at infinity can move only one of
them out of the affine line. Thus that product presentation cannot
satisfy the affine-divisor test. This is a statement about that cover and
its affine branch placement, not an exclusion of the natural action.

Suppose now that a degree-twelve cover of P^1 with this natural group
has genus zero and every *finite* branch inertia has a fixed sheet.
Finite inertia can have only orders 5 and 11, of indices 8 and 10.
The index at infinity belongs to {0,6,8,10}. Riemann--Hurwitz gives

where pi, the leading coefficient L and Disc(E) are units. Here L=pi if N=3 and L=aN*pi^N if N>=4. In particular aN is a unit in ranks at least four. This is an affine open of dimension N over R.

 C=x(5-3t)-x^3z-\sum_{j=4}^N(j-2)a_j(xq)^j,
 \tag{2}
\]
with output (Pi,-B/2,C). Its determinant is one. Over I_N its whole preimage is the finite etale algebra B_N=O_(I_N)[S]/E; the inverse-derivative localization is automatic on this chart.

The residual scaling is
\[
 a_j\mapsto\lambda^{j+1}a_j,\quad
 (\pi,b,c)\mapsto(\lambda^{-2}\pi,\lambda^{-1}b,\lambda c),
 \quad E_{\lambda p}(S)=\lambda E_p(S/\lambda).
 \tag{3}
\]

\[
 P(T)=\prod_i(T-r_i)=\sum_{j=0}^N d_jT^j,\qquad d_N=1.
\]

\[
 \pi=d_3/d_1,\quad b=d_2/d_1,\quad c=-2d_0/d_1,\quad
 a_j=d_jd_1^{j-1}/d_3^j

Indeed every term of C in (2) is divisible by x. Write C=xK. On C=1, x*K=1, so x is a unit. It is nonconstant: the specialization

 a_j=0,\quad x=s,\quad y=0,\quad

nodes.title: 6. Exact polynomial landing for coefficient profiles
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-RECEIVER, the named sub-result states:

The even-rank chart raises a more precise question: could its negative powers of Pi cancel in the original source coordinates? One all-degree rule answers this, and extends the earlier common positive power shifts.

**UAPROFILE1.** Replace each constant seed a_j in (2) by any rational function f_j(Pi) in k(Pi). The resulting rational map has determinant one wherever defined. The map extends polynomially on the original affine source if and only if:

- in characteristic zero, every f_j belongs to k[P];
- in odd characteristic p, every f_j is Laurent polynomial, with negative powers permitted only at indices j congruent to2 modulo p and only with pole order one or two.

At every pi!=0 where the profiles are defined, the complete fibre is exactly (1) with a_j=f_j(pi). For N>=4 with f_N nonzero the generic degree is N; the seed-free case has degree three. In characteristic zero its generic arithmetic and geometric monodromy are S_N, and every resulting polynomial map is absolutely stably atomic. No such general positive-characteristic monodromy claim is made.

For the Jacobian statement write A=DF_a with the seeds held fixed, and let v be the sum of f'_j(Pi)*partial_(a_j)F_a. Its first coordinate is zero. Since Pi is seed-independent, the total derivative is
\[
 A+v\,d\Pi,\qquad d\Pi\,A^{-1}=e_1^t.
\]
The determinant lemma therefore gives det(A+v*dPi)=det(A)*(1+e1^t*v)=1. This works for rational profiles and in every characteristic other than two.

First exclude every finite pole alpha!=0 after extending constants to an algebraic closure. The divisor Pi=alpha is prime: its equation is primitive and linear in z, and t is a unit there. With S=x/t one has
\[
 xq=\alpha S,\qquad
 t^2x^{j-2}q^j=\alpha^jS^{j-2}.
\]
The coordinate S is transcendental on that divisor. If the rational profiles have a pole of maximal order M at alpha with leading coefficients u_j, the B and C leading residues are respectively
\[
 \sum_j j u_j\alpha^jS^{j-2},\qquad
 -\sum_j(j-2)u_j\alpha^jS^j.
\]
Distinct j give distinct powers in each sum. Both residues can vanish only when j*u_j=(j-2)*u_j=0 for every j; since two is invertible, every u_j must be zero. This contradicts the maximal pole. Thus there are no finite nonzero poles, including inseparable denominator cases after constant extension. Every f_j is Laurent polynomial.

nodes.title: 7. A compiler-independent fixed-space obstruction
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-RECEIVER, the named sub-result states:

The inertia test concerns a receiver which retains a line. There is a second structural test even after that line is forgotten.

**UAEQUIV1.** Let G be a finite group and let F:V->W be a G-equivariant polynomial map between finite-dimensional linear representations over a characteristic-zero field, with constant nonzero Jacobian. For every subgroup H<=G, the restricted morphism
\[
 F^H:V^H\longrightarrow W^H
 \tag{21}
\]
is a Keller map between affine spaces of the same dimension. If y in W^G has finite etale fibre X, then its complete fibre in (21) is X^H, the finite set of H-fixed points with its scheme structure.

At every H-fixed source point, DF is an invertible H-equivariant linear map, and so is its inverse. Restricting to invariant tangent vectors gives an isomorphism. Hence the determinant of (21) never vanishes over an algebraic closure and is a unit of its polynomial coordinate ring, therefore a nonzero constant. The dimensions agree already from DF at the source origin. Fixed-point equalizers commute with the fibre product defining X, proving the assertion about the complete fibre. No generic-fibre or unmarked identification is substituted.

Suppose G=S_N and the marked fibre is its natural transitive N-point set, as required by a functorial realization of a rank-N algebra with its identification. It has no G-fixed point for N>=2. Thus the restriction F^G must be a Keller map with an empty geometric fibre.

In dimensions zero and one this is impossible: the zero-dimensional spaces are one point, and a one-variable characteristic-zero Keller polynomial is linear. Therefore
\[
 \boxed{\dim V^{S_N}\ge2.}                           \tag{22}
\]
If that dimension is exactly two, the construction supplies a non-surjective plane Keller map and hence a counterexample to JC(2). Conditional on JC(2), at least three invariant directions are required.

nodes.title: 1. A quadratic-tilt lemma in every odd characteristic
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-STRUCTURE, the named sub-result states:

**UAQTILT1.** Let K be any field of characteristic other than two, let h in K[S] have degree N>=3 and h'(0)!=0, and let B,C be independent indeterminates. Then
\[
 h(S)+BS^2-C
 \tag{1}
\]
has arithmetic and geometric Galois group S_N over K(B,C). Here geometric means after extending K to an algebraic closure; B and C remain variables. There is no restriction involving N, N-1, or the characteristic dividing N.

Cohen's 1980 Theorem 1 proves this immediately. In odd characteristic p, the functions 1,S^2,h(S) are linearly independent over K(S^p): the nonzero S coefficient of h gives a nonzero residue-one component, distinct from residues zero and two. His 1981 correction explicitly preserves Theorem 1. We give a direct proof to expose exactly where odd characteristic matters.

Extend K to an algebraic closure. The polynomial (1) is irreducible and separable: it is linear in the independent C, and its S derivative has nonzero constant term h'(0).

For double transitivity, divide the two-root equation by the diagonal:
\[
 A(X,Y)+B(X+Y)=0,\qquad
 A(X,Y)=\frac{h(X)-h(Y)}{X-Y}.                         \tag{2}
\]
The irreducible polynomial X+Y does not divide A, because
\[
 A(X,-X)=\frac{h(X)-h(-X)}{2X}
\]
has nonzero constant term h'(0). Thus (2), viewed as a polynomial linear in B, is primitive and irreducible in K[X,Y,B]. It stays irreducible over K(B). Localizing away from X=Y gives the integral incidence of two distinct roots of the generic fibre; its projection to C is dominant. Equivalently the point stabilizer is transitive on the other roots. The monodromy is doubly transitive.

There is also a transposition. A critical point r is nonzero and satisfies
\[
 B(r)=-\frac{h'(r)}{2r},\qquad
 C(r)=h(r)-\frac{rh'(r)}2.                           \tag{3}
\]
The rational function B(r) has a simple pole at zero, so B'(r) is not identically zero in any odd characteristic. The extension K(r)/K(B(r)) is finite separable. Differentiation with respect to B preserves its intermediate field K(B(r),C(r)); the identity
\[
 \frac{dC}{dB}=r^2                                  \tag{4}
\]
therefore places r^2 in that field. But B(r) is not in K(r^2), since every pole at zero of a function of r^2 has even order. As K(r)/K(r^2) is quadratic, this proves
\[
 K(B(r),C(r))=K(r).                                 \tag{5}
\]
The critical-value curve is birationally parametrized by r.

nodes.title: 2. One atomicity theorem for every coefficient section
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-STRUCTURE, the named sub-result states:

Use the normalized compiler
\[
 t=1+xy,\qquad q=t^2z+y^2(1+3t),\qquad \Pi=tq,
\]
\[
 B_0=y+3xq+\sum_{j=4}^N j a_jt^2x^{j-2}q^j,\qquad
 C_0=x(5-3t)-x^3z-\sum_{j=4}^N(j-2)a_j(xq)^j,
\]
with output (\Pi,-B_0/2,C_0). Substitute a_j=f_j(Pi), where the profiles lie in k(P). UAPROFILE1 already proves the rational Jacobian identity and the exact criterion for polynomial extension on the original affine source.

**UAALLATOM1.** For every field k of characteristic other than two, every such rational profile map with nonzero top profile f_N has generic degree N and arithmetic and geometric monodromy S_N. When the map extends polynomially, it is absolutely and stably atomic under polynomial composition. This includes the exceptional negative profiles in odd characteristic. The seed-free map has the same assertions with degree three.

Indeed over K=k(pi) the complete generic fibre has equation
\[
 E(S)=h(S)+bS^2-c/2,\qquad
 h(S)=S+\pi S^3+\sum_{j=4}^N f_j(\pi)\pi^jS^j.        \tag{6}
\]
Here h'(0)=1 and deg h=N. The source reconstruction in URKC1 identifies the full function-field extension with this polynomial. UAQTILT1 applies, including when p divides N. Applying it after algebraically closing k(pi) gives an S_N subgroup of geometric monodromy after algebraically closing k; therefore that geometric group and the arithmetic group are S_N.

For clarity, the atomicity step is characteristic-free. A polynomial factorization of a Keller map has Keller factors by the chain rule and the fact that polynomial-ring units are constants. A primitive generic permutation action admits no proper intermediate field, so one factor has generic degree one. An etale birational self-map of affine space is an open immersion by Zariski's Main Theorem. Its complement has no divisor, since such a divisor would restrict to a nonconstant unit on the source; normal Hartogs extension and affineness then make the immersion an isomorphism. Thus the degree-one factor is an automorphism. Constant-field extensions preserve the geometric action, and identity stabilizations adjoin purely transcendental variables without changing it.

nodes.title: 3. All exceptional pi-zero fibres
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-STRUCTURE, the named sub-result states:

Let k have odd characteristic p. The polynomial-landing classification says exactly
\[
 f_j(P)=g_j(P)+u_jP^{-1}+v_jP^{-2},\qquad g_j\in k[P],
 \tag{7}
\]
with u_j=v_j=0 unless j=2 mod p. Coefficients with j outside 4,...,N are absent. Define the separable polynomial
\[
 \phi(Y)=Y-\sum_{j=2\bmod p}v_j(-Y)^{j-2},
 \qquad \phi'(Y)=1,\qquad d=\deg\phi.                 \tag{8}
\]
Thus d=1 if every v_j vanishes; otherwise d is a positive multiple of p, at most N-2.

**UAMODBOUND1.** The complete fibre over (pi,b,c)=(0,b,c) is canonically, with the displayed coordinates,
\[
 \boxed{
 \operatorname{Spec}\bigl(k[S]/(S+bS^2-c/2)\bigr)[1/(1+2bS)]
 \ \sqcup\
 \operatorname{Spec}\bigl(k[Y,Y^{-1}]/(\phi(Y)-b)\bigr).
 }                                                       \tag{9}
\]
This is a scheme-theoretic whole-fibre formula, including all residue-field extensions, not a point count. Its geometric rank is
\[
 \boxed{
 \begin{cases}
 d,& b=0\ \text{or}\ 1+2bc=0,\\
 d+2,& b\ne0\ \text{and}\ 1+2bc\ne0.
 \end{cases}}
 \tag{10}
\]
It extends UABOUND1, whose regular-profile case has d=1.

To prove it, use the existing comaximality of t and q. On q=0, t is a unit and all negative-profile terms in B_0 vanish: their q exponents are j-1 or j-2, both positive. The original quadratic reconstruction applies:
\[
 D=1+2bS,\qquad y=-2b,\quad x=S/D,\quad
 z=-y^2(D^2+3D).
 \tag{11}
\]
This gives precisely the first component in (9), with ranks one if b=0, zero if b!=0 and 1+2bc=0, and two otherwise.

On t=0 one has y invertible, x=-1/y and q=y^2. The regular and simple-pole terms in B_0 vanish except for y+3xq=-2y. The double-pole terms give
\[
 -B_0/2=y-\sum v_j(-y)^{j-2}=\phi(y).
\]
The C_0 equation uniquely determines z:
\[
 z=y^3\left(c+\frac5y+
            \sum_{j=4}^N(j-2)g_j(0)(-y)^j\right).      \tag{12}
\]
Negative-profile C terms vanish because j-2=0 in k. This proves the second component and its inverse reconstruction. It has rank d for b!=0. For b=0, Y=0 is one simple root of phi, deleted by the localization, so the rank is d-1. Adding the quadratic component proves (10).

nodes.title: 4. Canonical constructions must be nonlinear in the moving variables
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-STRUCTURE, the named sub-result states:

This statement is independent of the quadratic-gauge compiler.

**UANORMAL1.** Let G be a finite group, let k be a field in which |G| is invertible, and let F:V->W be a G-equivariant polynomial Keller map between linear representations. Write
\[
 V=U\oplus T,\quad T=V^G,\quad U^G=0.
\]
Using the equivariant isomorphism DF(0) identifies W with V and the corresponding fixed and moving summands. In these coordinates write F=(F_U,F_T), and put f(t)=F_T(0,t). Then
\[
 A(t)=D_UF_U(0,t)
\]
is a polynomial G-equivariant matrix with nonzero constant determinant. It has a polynomial inverse. After a G-equivariant polynomial automorphism of the source one has the global normal form
\[
 \boxed{F(u,t)=\bigl(u+R(u,t),\ f(t)+Q(u,t)\bigr),\qquad
               R,Q\in (u)^2,\quad \det Df\in k^\times.} \tag{16}
\]
Here ideal membership means every monomial has moving-variable degree at least two; coefficient degrees in t are unrestricted.

The source normalization leaves the fixed target marked; it requires no inverse for the fixed-space Keller map f.

The fixed/moving splitting exists by averaging; characteristic zero is sufficient but not necessary. Equivariance gives F_U(0,t)=0, and there is no invariant linear map U->T, so the moving-linear part of F_T is zero. At u=0 the full derivative has diagonal blocks A(t),Df(t). Its constant determinant yields
\[
 \det A(t)\det Df(t)=\det DF\in k^\times.
\]
Both factors are polynomials, hence both are nonzero constants. Thus A(t)^{-1} is polynomial and G-equivariant. Precompose by
\[
 (u,t)\longmapsto(A(t)^{-1}u,t)
\]
to get (16).

In particular, suppose the moving component of the original F is affine linear in u, with arbitrary polynomial dependence on t. It must be exactly A(t)u. Since A(t) is everywhere invertible, the entire inverse image of W^G is V^G, scheme-theoretically. Every complete fibre over a G-fixed target therefore has trivial G action.

nodes.title: 5. What closes, and what remains
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of JAC-STRUCTURE, the named sub-result states:

UAQTILT1 and UAALLATOM1 replace many family-specific monodromy arguments by one quadratic-tilt rule, extending arbitrary rational profiles and their polynomial maps to every characteristic other than two. UAMODBOUND1 completes the exceptional boundary geometry. UANORMAL1 rules out all marked constructions affine linear in their moving variables, even after arbitrarily many trivial stabilizations.

These results do not improve the characteristic-zero target-dimension bounds, produce a receiver forgetting the generator line, solve JC(2), or prove stable equivalence of different compiler slices. The unresolved condition for canonical construction is a nonlinear equivariant polynomial realization which satisfies all subgroup-fixed restrictions and the normal form (16). For compression, another affine completion or another compiler is still required.

The [replay](verify.py) checks representative exact identities and whole quotient-algebra reconstructions, with [source pins](sources.json). The general monodromy, all-prime and normal-form results are written proofs. Formal verification, independent whole-proof replay, external review and a literature-priority claim remain absent.

nodes.title: 3. Why the standard exceptional families are not exceptions
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of FOUND-UM1, the named sub-result states:

The distinction to keep in view is

\[
 \text{monodromy of one slice }H(W)-s_0W+t
 \quad\hbox{versus}\quad
 \text{monodromy over }k(s,t).                     \tag{5}
\]

Specialization can lower monodromy.  The lemma says that only finitely many
tilts can fail the Morse criterion, while any one Morse tilt already detects
the full group of the two-parameter family.

| Polynomial phenomenon | Exceptional slice | What the moving parameter does |
|---|---|---|
| Monomial | For `H=W^n`, the slice `s=0` has cyclic geometric monodromy (smaller than `S_n` when `n>=3`). | If `sigma!=0`, the critical points satisfy `r^(n-1)=sigma/n`, and their critical values are `-(n-1)sigma*r/n`; they are simple and distinct. Thus every nonzero tilt is Morse. |
| Chebyshev | For `H=T_n`, the slice `s=0` has dihedral monodromy. Its critical values lie in `{+1,-1}` and collide when `n>=4`; the dihedral group is smaller than `S_n` when `n>=4`. | All but finitely many `sigma` make `T_n-sigma W` Morse, so those vertical slices and the full pencil have monodromy `S_n`. |
| Decomposable `H=A(B(W))` | The slice `s=0` is imprimitive. | All but finitely many linear tilts have monodromy `S_n`, hence are primitive and indecomposable. The decomposition of `H` is not a decomposition of the pencil over `k(s)`. |
| Large affine symmetry | A centered power, or another symmetric special slice, can have visible source automorphisms. | Pencil-compatible symmetries generally move `(s,t)` and are not target-fixed deck transformations. Full monodromy is unchanged. |
| Repeated or multiple critical values | At an exceptional `s_0`, (1) may have a cusp or several normalization points over one discriminant point. | These give only finitely many bad `s`-values. Away from them, all ramification in the vertical slice is simple with distinct branch values. |

nodes.title: 4. Deck transformations and affine symmetries
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of FOUND-UM1, the named sub-result states:

For a connected degree-`n` cover, target-fixed deck transformations form the
centralizer of the monodromy action on a geometric fiber.  In the natural
action of `S_n`, this centralizer is trivial for `n>=3`.  Therefore the
generic incidence cover has no nonidentity target-fixed deck transformation.

This does not say that the *family* has no automorphisms covering a change of
base coordinates.  For example, affine symmetries of a centered monomial may
act simultaneously on `W,s,t`.  Those are pencil self-equivalences, not deck
transformations over the fixed `(s,t)`-plane, and they do not contradict
UM1.

nodes.title: 3. A degree-one Keller map is an automorphism
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of FOUND-ATOMICITY, the named sub-result states:

We record the standard birational Keller lemma.

> **Lemma.** If a Keller self-map of `\mathbb A_k^d` has geometric degree
> one, it is a polynomial automorphism.

It is enough to prove this after passing to an algebraic closure, because
being an isomorphism descends under a faithfully flat field extension.  The
map is etale and birational.  An etale morphism is quasi-finite, so the
birational form of Zariski's Main Theorem, with normal target
`\mathbb A^d`, identifies it with an open immersion

\[
 \mathbb A^d\simeq U\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^d.          \tag{6}
\]

This open immersion cannot be proper.  If the complement contained a
divisor, factoriality of affine space would give an irreducible polynomial
vanishing exactly on that divisor.  Its restriction would be a nonconstant
unit on `U\simeq\mathbb A^d`, whereas affine space has only constant units.
Thus the complement has codimension at least two.  Normal Hartogs extension
then gives

\[
 \Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)=\Gamma(\mathbb A^d,\mathcal O)=
 k[x_1,\ldots,x_d].
\]

nodes.title: 1. Geometry behind the singular-Hessian theorem
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of HESS-TANG, the named sub-result states:

Tang Theorem 2.1 concerns a rational V in three variables with nilpotent
N=DV, symmetrized by a generically nonsingular **polynomial Hessian** H.
Its conclusion is that the image of V lies in an affine plane. Nonsingularity
means that det H is not identically zero, not that it is a unit. Polynomiality
is essential, as the rational counterexamples in HCTANG1 demonstrate.

At rank one, write V=A(t), t=p/q reduced, using the characteristic-zero
rank criterion and Luroth. Restriction to a suitable affine line shows
that the image curve is unirational, which supplies this application of
Luroth. If its image is nonplanar, the components of A' are independent.
Nilpotence gives A'(t).grad t=0. Clearing denominators, primitive
divisibility by p-Tq and comparison of source degrees give the stronger
identity A'(T).grad(p-Tq)=0 over C(T). The coefficient matrix of this last
gradient has rank at most two and entries affine in T.

At rank two its cross-product kernel has degree at most two. Independence
of A' makes its three coefficient vectors independent, so a constant
conjugation puts that kernel at (1,T,T^2). The resulting identities are
p_x=0, p_y=q_x, p_z=q_y, q_z=0. Integrating and comparing coefficients
forces p,q affine and makes the same coefficient matrix rank one, a
contradiction. At rank one, p-Tq depends on one linear form over C(T).
If its source degree is at least two, taking two T derivatives of its
top power forces that linear form to have constant coefficient ratios.
This would give a constant relation on A'. The remaining possibility is
that p,q are affine with independent linear parts.

Use p=x,q=y. Set F(t,y,z)=f(ty,y,z) and k=A'_3/A'_2. Self-adjointness
gives F_y+k F_z depending only on t. The coefficient of y^j z^ell in F
has t-degree at most j. Its highest z coefficient is therefore constant.
If the z degree is at least two, the next coefficient forces k to be
affine in t, giving a constant relation on A'. At z degree at most one,
the same degree constraint makes f affine. Both alternatives contradict
the hypotheses. This is an all-degree argument, not a bounded search.

nodes.title: 2. Common rules for changing weights
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of HESS-TANG, the named sub-result states:

Let E be the leading weight and W=4E-2 sum(w_i). The determinant-weight
identity gives W>=0. If W>0 the leading Hessian is singular; if W=0 its
determinant is the same nonzero constant as the full determinant.
Finite support supplies a strict gap until the first new wall.

At W=0 with positive weights, write A=Hess P(0). Both A and A^-1 pair
only complementary weight blocks. Consequently A^-1 grad f has ith
component of weight at most w_i and linear part x_i within its own
weight block. A nonlinear monomial of that weight uses only lower-weight
variables. Successive substitution supplies an actual polynomial inverse.
This also justifies stopping at W=0 when another term ties there.

The primary [de Bondt Corollary 7.3 and Theorem 7.2](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.03904v2)
give the singular forms used here. At rank three, one apex gives a
rank-one complementary Hessian over the active-variable field; two give
joint affineness in the complementary pair; three give a constant kernel
line. At rank two, the alternatives are a constant two-dimensional
kernel or one apex with a complementary affine triple. At rank one
there is a three-dimensional constant kernel. Homogeneous tops of rank
at most three depend on exactly that many variables after a constant
change. The extra algebraic-dependence conditions in de Bondt's formulas
are respected; the common binary coefficient pair is not assumed free.

Apex spaces and constant kernels split across equal-weight blocks by
equivariance. Old homogeneous minors survive as leading parts at a wall.
If a passive vector has a unique coordinate of greatest old weight and
the corresponding principal cofactor is nonzero, its adjugate contraction
cannot vanish. An apex must have zero such contraction. This remains
usable when the new weights coincide.

For an apex plane that is a graph from base to fibres, the transpose
source shear aligns it with the target base plane. It preserves new
weights. In every continuing use, the replacement variable has strictly
smaller old weight, so it also preserves the old leading form. This
direction of the shear is essential.

nodes.title: 3. Lemmas 3.2–3.8: coverage and termination
nodes.scope:
In the exact setting/notation of HESS-TANG, the named sub-result states:

**3.2, genuinely binary common coefficient.** The curvature polynomial
U=S_y^2 S_xx-2 S_x S_y S_xy+S_x^2 S_yy is nonzero. Indeed U=0 would
make generic irreducible polynomial level components lines, and comparison
of lines in different levels makes them parallel, contrary to genuine
binary dependence. For H=z A+w B the two fibre cofactors and every
mixed base/fibre minor are nonzero, by the displayed cofactor formulas.
Raise both fibres with slope one. E has slope one and W is constant.
At a wall, the cofactors exclude an apex in the fibre plane. A single
apex would have an annihilating old-homogeneous base direction and the
other fibre axis; their nonzero surviving minor contradicts complementary
rank at most one. Three apices also intersect that fibre plane. Thus
the apex plane is a graph over the base. The graph shear restores H
exactly: a new tied fibre-degree-j term had old weight E+(1-j)tau,
so no fibre-free term is present and the fibre-linear part is unchanged.
Each genuine continuing wall is a base/fibre weight equality. There
are at most four. Beyond them no fibre-degree-at-least-two term can
remain, since it would eventually overtake H. The full f is cotangent.

**3.3, three distinct phase entries.** For F(x,L), L=ell(x).Y, the
cofactor deleting a passive variable is
-F_LL F_L^2(ell'_i ell_j-ell'_j ell_i)^2. All three are nonzero for
phase entries proportional to 1,x^r,x^s with distinct integral exponents.
Raising all passive weights gives W slope 4m-6>0. At every wall the
apex is the active axis. The old passive-degree-m coefficients recover
exactly the same phase. A genuine continuation strictly increases m.
Ordinary polynomial degree bounds these increases.

At the final maximal passive degree D, its whole homogeneous passive
part N_D still has the three cofactors. Weights (0,1,1,1) and the old
contraction test force its only apex to be active. Thus
N_D=a(x)(ell(x).Y)^D. Its three rational phase coefficients are independent
over C, or a constant kernel would make a rank-three image a hyperplane
with three apices. Their Wronskian is nonzero. At a regular x0 choose
passive coordinates from ell,ell',ell''/2 and write x=x0+xi. Every
monomial xi^k u^i v^j t^h of N_D has k>=j+2h, with equality part
a(x0)(u+xi v+xi^2 t)^D.
